performance.name: Performance
performance.desc: Playing, singing, keeping a steady beat and performing for others: MIDI MUSIC, Tap Tempo challenges, Rhythm Rock Stars, Looper.

composition.name: Composition
composition.desc: Making up and writing down original music: Staff Composer, Beat Machine, Type Beat, Sound Blocks.

form.name: Arranging & Form
form.desc: Organizing music into sections (AB, ABA, rondo, verse/chorus), layering parts and arranging: Studio DAW, Sound Blocks, Looper.

literacy.name: Music Literacy
literacy.desc: Reading and writing notation: note names, rhythms, solfège and the staff: Staff Wars, Rhythm Rock Stars, Do-Re-Mi Trainer.

knowledge.name: Instruments & Symbols
knowledge.desc: Knowing the instruments, their families and sounds, and the symbols and terms of music: Instrument Zoo, Symbol Match, Tuner, Metronome.

listening.name: Listening & Responding
listening.desc: Describing, comparing and judging music with music words: Dynamic Ears, Instrument Zoo, Chrome Music Lab EXTRA.

anchors.name: Generate and conceptualize artistic ideas and work
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: Musicians' creative ideas, concepts and feelings come from many sources.
anchors.essentialQuestion: How do musicians come up with creative ideas?

anchors.name: Organize and develop artistic ideas and work
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: Musicians' creative choices are shaped by their expertise, context and expressive intent.
anchors.essentialQuestion: How do musicians make creative decisions?

anchors.name: Refine and complete artistic work
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: 3.1: Musicians improve their work through openness to new ideas, persistence and clear criteria. 3.2: Sharing creative work completes a process of creating and communicating.
anchors.essentialQuestion: 3.1: How do musicians improve the quality of their creative work? 3.2 (NCAS): When is creative work ready to share?

anchors.name: Select, analyze and interpret artistic work for presentation
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: 4.1: Interest, knowledge, technical skill and context shape repertoire choice. 4.2: Analyzing creators' context and use of elements informs performance. 4.3: Performers make interpretive decisions based on context and expressive intent.
anchors.essentialQuestion: 4.1: How do performers select repertoire? 4.2: How does understanding structure and context inform performance? 4.3: How do performers interpret musical works?

anchors.name: Develop and refine artistic techniques and work for presentation
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: Musicians analyze, evaluate and refine their performance over time through openness, persistence and appropriate criteria.
anchors.essentialQuestion: How do musicians improve the quality of their performance?

anchors.name: Convey meaning through the presentation of artistic work
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: Performance quality is judged by criteria that vary across time, place and culture; context and presentation shape audience response.
anchors.essentialQuestion: When is a performance ready to present? How do context and manner of presentation affect audience response?

anchors.name: Perceive and analyze artistic work
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: 7.1: People choose music based on interests, experiences, understandings and purposes. 7.2: Responses to music are informed by context and how creators/performers use the elements.
anchors.essentialQuestion: 7.1: How do individuals choose music to experience? 7.2: How does understanding the structure and context of music inform a response?

anchors.name: Interpret intent and meaning in artistic work
anchors.nyName: Interpret meaning in artistic work (NY EU/EQ table and poster wording)
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: Creators and performers give clues to their expressive intent through the elements and structures of music.
anchors.essentialQuestion: How do we discern the creators' and performers' expressive intent?

anchors.name: Apply criteria to evaluate artistic work
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: Personal evaluation of music and performances is informed by analysis, interpretation and established criteria.
anchors.essentialQuestion: How do we judge the quality of musical works and performances?

anchors.component: Connect (NCAS names no separate component; NY: Relate)
anchors.name: Synthesize and relate knowledge and personal experiences to make art
anchors.nyName: Relate and synthesize knowledge and personal experiences to inspire and inform artistic work
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: NCAS: Musicians connect personal interests, experiences, ideas and knowledge to creating, performing and responding.
anchors.essentialQuestion: NCAS: How do musicians make meaningful connections to creating, performing and responding?

anchors.component: Connect (NCAS names no separate component; NY: Interrelate)
anchors.name: Relate artistic ideas and works with societal, cultural and historical context to deepen understanding
anchors.nyName: Investigate ways that artistic work is influenced by societal, cultural and historical context and, in turn, how artistic ideas shape cultures past, present and future
anchors.enduringUnderstanding: NCAS: Understanding connections to varied contexts and daily life enriches creating, performing and responding.
anchors.essentialQuestion: NCAS: How do the other arts, other subjects, contexts and daily life inform creating, performing and responding to music?

nyNotes: **National + New York.** Both frameworks share the same 11 anchor standards and code format (MU:Cr1.1.3a = Music, Creating anchor 1, grade 3, indicator a). New York (adopted 2017; full implementation by 2021-22) calls them Performance Indicators and changes a few things: **Connecting** uses grade-specific MU:Cn10.1 (Relate: soundscapes, reasons for music, folk dance, manipulating concepts) and MU:Cn11.1 (Interrelate: folk music of many cultures, documenting music) instead of the national Cn10.0/Cn11.0; NY adds **Pr5.1c / Pr6.1c** (respond to aural and visual cues such as a conductor’s); and NY drops Cr3.1b in grades 3-5. Rows marked **NY** or **NCAS** exist in only that framework. Wording here is a short teacher-friendly paraphrase: check the official documents (Sources, below) for the exact text.

tools.name: Staff Composer
tools.summary: A full notation editor: write notes on the staff, hear them, add instruments, print real sheet music and share a link.
features: Click notes onto the staff, or play them on the on-screen piano or a MIDI keyboard.
Three levels: **Easy** (colored, labeled notes), **Standard**, and **Advanced** (16ths, accidentals, dots, ties, dynamics, articulations, glissando).
Helpers menu: note letters, fixed or movable-do solfège, scale degrees, counting (1 e & a or Kodály ta/ti-ti), Boomwhacker colors, beat ruler, count-in.
Time signatures 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, 5/4, 6/4, 6/8, 7/8; all 15 major keys; tempo 40-208; dynamics pp-ff; repeats and 1st/2nd endings; lyrics.
About 90 instrument sounds; a mixer; 19 ensemble templates (string quartet, concert band, Orff percussion, rock band, choir SATB and more); 26 drum grooves.
Templates with classroom challenges (fill in the missing notes of Ode to Joy and Twinkle).
Transpose by octave/half step or for B♭ instruments.
Print / PDF, MIDI and MusicXML export, WAV download, public share link, and saving to the class account.
**Big Staff** ([/?app=big-staff](/?app=big-staff)) for K-1: one huge measure, Ta / Ti-Ti / Shh buttons, turtle-walk-rabbit tempos.
tips: Start K-2 in Big Staff, grade 3 in Easy mode, grades 4-6 in Standard; open Advanced only when you teach 16ths or accidentals.
Turn on Helpers → Note Letters while students learn, then turn it off for the assessment.
Teachers signed in to the class account can “Assign Song to Class” to push a starter file to every student.
Print the class’s compositions and post them: real sheet music is a powerful motivator.
tools.data: Saves to a student’s class account when they sign in (first name + initial, class, PIN). Share links contain only the music.

tools.name: Beat Machine
tools.summary: A step sequencer for drums, melody and bass, plus the Beat Detective echo game and a button that turns any beat into notation.
features: Drum Beat, Rainbow Melody (pentatonic xylophone) and Bass grids; 8 or 16 steps per measure, 1-4 measures; tempo with tempo words.
8 sound packs (acoustic kit, TR-808, world percussion & congas, jazz brushes, mallets, beatbox & voice lab and more).
Ready Grooves, Magic Beat/Tune/Bass generators, Live Pads and the Sound Explorer.
**Beat Detective**: Barnaby the Beat Bear plays a pattern, students tap it back (5 levels from Stomp & Clap to Master Beat Champ).
**Notate Song**: turns the beat into quarter/eighth/sixteenth notation with rests; print it or save as PNG.
Voice Lab: record your own sound with fun voice effects.
Share link, audio export and saving to the class account.
tips: Use 8 steps for K-3 (each step = an eighth note), 16 for grades 4-6.
Notate Song is the bridge from “making a beat” to “reading rhythm”: always end a beat lesson by looking at the notation.
Beat Detective is an excellent 5-minute warm-up on the projector.
tools.data: Class-account saving when signed in; share links hold only the beat. Voice Lab recordings stay in the browser.

tools.name: Studio DAW
tools.summary: A real browser recording studio: 2,000+ CC0 loops that follow the song tempo and key, instruments, a piano roll, drum grid, microphone recording, effects and a mixer.
features: Start screen templates: Make a Beat, Pop Song, Lo-Fi Hip-Hop, Funk Groove, Folk & Country, Jazz Club, Movie Soundtrack, Soundscape, Empty Song.
Loop library with filters for instrument, genre, mood, key and BPM; loops follow the song tempo and key.
Track types: audio (mic recording with count-in and voice changer), instrument (about 50 sampled instruments), drum machine, and video (for scoring a film clip).
Piano roll with Chord tool, Arpeggiate, quantize, swing, humanize and strum.
Effects (EQ, compressor, reverb, echo, chorus, phaser, distortion, filter, robot) with presets; mixer and automation; a tuner.
A 7-step guided tutorial; saves on the device and to the class account; exports WAV/MP3; share link that opens as a credited remix.
tips: Have every student complete the built-in 7-step tutorial in the first session.
Teach form first (intro/verse/chorus/outro) and let the loops do the harmony; add the piano roll later.
Plug Chromebooks in during DAW work, and use wired headphones for recording.
tools.data: Projects save on the device and to the class account; microphone recordings stay on the device.

tools.name: Sound Blocks
tools.summary: A picture-only song maker: pick a world, drag loop blocks onto colored tracks, add effects and your own voice, press play, share a link.
features: 12 worlds with their own tempo and key: Playground, Parade, Sunny Day, Jungle, Dreamy Sky, Spooky, Hero, Chill, Fiesta, Funk, Hip-Hop, Country.
14-16 loop blocks per world plus a fun-sound row (bells, horns, boings).
6 measures to start, up to 12 with the + button; 4 to 8 tracks; a volume slider per track.
Effects: echo, reverb, muffle, crunch. A microphone block records one measure of your voice after a 3-2-1 countdown.
Click a measure’s top bar to start playback there; undo; autosave; short share link with a QR code.
Almost no words on screen: ideal for pre-readers and English learners.
tips: Each world’s loops are in the same key and tempo, so every combination “works”: students can focus on form and texture.
Have students put the same column of blocks in two places to *see* a repeated section (the A in ABA).
The QR code on the share screen lets you scan student songs with a teacher iPad.
tools.data: Songs autosave on the device. Voice recordings never leave the device and are left out of share links.

tools.name: MIDI MUSIC
tools.summary: A keyboard studio for USB MIDI keyboards (or computer keys): 130+ instruments, a song guide, 36 scored challenges and a two-player Duet mode.
features: Plays a USB MIDI keyboard with very low delay; also the computer keys and on-screen keys.
Song guide with public-domain songs (Hot Cross Buns, Ode to Joy, When the Saints, The Entertainer and more) that lights up the next key.

Challenges with stars: Keyboard Basics (find C D E, all white keys, sharps & flats), Scales (C, G, F, A minor, black-key), Ear Training (echo me), Chords (C F G, major/minor, pop chords, 12-bar blues), Make It Up (black-key jam, blues solo), Partners.
Duet mode for two keyboards; Partner challenges (harmony parts, question & answer, ostinato + solo).
Sampler and recording; recordings can be downloaded.
Teacher links: `/midimusic/?challenge=<id>` and `/midimusic/?song=<id>` open straight to a challenge or song.
tips: Plug the keyboard in before opening the page. iPads have no Web MIDI: use the on-screen keys.
Project a challenge first and solve it together, then release students to earn stars.
Stars are saved per device: ask students to show you their star screen as a quick check.
tools.data: Stars and settings stay on the device; nothing is uploaded.

tools.name: Chrome Music Lab EXTRA
tools.summary: Five playful experiments in one page: Song Maker, Kandinsky, Shared Piano, Rhythm and Sketch Studio.
features: **Song Maker**: paint melody and drums on a grid; 1-16 bars, 2-7 beats per bar; major, minor, pentatonic, blues, dorian and chromatic scales; magic tools (arpeggio, invert, reverse, transpose); share link, WAV/MIDI export.
**Kandinsky**: draw lines, circles and triangles that become melody, singing faces and percussion.
**Shared Piano**: a big piano with letter or solfège labels, sustain, transposing, and “Play Together” rooms across devices.
**Rhythm**: animated players on a 3-track sequencer in 3/4, 4/4, 5/4 and 6/4.
**Sketch Studio**: draw music with chalk, crayon, neon or watercolor; line thickness = volume; step or glide; backing beats.
tips: Rhythm is a perfect visual for meter: compare 3/4 and 4/4 side by side.
Song Maker in Pentatonic scale makes every K-3 melody sound good; switch to Major or Minor for grades 4-6 mood lessons.
Play Together rooms need the live site (they don’t work on test copies).
tools.data: Song Maker share links store the song only. Nothing else is saved.

tools.name: Looper
tools.summary: A 24-slot loop station: record a short loop with the microphone, then layer more loops on top, all locked in time.
features: The first loop sets the length; every other loop snaps to it (or 2× / 4×).
Record, overdub, undo, mute, clear; volume and left/right pan per loop.
Metronome with count-in and drum grooves to record over.
Effects per loop: Echo, Big Room, Underwater (filter), Crunchy.
A one-time sound check to line up recordings; save sessions on the device; export a WAV (the export leaves out effects).
tips: Run Sound check once per device through the speakers (it can’t hear headphones), then record with headphones on.
Model “say it, then loop it”: chant a rhythm first, then record it.
Assign loop roles (beat keeper, bass voice, melody, sound effect) so groups build a texture together.
tools.data: Recordings and sessions stay on the device; WAV export downloads a file only if the student chooses.

tools.name: Type Beat
tools.summary: Type letters and hear a drum loop: every letter is a drum sound, a space is a rest, (parentheses) make triplets, CAPITALS are loud.
features: Each letter = one sixteenth note; space or period = rest.
Letters in ( ) play as triplets; CAPITAL letters are accented (louder).
Tempo 50-180, volume, four drum kits (acoustic, 808, jazz, Latin).
The beat is shown as colored blocks that light up as they play; the share link carries the beat.
tips: Names and words make instant rhythm patterns: syllables become drum hits.
Use capitals to teach accents and the strong beat.
Because 4 letters = 1 beat, “boom” or “k.s.” style words line up neatly with 4/4.
tools.data: Nothing is saved on a server; the beat lives in the share link.

tools.name: Staff Wars
tools.summary: A space game for note-name fluency: notes fly toward the clef and students name them to blast them.
features: Treble, bass, alto clef and grand staff.
Levels: Cadet (lines & spaces), Pilot (middle C + 1 ledger line), Jedi Master (full range), Custom Range.
Answer with buttons/keys (letters or solfège) or with the **Live Microphone** by playing the note on a real instrument.
Transposition for B♭, E♭ and F instruments so band students read their own written pitch.
Leaderboards (main, bass, alto, grand) for signed-in students.
tips: Short daily rounds (3-5 minutes) build fluency faster than one long session.
Have band students use Live Microphone with their instrument and their transposition.
tools.data: Scores go to the class leaderboard only when a student is signed in.

tools.name: Rhythm Rock Stars
tools.summary: A rhythm game with four modes (listen, tap, build, quiz) and seven levels from quarter notes to syncopation and triplets.
features: Modes: **Beat Decoder** (hear it, pick the notation), **Rhythm Tapper** (tap in time; Perfect/Great/Missed), **Beat Builder** (build a measure to match a groove), **Rhythm Quiz** (note values, beat sums, syllables).
Levels: 1 quarter, half, quarter rest · 2 eighths and eighth rests · 3 sixteenths · 4 ti-tika, tika-ti, dotted eighth-sixteenth · 5 triplets and syncopa · 6 mixed · 7 secret.
Counting in numbers (1 e & a) or Kodály syllables; count-in; tempo 70/96/130; eight instrument sounds.
Badges, Fame Score and a class leaderboard.
tips: Choose Kodály syllables for K-3 and numbers for 4-6 (or both, to bridge).
Use the Slow Practice tempo (70) for the first try of any new level.
tools.data: Leaderboard entries use a display name: teach students to use a first name or nickname only.

tools.name: Do-Re-Mi Trainer
tools.summary: Eight colored bells from do to high do with Curwen hand-sign descriptions, pattern songs and an ear-training challenge.
features: Bells do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti-do (C major), played by tapping or keys 1-8; six instrument sounds.
Hand-sign name for each syllable.
“Play Songs” patterns: sol-mi, mi-re-do / Hot Cross Buns, the scale.
Ear Training Challenge levels: Do-Re-Mi, Triad, All 8, with points and streaks.
Print a Do-Re-Mi chart (syllables, notes, hand signs).
tips: Always pair the bells with singing and hand signs: the tool is the reference pitch, students are the instrument.
Project it and let a student be the “bell captain” for echo games.

tools.name: Symbol Match
tools.summary: Memory and speed games with 27 music symbols: notes, rests, dynamics, clefs, accidentals and articulations.
features: Modes: Memory Match, Speed (45 seconds, score and streak) and a Study Guide.
Categories: Notes & Rests, Dynamics (pp-ff), Clefs & Accidentals, Articulations.
Symbols include whole to sixteenth notes and rests, dotted half, pp-ff, crescendo/decrescendo, treble/bass clef, sharp/flat/natural, fermata, repeat sign, staccato, accent.
tips: Filter to one category per lesson for K-3.
The Study Guide on the projector makes a quick word-wall review.

tools.name: Instrument Zoo
tools.summary: 17 instrument cards with real recorded sounds, family, clef, range and a “Did you know?” fact.
features: Strings: violin, cello, acoustic guitar, harp. Woodwinds: flute, recorder, clarinet, oboe. Brass: trumpet, trombone, French horn, tuba.
Percussion: xylophone, marimba, timpani. World & popular: ukulele, Andean pan flute.
Family filter; each card plays a note and a full arpeggio and lists clef and range.
tips: There is no built-in quiz: hide the screen, play a card, and let the class guess (the lesson plans do this).
Pair with live instrument demos by older students or band teachers.

tools.name: Dynamic Ears
tools.summary: A live microphone loudness meter that shows dynamics from pianissimo to fortissimo, plus the Classroom Quiet Challenge.
features: Six dynamics, pp to ff, with pronunciation and meaning.
Live mic meter (or buttons if there is no mic).
Classroom Quiet Challenge: keep the room at piano for 60 seconds and keep your 5 stars.
Print a dynamics chart.
tips: Students sing or play into the mic and try to hit a target dynamic.
The Quiet Challenge doubles as a classroom-management tool.
tools.data: The microphone is only measured live; nothing is recorded or saved.

tools.name: Metronome
tools.summary: A classroom metronome with animal tempo presets, Italian tempo terms, accents, subdivisions and a flash option.
features: 30-250 BPM; animal presets from Sleepy Turtle (Largo) to Supersonic Rocket (Prestissimo).
1-8 beats per measure with an accented downbeat; subdivisions quarter, eighth, triplet, sixteenth.
Click sounds (woodblock, beep, drumstick, cowbell, silent) and a screen flash for visual beat.
Print a tempo chart.
tips: The animal presets make tempo words memorable for K-3.
Use silent + flash for students with hearing differences or for “internal beat” games.

tools.name: Tap Tempo & Tempo Challenge
tools.summary: Tap along to find the BPM of any music, then take the Tempo Challenge: keep a steady beat alone for 32 taps.
features: Tap the button or Space bar to see BPM, the matching animal and Italian tempo term.
Tempo Challenge (tab): target 60, 80, 100 or 120 BPM, Starter (±5) or Pro (±2) zone, 4-click count-in, then 32 taps alone with “Rushing” / “Dragging” feedback; best score saved per tempo.
Print a tempo chart.
tips: Project the Tempo Challenge and let one student tap while the class pats silently: everyone practices the internal beat.
Have students find the BPM of a song they love and compare it to the tempo chart.
tools.data: Best scores stay on the device.

tools.name: Instrument Tuner
tools.summary: A microphone tuner with presets for guitar, ukulele, violin, viola, cello and bass, plus a chromatic mode for any instrument or voice.
features: Presets: Chromatic, Guitar (standard, drop D), Ukulele, Violin, Viola, Cello, Bass.
Tolerance Kids ±8¢, Standard ±5¢, Pro ±2¢; A4 reference 415-466 Hz; sharps or flats; B♭/E♭/F transposition.
Needle, history and strobe views; a speaker button plays the reference pitch.
tips: Use the history view to *see* whether a sung note stays steady.
Band students choose their transposition so the tuner shows their written note.
tools.data: The microphone is only measured live; nothing is recorded.

lessons.title: Big Staff: My First 4-Beat Song
lessons.summary: Young students build one big 4-beat measure with Ta, Ti-Ti and Shh buttons, hear notes go high and low on the staff, and play their song at turtle, walking and rabbit speed.
objectives: build a 4-beat pattern using ta, ti-ti and shh (rest)
place notes high and low on the staff and hear the difference
read their own pattern aloud with rhythm syllables while keeping a steady beat
choose a tempo (turtle, walking, rabbit) to match an idea
iCan: I can make a song with 4 beats.
I can say ta, ti-ti and shh.
I can make notes go high and low.
I can play my song slow like a turtle or fast like a rabbit.

vocabulary.def: The steady heartbeat of the music.
One sound on one beat.
Two quick sounds on one beat.
A beat with no sound. We stay quiet.
The five lines where we write music.
How fast or slow the music goes.

materials: Projector with [Big Staff](/?app=big-staff)
Student devices (tablets or Chromebooks), one per student or pair; headphones if available
Four large beat cards (heart pictures) or four paper plates for the floor
Picture cards: turtle, walking person, rabbit
prep: Open [Big Staff](/?app=big-staff) on the projector and check the sound.
Practice the buttons once: Ta, Ti-Ti, Shh! (Rest), Play, and the Slow / Medium / Fast tempo buttons (turtle 72, walking 96, rabbit 126).
Put four heart cards on the board in a row for the 4 beats.
Decide partners if devices are shared (one clicks, one reads; switch halfway).

steps.do: Students pat a steady beat on their knees while you chant a short rhyme. Then point to the four heart cards and pat-say ta ta ta ta. Change one heart to two small hearts and say ta ta ti-ti ta. Change one to an empty heart: shh.
steps.say: Every song has a heartbeat. Let’s keep it together.
steps.check: Pats stay steady; students are silent on the shh beat.

steps.do: Show the turtle, walking and rabbit cards. Pat the same pattern slow, medium and fast. Students move hands like each animal.
steps.say: The rhythm stays the same, but the speed can change. That speed is called tempo.

steps.do: On the projector, click Ta, Ta, Ti-Ti, Shh! to fill the big measure. Click a note high on the staff, then one low, and press Play so students hear high and low. Press Slow, then Fast, and play again.
steps.say: Up high on the staff sounds high. Down low sounds low. Show me with your hands.
steps.check: Students raise hands for high notes and lower them for low notes.

steps.do: Students read the projected pattern with syllables while you point. Invite two volunteers to change one beat each on the projector. The class reads the new pattern.
steps.check: Students say ti-ti for two eighth notes and whisper shh on the rest.

steps.do: Students open Big Staff and make their own 4-beat song. **Task card:** 4 beats are full; use at least one ta, one ti-ti and one shh; at least one high note and one low note; choose turtle, walking or rabbit. They press Play and say their pattern with the computer.
steps.say: Make it, play it, say it.
steps.check: Circulate: ask each student to point and read their four beats.

steps.do: Three or four students read their pattern aloud while the class pats the beat, then the student plays it at the tempo they chose. Class guesses the animal.
steps.say: Was that a turtle, a walker or a rabbit? How do you know?

steps.do: Exit ticket: hold up the heart cards with one pattern; students show a thumb up if it has a shh beat.

support: Give a starter pattern (ta ta ta ta) and ask the student to change just one beat.
Partner a confident reader with a new student; one clicks, one says the syllables.
extend: Click Add Bar to make a second measure that is different from the first.
Try the Half (ta-a) button and explain why it fills two beats.
access: Students who cannot click easily can point and tell a partner which button to press.
For ELL students, use the heart and animal picture cards; syllables are the same in any language.
Headphones or a low volume help students with sound sensitivity.

formative: Students say ta, ti-ti and shh correctly during the projected reading.
Students show high and low with their hands when notes change.
Each student can point and read their four beats.
assessment.summative: Each student reads and plays their 4-beat song for the teacher or a partner; note on a class checklist: 4 beats full, uses ta/ti-ti/shh, shows high and low, chose a tempo.

levels: Makes more than one full measure using ta, ti-ti and shh, and explains each.
Fills 4 beats using ta, ti-ti and shh.
Fills 4 beats but uses only one kind of note.
Places notes but the measure is not full or the pattern is not finished.
Reads own and a classmate’s pattern with correct syllables and a steady beat.
Reads own pattern with correct syllables, silent on the rest.
Reads with some syllable errors or loses the beat.
Needs the teacher to read with them.
Uses high and low notes on purpose and explains the tempo choice (“rabbit because it is exciting”).
Uses at least one high and one low note and picks a tempo.
Uses only high or only low notes, or does not try a tempo.
Cannot yet show high vs. low.

lessons.exitTicket: Show ta ta ti-ti shh on the heart cards: thumbs up if there is a quiet beat, and say the pattern together.
tips: K students do best in pairs with one device: one clicks, one says the syllables.
If a student fills the measure by accident, show the Play button first; hearing it fixes most mistakes.
Keep the projector on Big Staff during the Create time so students can copy the model if stuck.

lessons.title: Sol-Mi-La Melody Makers
lessons.summary: Students compose a 4-measure melody in 4/4 using sol, mi, la (and do) in Staff Composer Easy mode, with movable-do and Kodály counting helpers on, end on do, and sing their song for the class.
objectives: compose a 4-measure melody in 4/4 using sol, mi, la and do
use ta, ti-ti and rests so each measure has 4 beats
end the melody on do so it sounds finished
sing their melody with solfège and hand signs
iCan: I can write a song with sol, mi and la on the staff.
I can make every measure have 4 beats.
I can end my song on do so it sounds finished.
I can sing my song with hand signs.

vocabulary.def: Singing names for notes. Sol is higher than mi; la is one step above sol; do is home.
A box of beats. In 4/4 each measure has 4 beats.
A tune: notes that go up, down or stay the same.
The note that makes a song sound finished.
The numbers that say 4 beats in every measure.

materials: Projector with [Staff Composer](/?app=staff-composer)
Student devices with headphones
[Do-Re-Mi chart](/?app=solfege-trainer&focus=1) (print it from the Do-Re-Mi Trainer) for the board
Optional: class account sign-in cards so students can save
prep: Open Staff Composer, choose **Easy** mode, 4/4, key of C.
Open Helpers and turn on **Solfege - Movable Do** and Counting with **Kodály Syllables**.
Write a model 4-measure melody (example: sol sol mi mi | sol sol mi shh | la la sol mi | sol mi do shh) and keep it in a second tab.
Write the task card on the board (see Create step).

steps.do: Echo-sing sol-mi patterns with hand signs (sol = flat hand, mi = hand level like a table). Add la (hand drooping) and low do (fist). Sing a familiar sol-mi-la playground chant such as “Rain, Rain, Go Away” with hand signs.
steps.say: Sol and mi are like stairs. La is one more step up. Do is home.
steps.check: Hand signs match pitch; voices go up for la.

steps.do: Play the model melody from the second tab. Ask: does it sound finished? Then change the last note to sol and play again.
steps.say: Which ending sounds like we got home? That is why we end on do.

steps.do: On the projector, build measure 1 by clicking notes onto the staff: point out the solfège letters under each note and the ta / ti-ti counting. Show how a rest fills a beat. Point to where sol, mi, la and do sit (in C: G, E, A, C). Press Play after each measure.
steps.check: Students can tell you which line or space is sol and which is mi.

steps.do: Class composes measure 2 together: students vote on the rhythm, then on sol or mi for each note. Sing it with hand signs before pressing Play.
steps.say: Sing it first, then let the computer check us.

steps.do: Students compose their own melody. **Task card:** 4 measures, 4 beats each; use sol, mi and la (do is a bonus); use at least one ti-ti and one rest; the last note is do. Press Play after each measure and sing along. Signed-in students save; others copy the share link.
steps.check: Circulate: is every measure full? Does it end on do? Can the student sing measure 1?

steps.do: Volunteers sing their melody with solfège and hand signs, then press Play so the class hears if it matched. Class gives one star (something that worked) and one wish.
steps.say: Did the singing match the computer? What made the ending sound finished?

steps.do: Exit ticket: sing a sol-mi-la pattern; students show it with hand signs and then hold up fingers for how many beats it has.

support: Limit to sol and mi only, then add la.
Start from the class model and change only the rhythm in measures 3-4.
extend: Add re (between mi and do) and make a melody that steps down mi-re-do at the end.
Add lyrics under the notes and sing the words.
access: Turn on Boomwhacker colors as well as solfège for students who rely on color.
Students who are not comfortable singing alone can sing with a partner or play their song on a barred instrument.
For ELL students, post the solfège ladder with hand-sign pictures.

formative: Hand signs match pitch in the warm-up.
Measures show 4 beats in Kodály counting.
Melody ends on do when you check it.
assessment.summative: Student sings their 4-measure melody with solfège; the saved file or share link is posted to Google Classroom (or the class account) and scored with the rubric.

levels: Uses sol, mi, la and do with a clear shape (goes up and comes home) and explains it.
Uses sol, mi and la and ends on do.
Uses sol and mi only, or does not end on do.
Notes are placed but not on the target pitches.
All 4 measures have 4 beats with varied rhythms (ta, ti-ti, rest, half note).
All 4 measures have 4 beats with at least one ti-ti and one rest.
One or two measures have too many or too few beats.
Most measures do not have 4 beats.
Sings in tune with correct solfège and hand signs, steady tempo, with expression.
Sings with correct solfège and hand signs; mostly in tune.
Sings with some wrong syllables or loses the beat.
Needs the teacher to sing along to get through it.

lessons.exitTicket: I sing sol-sol-mi-la: show it with hand signs. Then: which note makes a song sound finished?
tips: Easy mode colors and labels the notes, so students can focus on sound. Turn helpers off later for a reading check.
If students’ melodies jump around, remind them that sol-mi-la live next to each other on the staff.
Sing everything before pressing Play: the computer checks the singing, not the other way around.

lessons.title: Question and Answer Melodies
lessons.summary: Students compose an 8-measure melody in Standard mode: a 4-measure question that ends on a non-tonic note and a 4-measure answer that ends on C (do). They add dynamics, revise with peer feedback, print the score and share a link.
objectives: compose an 8-measure melody in 4/4 in C major organized as a question phrase and an answer phrase
end the question on an unstable note (re, sol or ti) and the answer on C (do)
add at least two dynamics that support the mood
revise using peer feedback and explain one change
present a printed score and share link
iCan: I can write a musical question that sounds unfinished and an answer that sounds finished.
I can use dynamics to shape my melody.
I can explain a change I made after feedback.

vocabulary.def: A musical sentence, often 4 measures long.
Fancy names for the question phrase and the answer phrase.
The home note of the key. In C major it is C (do).
The ending of a phrase; it can sound open (question) or closed (answer).
How loud or soft the music is: p, mp, mf, f.
A short idea that can be repeated or changed.

materials: Projector with [Staff Composer](/?app=staff-composer)
Student devices with headphones; class account sign-in cards
Printer or PDF print for final scores
Peer feedback slips (two stars and a wish)
prep: Set Staff Composer to **Standard** mode, 4/4, key of C, tempo about 100.
Prepare a model: a question ending on D or G and an answer that starts the same way but ends on C. Save it to the class account.
Optional: sign in and use **Assign Song to Class** to push a blank 8-measure starter file.
Post success criteria on the board.

steps.do: Call-and-response singing: you sing a 4-beat phrase that ends up high, students answer with a phrase that ends on do. Then play a question on the projected piano and ask a volunteer to sing an answer.
steps.say: A question sounds like it wants to keep going. An answer sounds like a period at the end of a sentence.

steps.do: Play the model. Then play only the question phrase and stop. Ask students to describe what they feel. Play the answer.
steps.check: Students use words like unfinished, open, hanging, finished, home.

steps.do: Show how the model is built: measures 1-4 end on G (or D); measures 5-8 repeat the first measure’s idea and end on C. Turn on Helpers → Note Letters and Counting (numbers) to read it. Show how to add dynamics (p, mf, f) to a note.
steps.say: Good composers reuse an idea. Your answer can start like your question and change at the end.

steps.do: Students compose. **Success criteria:** 8 measures in 4/4; measure 4 ends on a note that is not C; measure 8 ends on C; the answer reuses an idea from the question; mostly steps with a few leaps; two or more dynamics. Save to the class account before the end.
steps.check: Check measure 4 and measure 8 endings with each student; ask them to play just the question.

steps.do: Students write on a sticky note: my question ends on ___ and my answer ends on ___.

Partners listen to each other’s melody with headphones split or at low volume. Each writes two stars and a wish using the success criteria, e.g. “Your question ends on D and sounds open” / “Wish: try p at the start so the f stands out.”
Students make at least one change from the feedback and write one sentence about why. Then they print (Print / PDF) and copy the share link into Google Classroom.
steps.check: Every student can name the one change they made.

steps.do: Gallery: post printed scores; 4-6 students play their melody for the class and explain how the dynamics fit the mood. Class identifies where the question ends.
steps.say: Raise your hand when you hear the question end. Was it open or closed?

support: Provide the first measure; the student repeats it to start the answer.
Use Easy mode or Helpers → Note Letters so note names are visible.
extend: Write in G major and end the answer on G; explain which note is the tonic now.
Add a second instrument from the mixer playing long C and G notes underneath.
access: Students can enter notes with the on-screen piano or a MIDI keyboard instead of clicking the staff.
Provide a printed staff with C and G highlighted for students who need a visual anchor.
ELL: pair the words question/answer with ? and . symbols on the board.

formative: Sticky note: ending notes of the question and answer.
Partner feedback slips use the success-criteria vocabulary.
Students identify the question ending when classmates play.
assessment.summative: Printed score plus share link posted to Google Classroom, with a one-sentence revision note; scored with the rubric.

levels: Question ends on an unstable note, answer ends on C, and the answer clearly reuses and varies the question’s idea.
Question ends on a note other than C; answer ends on C; 8 measures.
Endings are present but the question also ends on C, or the piece is incomplete.
No clear phrases or endings.
All measures correct in 4/4; three or more dynamics placed to shape the phrases.
All measures correct in 4/4; at least two dynamics.
Some measures have the wrong number of beats, or only one dynamic.
Many measures incomplete; no dynamics.
Makes several purposeful revisions and explains each with musical vocabulary.
Makes at least one revision from feedback and explains why.
Makes a change but cannot explain it.
No revision.

lessons.exitTicket: Write the letter name your question ends on and the letter name your answer ends on. Which one is the tonic?
tips: Students often end every phrase on C; play their question alone so they hear it sounds finished already.
Remind students to save before the bell; unsaved work is lost if the tab closes.
The share link holds only the music, so it is safe to post in Google Classroom.

lessons.title: Arrange It! Ode to Joy for an Ensemble
lessons.summary: Students arrange a public-domain tune (Beethoven’s Ode to Joy or Twinkle) for an ensemble template such as String Quartet, Brass Quintet, Elementary Orff Percussion or Rock Band: melody, a bass line on chord roots and a harmony or rhythm part, balanced in the mixer.
objectives: complete a melody from the “Challenge: Beethoven’s Ode to Joy” (or Twinkle) template
write a bass line using the roots of I (C) and V (G) chords
add a harmony or rhythm part that supports the melody
balance parts in the mixer and explain instrument choices
explain why B♭ instruments read music written a step higher than they sound
iCan: I can arrange a melody for a group of instruments.
I can write a bass line on chord roots.
I can explain how each part supports the melody.

vocabulary.def: A version of a piece written for particular instruments or voices.
The lowest part; it often plays the root of each chord.
The note a chord is built on (C for a C chord, G for a G chord).
Notes that sound at the same time as the melody to support it.
A group of musicians performing together.
An instrument (like clarinet or trumpet in B♭) whose written note is different from the sound.
How loud each part is compared to the others.

materials: Projector with [Staff Composer](/?app=staff-composer)
Student devices with headphones; class account sign-in cards
Chord chart on the board: C (C-E-G) and G (G-B-D)
Optional: band students’ instruments for a live demo
prep: Open the template **Challenge: Beethoven’s Ode to Joy** (alternative: Challenge: Twinkle Twinkle Little Star) and complete it yourself so you know the missing notes.
Try the ensemble templates String Quartet, Brass Quintet, Elementary Orff Percussion and Rock Band; decide which ones to offer (2-3 choices is plenty).
Mark on your model which measures use the C chord and which use G (Ode to Joy in C mostly alternates C and G).
Plan groups of 2-3 students per arrangement.

steps.do: Sing or hum Ode to Joy on solfège (mi mi fa sol sol fa mi re …). Listen to a short public-domain recording or play the template. Ask: what is the melody? What else could be happening underneath?
steps.say: Beethoven wrote this melody 200 years ago. Today you are the arranger.

steps.do: Students open the Ode to Joy challenge template and fill in the missing notes, checking by ear and with Helpers → Note Letters.
steps.check: Melody matches what the class sang.

steps.do: Project the C and G chord chart. Show measure by measure: if the melody uses C, E or G, the bass plays C; if it uses G, B or D, the bass plays G. Write half or whole notes in the bass. Transpose the bass down an octave if needed and choose a cello, tuba or bass guitar sound.
steps.say: The bass is the floor the melody stands on. Find the chord root.

steps.do: Groups pick an ensemble template (String Quartet, Brass Quintet, Elementary Orff Percussion, Rock Band) and copy the melody into the top part. Save to the class account.

**Task card:** melody part complete; bass line on chord roots for every measure; one more part: harmony (thirds below the melody or long chord tones) or a rhythm/drum part from the grooves; use the mixer to set balance so the melody is clearest; add dynamics. Save often.
steps.check: Visit each group: play the bass alone, then with the melody. Does it fit? Is the melody audible in the mixer?

steps.do: Show Transpose for B♭ instruments on the model. Ask band students to play written C on clarinet or trumpet while you play concert B♭. Discuss why the written part changes.
steps.say: A B♭ trumpet plays a written C and we hear a B♭. The arranger has to write it a step higher.

steps.do: Peer listening with a checklist (melody clear, bass on roots, extra part fits), 15 minutes revising, then each group plays its arrangement and explains one instrument choice. Print or share the link to Google Classroom.
steps.check: Groups name which part they changed after feedback and why.

support: Give a bass line starter with the first 4 measures written.
Use Twinkle (C-F-G only) or keep the extra part to a single drum groove.
extend: Write a countermelody instead of plain harmony.
Add a 1st/2nd ending or an introduction; arrange in G major for the Brass Quintet and transpose the trumpet parts for B♭.
access: Allow MIDI keyboard or on-screen piano entry.
Assign roles in groups (melody checker, bass writer, mixer engineer) so every student has a clear job.
Provide the chord chart with color coding for C and G measures.

formative: Completed challenge melody after Session 1.
Bass notes match chord roots when checked measure by measure.
Group explains balance choices during check-ins.
assessment.summative: Group arrangement shared via link or class account plus each student’s short written explanation of one part they wrote and why; scored with the rubric.

levels: Bass is correct on every measure and adds movement (passing notes or octave jumps) that fits.
Bass plays the correct root (C or G) for every measure.
Bass is correct for some measures; some clash with the melody.
Bass is missing or random notes.
Three or more parts with distinct roles; balance and dynamics make the melody stand out; uses instrument ranges sensibly.
Melody, bass and one harmony or rhythm part; melody is clearly heard.
Parts are present but cover the melody or are unfinished.
Only the melody is complete.
Explains instrument choices, balance and transposition using correct vocabulary.
Explains why one part or instrument supports the melody.
Describes choices only as “it sounds cool”.
Cannot explain choices.

lessons.exitTicket: A measure of the melody uses B, D and G. Which bass note fits: C or G? Why?
tips: Ode to Joy in C fits almost entirely on C and G chords, which keeps the bass line achievable.
If playback sounds muddy, have students lower the harmony volume in the mixer before changing notes.
Ask your band teacher to visit for the transposition talk; students love hearing real instruments.

lessons.title: Staff Wars Cadets: Treble Clef Lines and Spaces
lessons.summary: Third graders learn treble clef line notes (E G B D F) and space notes (F A C E), then build fluency in Staff Wars at Cadet level with short timed rounds and a personal best goal.
objectives: name the treble clef lines E G B D F and spaces F A C E
identify notes on the treble staff quickly and accurately in Staff Wars Cadet level
track a personal best and set a practice goal
use a rehearsal strategy (short rounds, mnemonic) to improve
iCan: I can name the lines and spaces of the treble clef.
I can blast notes in Staff Wars by naming them.
I can beat my own best score.

vocabulary.def: The curly G clef used for higher notes.
A note with a line going through its middle.
A note that sits between two lines.
The treble lines from bottom to top: Every Good Bird Does Fly.
The treble spaces from bottom to top spell FACE.
Your highest score so far.

materials: Projector with [Staff Wars](/?app=staff-wars)
Student devices with headphones
Large staff on the board or a floor staff made of tape
Personal best tracking cards (index cards)
prep: Open Staff Wars, choose treble clef and **Cadet** level (lines & spaces), letter-name answers.
Draw a big treble staff on the board; prepare note magnets or sticky notes.
Decide if students sign in (scores go to the leaderboard only when signed in) or just record scores on cards.

steps.do: Hand staff: hold your hand sideways, five fingers are the five lines, gaps are the spaces. Point to a finger and students say the line name (pinky = E … thumb = F). Then point to gaps for F A C E.
steps.say: Your hand is a staff you always carry with you.

steps.do: Project Staff Wars and play 30 seconds yourself, missing a few on purpose. Ask: how can we get faster?
On the board staff, teach EGBDF (class makes its own sentence, e.g. Every Good Bird Does Fly) and FACE. Place sticky notes; students say line or space first, then the letter.
steps.say: First ask: line or space? Then which one?
steps.check: Students answer line/space before the letter.

steps.do: Play Staff Wars on the projector with the class calling answers; a student volunteer clicks. Pause and use the line-or-space question on any mistake.

Students play three short Cadet rounds (about 2-3 minutes each). After each round they write the score on their card and circle the best. Between rounds: 30 seconds of hand-staff review with a partner.
steps.check: Scores rise from round 1 to round 3 for most students.

steps.do: Students write a goal on their card: “Next time I want to reach ___ by practicing ___.” Share one strategy that helped.
steps.say: Your best score only competes with you.

steps.do: Exit ticket on the board staff (see below).

support: Start with lines only (E G B D F) or spaces only for the first round.
Keep the hand-staff picture on the desk.
extend: Move to Pilot level (middle C and one ledger line).
Answer with solfège instead of letters.
access: Allow keyboard keys or buttons, whichever is easier to reach.
Students with processing needs can compete only against their own score with no leaderboard.
Large-print staff card for visual impairments; project at large zoom.

formative: Hand-staff responses in the warm-up.
Line-or-space reasoning during guided practice.
Score growth across three rounds on the tracking card.
assessment.summative: Each student names 10 notes on a printed or projected treble staff (5 lines, 5 spaces); record accuracy, plus the best Staff Wars Cadet score from the tracking card.

levels: Names all line notes instantly and can find a given letter on the staff.
Names all line notes correctly.
Names 3-4 line notes correctly.
Names 0-2 line notes correctly.
Names all space notes instantly and can find a given letter on the staff.
Names all space notes correctly.
Names 2-3 space notes correctly.
Names 0-1 space notes correctly.
Improves across rounds, sets a specific goal and names a strategy that worked.
Records all scores and sets a goal.
Records scores but no goal.
Does not track scores.

lessons.exitTicket: Teacher places three notes on the board staff (one line, two spaces). Students write the letter names on a sticky note.
tips: Short daily rounds (3-5 minutes) work better than one long session; reuse this as a weekly warm-up.
Teach students to use first name or nickname only if they sign in for the leaderboard.
If students guess randomly for speed, ask them to say line or space out loud before answering.

lessons.title: Staff Wars Pilots: Bass Clef and the Grand Staff
lessons.summary: Students extend note reading to bass clef and the grand staff, connect both clefs through middle C, play Staff Wars at Pilot level and Custom Range, and band students practice with Live Microphone and their instrument’s transposition.
objectives: name bass clef lines (G B D F A) and spaces (A C E G)
locate middle C and one ledger line above and below on the grand staff
build reading fluency at Pilot level and with a Custom Range targeted at their weak notes
band students: play written notes on their instrument using Live Microphone and the correct transposition
iCan: I can read notes in bass clef and on the grand staff.
I can find middle C in both clefs.
I can choose a practice range that targets the notes I miss.

vocabulary.def: The F clef; its two dots surround the F line. Used for lower notes.
A treble and a bass staff joined together, as in piano music.
The C between the two staves, written on a ledger line.
A short extra line above or below the staff.
Changing the written note so an instrument in B♭, E♭ or F sounds the right pitch.
The actual sounding pitch, the same as piano.

materials: Projector with [Staff Wars](/?app=staff-wars)
Student devices with headphones
Band instruments for band students (and a quiet corner); device microphone
Grand staff handout or board drawing
prep: In Staff Wars set bass clef, **Pilot** level; also try grand staff and **Custom Range** so you can demonstrate.
Ask band students to bring instruments; check the Live Microphone setting and the B♭ / E♭ / F transposition options.
Draw a grand staff with middle C circled.

steps.do: Quick treble review: 60 seconds of Cadet treble on the projector, class calls answers.

steps.phase: Model: bass clef and middle C
steps.do: On the grand staff drawing, show that bass clef lines are G B D F A (Good Boys Do Fine Always) and spaces A C E G (All Cows Eat Grass). Show middle C as one ledger line below treble and one above bass: the same note. Count up from middle C into treble and down into bass.
steps.say: Middle C is the bridge between the two clefs.
steps.check: Students can point to middle C in both clefs.

steps.do: Project Staff Wars, bass clef Pilot. Students answer on mini whiteboards before the volunteer clicks; reveal and compare.
Students play two rounds of bass clef Pilot and one round of grand staff. They tally which letters they missed most.
steps.check: Each student has a list of 2-3 trouble notes.

steps.do: Students set a **Custom Range** covering their trouble notes and play two short rounds. Band students instead turn on **Live Microphone** with their instrument’s transposition (B♭ clarinet/trumpet, E♭ alto sax, F horn; concert pitch for flute, trombone, baritone, tuba) and play each note to blast it.
steps.say: Practice what you miss, not what you already know.

steps.do: Written reflection: Which clef is harder for you and why? What strategy helped? Band students explain why a trumpet’s written C is not concert C.
Exit ticket (see below).

support: Begin with bass clef Cadet level (lines and spaces only) before Pilot.
Provide a grand staff card with the mnemonics.
extend: Try Jedi Master level or alto clef (viola reading).
Compare transpositions: what does a B♭ trumpet play to sound concert F?
access: Live Microphone needs a quiet space; offer button answers as an equal alternative.
Allow letter keys on the keyboard for students who prefer typing.
Students with visual needs can zoom the browser; pair with a reader who says “line” or “space”.

formative: Mini whiteboard answers during guided practice.
Trouble-note lists and the Custom Range chosen.
Band students’ correct use of transposition setting.
assessment.summative: Grand staff quiz: name 12 notes (bass lines, bass spaces, middle C, ledger notes) and submit a written reflection; band students may instead show 8 correct notes played with Live Microphone.

levels: Names all bass lines and spaces instantly, including ledger notes.
Names bass lines and spaces correctly.
Confuses bass with treble names on some notes.
Reads bass clef with treble names throughout.
Explains middle C in both clefs and reads notes moving across the staves.
Locates middle C in both clefs and names notes within one ledger line.
Locates middle C in one clef only.
Cannot locate middle C.
Chooses a precise Custom Range (or transposition) and explains how it improved accuracy.
Identifies trouble notes and practices them.
Plays rounds but does not adjust the range.
Does not complete practice rounds.

lessons.exitTicket: Draw a grand staff: circle middle C in both clefs, and write the letter names of the bass clef lines from bottom to top.
tips: Students who play piano or band often know one clef well; pair them across strengths.
If Live Microphone misses notes, lower background noise and have students play long, steady tones.
Leaderboards include main, bass, alto and grand; remind students to use a first name or nickname only.

lessons.title: Rhythm Rock Stars: Ta, Ti-Ti and Shh
lessons.summary: Students read and perform quarter notes, half notes, quarter rests and eighth notes with Kodály syllables, first by listening and choosing in Beat Decoder, then by tapping in time in Rhythm Tapper at tempo 70.
objectives: say and clap ta, ta-ah, ti-ti and shh patterns
match a heard 4-beat pattern to its notation (Beat Decoder)
tap rhythms in time at a slow tempo (Rhythm Tapper, 70)
perform a folk chant with correct rhythm
iCan: I can read ta, ti-ti and shh.
I can find the rhythm I hear.
I can tap a rhythm right on time.

vocabulary.def: Quarter note: one sound on one beat.
Two eighth notes: two even sounds on one beat.
Half note: one sound held for two beats.
Quarter rest: one beat of silence.
A beat that stays the same, like a clock.

materials: Projector with [Rhythm Rock Stars](/?app=rhythm-rockstars)
Student devices with headphones (tablets work well for tapping)
Rhythm flashcards: ta, ti-ti, ta-ah, shh
Words to the Mexican folk chant “Bate, bate, chocolate” on the board
prep: Open Rhythm Rock Stars, set counting to **Kodály syllables**, tempo **70** (Slow Practice), Level 1.
Try Beat Decoder and Rhythm Tapper once each so you know the screens.
Write the chant rhythm on the board in stick notation: ti-ti ti-ti | ti-ti ta.

steps.do: Teach “Bate, bate, chocolate” (a Mexican folk chant sung while stirring hot chocolate). Students pat the beat, then clap the words. Point out that two sounds on one beat are ti-ti. Ask who has a stirring or cooking chant at home.
steps.say: This chant comes from Mexico. Families say it while stirring chocolate.

steps.do: Flash rhythm cards; students echo with syllables and claps. Add shh with hands open and silent.
On the projector open **Beat Decoder**, Level 1. A rhythm plays; class says what they heard with syllables, then a volunteer chooses the notation. Repeat with Level 2 (ti-ti and eighth rests).
steps.say: Listen, say it, then find it.
steps.check: Students say the syllables before choosing.

steps.do: Students play Beat Decoder on their own, Level 1 then Level 2 when they get 5 in a row.
Model **Rhythm Tapper** at tempo 70 with the count-in: say the syllables quietly while tapping. Students then play Level 1 and Level 2, aiming for more Perfect and Great taps.
steps.check: Listen for steady taps; watch for students rushing ti-ti.

steps.do: Whole class performs the chant twice: once clapping the rhythm, once with a student keeping the beat on a drum. Ask: which was easier, finding the rhythm or tapping it? Why?
Exit ticket (see below).

support: Stay on Level 1 (ta, ta-ah, shh) until 5 correct in a row.
Partner tapping: one student taps, the other says syllables.
extend: Move to tempo 96 in Rhythm Tapper.
Try Rhythm Quiz on Level 2.
access: Students with motor challenges can tap a large key or touch the screen instead of a small button.
Visual beat cards on the desk for students who need a reference.
ELL: syllables work in every language; let students teach a chant from their culture.

formative: Echo accuracy with flashcards.
Beat Decoder streaks.
Perfect/Great counts in Rhythm Tapper.
assessment.summative: Teacher points to four flashcards in a row; each student (or small group) claps and says the 4-beat pattern; record on a class checklist.

levels: Reads any 4-beat pattern with ta, ti-ti, ta-ah and shh instantly, including new combinations.
Reads 4-beat patterns with correct syllables.
Mixes up ti-ti and ta or forgets the rest.
Needs the teacher to model each pattern.
Chooses the correct notation in Beat Decoder Level 2 consistently.
Chooses correctly most of the time at Levels 1-2.
Correct at Level 1 only.
Guesses without saying the rhythm.
Taps and claps with a steady beat at 70 and 96.
Taps and claps steadily at tempo 70.
Rushes or slows during ti-ti or rests.
Does not keep a steady beat.

lessons.exitTicket: Clap and say the pattern on the board: ta ti-ti shh ta. Then show with fingers how many sounds it has (4).
tips: Always start new levels at tempo 70; speed comes later.
Headphones help tapping accuracy because students hear their own taps.
Leaderboard names: first names or nicknames only.

lessons.title: Rhythm Rock Stars: Sixteenths, Triplets and Syncopation
lessons.summary: Students read, count and perform sixteenth-note patterns, ti-tika and tika-ti, dotted eighth-sixteenth, triplets and syncopa (Levels 3-5) using number counting, build rhythms in Beat Builder, then compose and perform their own 4-beat pattern.
objectives: count sixteenth, dotted eighth-sixteenth, triplet and syncopated patterns with numbers (1 e & a, 1-trip-let)
match and build patterns in Beat Builder at Levels 3-5
compose a 4-beat rhythm using at least two new patterns and notate it on paper
perform their rhythm accurately and identify syncopation in a folk song
iCan: I can count sixteenths, triplets and syncopation with numbers.
I can build a rhythm that matches a groove.
I can compose and perform my own 4-beat rhythm.

vocabulary.def: Four sounds per beat, counted 1 e & a.
A long-short pattern in one beat, counted 1 (e &) a.
Three even sounds in one beat, counted 1-trip-let.
An accent on a weak part of the beat; syncopa is short-long-short (ti-ta-ti).
Splitting the beat into smaller equal parts.

materials: Projector with [Rhythm Rock Stars](/?app=rhythm-rockstars)
Student devices with headphones
Rhythm composition worksheet (4 empty beats) and pencils
Recording or your own singing of “Li’l Liza Jane” (traditional African American folk song)
prep: Set Rhythm Rock Stars counting to **numbers** (switch to Kodály syllables later to bridge), tempo 70, Level 3.
Write on the board: 1 e & a | 1 & a (ti-tika) | 1 e & (tika-ti) | 1 a (dotted) | 1-trip-let | syncopa.
Print the composition worksheet.

steps.do: Body-percussion echo: you pat 4-beat patterns using sixteenths and ti-tika; students echo and count aloud. Then sing “Li’l Liza Jane” and clap the chorus rhythm.
steps.say: Listen to “Liza Jane”: the accent jumps off the beat. That is syncopation.
steps.check: Students notice the short-long-short rhythm.

steps.do: Project Rhythm Tapper or Beat Decoder Level 3, then 4 and 5. For each new pattern, count it with numbers, clap it, then let the tool play it. Show the gallop (ti-tika), the snap (tika-ti), the dotted march and triplets.
steps.say: Count first, clap second, check third.

steps.do: Open **Beat Builder** at Level 3. A groove plays; the class decides which pattern fits each beat; volunteers build it. Repeat at Level 4.
steps.check: Students justify choices by counting (“beat 2 has four sounds, so it’s 1 e & a”).

steps.do: Students play Beat Builder Levels 3-5 at their own pace, then try one round of Rhythm Tapper at tempo 70 on their best level.

**Task card:** On the worksheet, compose a 4-beat rhythm in 4/4. Use at least two patterns from today (sixteenths, ti-tika, tika-ti, dotted, triplet, syncopa). Write the counting under every beat. Practice clapping it four times without stopping.
steps.check: Every beat adds up to one beat; counting is written correctly.

steps.do: Students perform for a partner, then 4-6 volunteers perform for the class while others keep the beat. Class names which patterns they heard.
steps.say: Which pattern made the rhythm feel exciting or off-balance?

steps.do: Exit ticket (see below). Collect worksheets.

support: Use only sixteenths and ti-tika/tika-ti (Level 3-4) in the composition.
Provide a word bank: “huckleberry” (sixteenths), “blueberry” (triplet), “pizza-pie” (syncopa, short-long-short).
extend: Compose 8 beats with a syncopation across the bar line and notate it in Staff Composer.
Try Level 6 (mixed) at tempo 96.
access: Allow students to perform their rhythm on a drum or with body percussion as preferred.
Students with fine-motor needs can build their composition with rhythm cards instead of writing.
ELL: number counting is visual on the board; pair with a buddy.

formative: Echo accuracy during the warm-up.
Beat Builder justifications using counting.
Rhythm Tapper Perfect/Great at tempo 70.
assessment.summative: Composition worksheet with counting written in plus a live performance of the 4-beat rhythm (teacher checklist or a short video in Google Classroom).

levels: Counts all Level 3-5 patterns correctly and explains how they divide the beat.
Counts sixteenth, dotted, triplet and syncopa patterns correctly.
Counts some patterns; confuses ti-tika with tika-ti or triplets with sixteenths.
Cannot yet count subdivided patterns.
4 beats correct, three or more new patterns, counting accurate, purposeful accents or syncopation.
4 beats correct, two new patterns, counting written under every beat.
One beat is too long or short, or counting is incomplete.
Pattern does not add up to 4 beats.
Performs the rhythm accurately, steady, with dynamics or accents, and repeats it from memory.
Performs accurately with a steady beat.
Performs with some hesitation or rhythm errors.
Cannot perform the rhythm without help.

lessons.exitTicket: Write the counting for a triplet and for a beat of four sixteenth notes. Which one has more sounds?
tips: Students confuse triplets and sixteenths; contrast “blue-ber-ry” (3) and “hum-ming-bird-ie” (4) on the same beat.
Switch counting to Kodály syllables briefly if students learned them in K-3; it helps bridge.
Use tempo 70 for every new level; 96 and 130 are for mastery.

lessons.title: Symbol Detectives: Notes, Rests and Dynamics
lessons.summary: Students play Memory Match with Notes & Rests and then Dynamics, and connect each symbol to a sound or movement: stepping note values, freezing for rests, and singing p, mp, mf and f.
objectives: match note and rest symbols to their names
match dynamic symbols (pp to ff, crescendo, decrescendo) to their meanings
show the meaning of a symbol with sound or movement
explain how dynamics change the feeling of music
iCan: I can match music symbols to their names.
I can show what a symbol means with my voice or body.
I can tell how loud or soft music should be from its symbol.

vocabulary.def: A sign that tells musicians what to do.
A symbol for silence.
Soft.
Loud.
Gradually getting louder.
Gradually getting softer.

materials: Projector with [Symbol Match](/?app=music-symbol-match&focus=1)
Student devices (pairs work well)
Large symbol cards: quarter note, half note, whole note, quarter rest, p, f, crescendo, decrescendo
prep: Open Symbol Match, choose **Memory Match**, category **Notes & Rests**.
Open the **Study Guide** in a second tab for review.
Clear floor space for movement.

steps.do: Movement: hold up a quarter note card, students walk one step per beat; half note, step and hold; whole note, step and hold for 4; quarter rest, freeze. Hold up p and f while singing a familiar song softly and loudly.
steps.say: Musicians read symbols like detectives read clues.

steps.do: Project the Study Guide and reveal symbols one at a time; students guess the name before you click.
Play one Memory Match turn on the projector: flip two cards, say the names, explain matches. Model saying the meaning when you find a match.
steps.say: When you find a match, say what it means or show it.

steps.do: Pairs play Memory Match with **Notes & Rests**. Rule: every match, both partners show the symbol with movement or claps.
steps.check: Partners act out each match, not just click.

steps.do: Switch to category **Dynamics**. Every match, partners say “hello” at that dynamic (pp whisper to ff strong voice, never yelling). For crescendo and decrescendo they grow or shrink their voice.
Sing a short song twice, once all p and once all f. Ask: which fits a lullaby? A parade? Students show crescendo with arms opening wide.
steps.say: Dynamics help music tell a story.

steps.do: Exit ticket (see below).

support: Use fewer cards: Notes & Rests only, or play together on the projector.
Keep the Study Guide open beside the game.
extend: Try Speed mode with Dynamics.
Add Clefs & Accidentals and explain one new symbol to the class.
access: Students who cannot move freely can use hand motions or voice instead.
Large symbol cards and projector zoom for visual needs.
ELL: Italian dynamic words are new to everyone; add home-language words for loud and soft.

formative: Movement responses in the warm-up.
Partners demonstrate each match.
Voice level matches dynamic symbol.
assessment.summative: Teacher holds up 5 symbol cards; each student shows or says the meaning; record on a class checklist.

levels: Names and shows all note values and rests, including how many beats each lasts.
Matches and names quarter, half, whole notes and quarter rest.
Matches most cards but confuses half and whole note.
Matches cards by shape only, without names.
Performs pp to ff and crescendo/decrescendo accurately and explains when to use each.
Performs p, mp, mf, f and crescendo/decrescendo with the voice.
Shows loud and soft but not the in-between levels.
Does not change voice level to match symbols.
Explains how a symbol changes the mood of a song with an example.
Shows each symbol’s meaning with movement or sound.
Shows some symbols with help.
Cannot yet connect symbols to sounds.

lessons.exitTicket: I hold up a symbol (p, f or a quarter rest): students show it silently: tiny hands for p, big hands for f, freeze for rest.
tips: Filter to one category per round for K-3; mixing categories confuses younger students.
Set a voice rule for ff (strong, not screaming) before the Dynamics round.
The Study Guide on the projector makes a quick word-wall review for the next class.

lessons.title: Score Scavenger Hunt
lessons.summary: Students race through Symbol Match Speed mode, hunt for symbols in a real projected or printed score (the Ode to Joy template with added dynamics, articulations and repeats), then add five symbols to their own Staff Composer piece and explain the effect.
objectives: identify notes, rests, dynamics, clefs, accidentals and articulations quickly in Speed mode
locate and explain symbols in a real score
add five purposeful symbols to their own composition
explain how symbols change a performance
iCan: I can name music symbols quickly.
I can find symbols in a real score and tell what they mean.
I can add symbols to my own music on purpose.

vocabulary.def: Printed music showing all the notes and symbols of a piece.
How a note is played: staccato (short), accent (strong).
Hold the note longer than its value.
Go back and play the section again.
A sharp, flat or natural that changes a note’s pitch.
Symbols for volume, from pp (very soft) to ff (very loud).

materials: Projector with [Symbol Match](/?app=music-symbol-match&focus=1) and [Staff Composer](/?app=staff-composer)
Student devices with headphones
Printed score: Ode to Joy template with your added symbols (one per pair)
Scavenger hunt sheet (list of 10 symbols with blanks for measure number and meaning)
prep: In Staff Composer open **Challenge: Beethoven’s Ode to Joy**, complete it, switch to **Advanced** mode and add: p, f, crescendo, decrescendo, staccato, accent, a fermata on the last note, and a repeat sign. Print it (Print / PDF).
Make a scavenger hunt sheet: find each symbol, write its measure number and meaning.
Make sure students have a saved Staff Composer piece (e.g. from the Question and Answer lesson) or a blank file.

steps.do: Students play two 45-second rounds of Symbol Match **Speed** mode (all categories) and record their best score and streak.
steps.say: Speed shows what you know by heart. Remember the symbols you missed.

steps.do: Play the Ode to Joy model twice: once with no symbols, once with your symbols. Ask what changed.
steps.check: Students mention louder/softer, short notes, holding the end, repeating.

steps.do: Pairs get the printed score and hunt sheet. Find each symbol, write the measure number and its meaning. Then pick two symbols and perform their effect (sing or clap that measure).
steps.check: Measure numbers are correct; meanings use musical vocabulary.

steps.do: Go over answers on the projected score; students come up to point. Play the measure to hear each symbol.
steps.say: Every symbol is an instruction from the composer.

steps.do: Students open their own Staff Composer piece (Advanced mode). **Task card:** add five symbols from at least three categories (dynamics, articulation, repeat/fermata); play back after each; write one sentence per symbol explaining why it is there. Save and copy the share link.
steps.check: Five symbols present; reasons connect symbol to effect.

steps.do: Three or four students play their piece; class names the symbols they hear. Exit ticket (see below).

support: Shorten the hunt to five symbols with pictures on the sheet.
Allow Symbol Match Study Guide during the hunt.
extend: Add a 1st/2nd ending and explain how it changes form.
Hunt in a second public-domain score (e.g. a Sousa march) and compare symbol use.
access: Enlarge the printed score; provide a projected version.
Students may record explanations orally instead of writing.
ELL: hunt sheet includes the symbol drawing next to each word.

formative: Speed mode scores and missed symbols.
Scavenger hunt sheet accuracy.
Performed effect of chosen symbols.
assessment.summative: Staff Composer piece with five added symbols and a written reason for each, shared via link to Google Classroom.

levels: Finds and explains all symbols in the score, including measure numbers, with no help.
Finds and explains at least 8 of 10 symbols.
Finds 5-7 symbols or explains meanings incompletely.
Finds fewer than 5 symbols.
Adds more than five symbols from four or more categories, all correctly placed.
Adds five symbols from at least three categories, correctly placed.
Adds fewer than five symbols or from only one category.
Adds symbols incorrectly or none.
Explains how each symbol shapes the mood or form, using vocabulary and examples.
Explains the purpose of each symbol in a sentence.
Explains some symbols only by name.
No explanation.

lessons.exitTicket: Draw one symbol you added and write how it changes the sound of your music.
tips: Advanced mode is needed for articulations; make sure students switch modes before adding symbols.
If printing is limited, project the score and have pairs use the hunt sheet only.
Speed mode scores are not saved; have students write them down if you want to track growth.

lessons.title: Beat Detective: Beat vs. Rhythm
lessons.summary: Students feel the difference between the steady **beat** and the **rhythm** of the words, echo Barnaby the Beat Bear in Beat Detective, build an 8-step drum beat with the kick on the beat, and use Notate Song to read their beat as ta and ti-ti.
objectives: tell the steady beat apart from the rhythm of the words by patting and clapping
echo short drum patterns accurately in Beat Detective levels 1-2
build an 8-step drum beat with the kick on every beat and a clap or snare on beats 2 and 4
read their own beat in standard notation using ta, ti-ti and shh
iCan: I can pat the steady beat and clap the rhythm of the words.
I can echo Barnaby’s drum pattern.
I can make a drum beat and read it with ta and ti-ti.

vocabulary.def: The steady pulse of music, like a heartbeat. It never changes.
The pattern of long and short sounds, like the words of a song.
One sound on one beat (a quarter note).
Two even sounds on one beat (two eighth notes).
A beat with no sound (a quarter rest).
The big low drum that keeps the beat.

materials: Projector and speakers
One device per student or pair, with headphones
[Beat Machine](/?app=beat-machine)
Whiteboard with four heart shapes drawn in a row
prep: Open [Beat Machine](/?app=beat-machine) on the projector and test the sound.
Open Beat Detective once so you know where the pads are; start at Level 1: Stomp & Clap.
Set the Drum Beat grid to **8 steps** and 1 measure; press Reset all drum beats.
Draw four hearts (the beats) on the board, with space under them to write ta / ti-ti.

steps.do: Chant the Mexican folk rhyme “Bate, bate, chocolate.” First everyone pats the steady beat on their legs while you chant. Then chant again while students clap the words. Ask: which one stayed the same the whole time? Point to the four hearts: the beat. The words make the rhythm.
steps.say: Your pat is the beat. It is steady like your heart. Your clap is the rhythm. It follows the words.
steps.check: Pats stay even while claps change; students can name which is which.

steps.do: Open Beat Detective on the projector. Barnaby the Beat Bear plays a pattern; the class stomps and claps it in the air, then one student taps it back on the pads (kick, snare, clap, boing). Play Level 1: Stomp & Clap, then Level 2: Snappy Bounce. Use the hear-it-again button whenever needed.
steps.say: Detectives listen first. Hands still, ears open, then tap.
steps.check: Volunteers tap the right pads in the right order on the first or second try.

steps.do: Close Beat Detective. On the 8-step grid, each pair of steps is one beat (one heart). Click the kick on steps 1, 3, 5 and 7: kick on every beat. Press Play and pat along. Add a clap (or snare) on steps 3 and 7 (beats 2 and 4). Play again and let students stomp the kick and clap the clap.
steps.say: Kick on every heart keeps the beat. Now let’s add some rhythm on top.
steps.check: Class stomps on the kick and claps on 2 and 4 in time.

steps.do: Students open Beat Machine on their device (8 steps, 1 measure). Task card on the board: 1) kick on all four beats (steps 1, 3, 5, 7); 2) clap or snare on beats 2 and 4; 3) add one more sound anywhere to make your own rhythm (hi-hat on every step, or a clap on an in-between step). Play it, pat along, fix anything that wobbles.
steps.check: Circulate: kick lands on 1-3-5-7; students can pat the beat while their beat plays.

steps.do: Model on the projector: press **Notate Song** on your demo beat. Point to the kick line: one note per beat = ta. Change it so the kick plays on steps 1 and 2: two notes on one beat = ti-ti. Then students press Notate Song on their own beat and read one line aloud with ta, ti-ti and shh while pointing.
steps.say: Your beat is now real music notation. Let’s read it like musicians: ta, ta, ti-ti, ta.
steps.check: Students say ta for a single note and ti-ti for two beamed notes.

steps.do: Two or three students play their beat while the class pats the steady beat. Then the exit ticket.
steps.check: The class can keep the beat over a classmate’s rhythm.

support: Give a starter card with the exact steps to click (kick 1-3-5-7, clap 3-7).
Pair a beginner with a “beat buddy” who pats the beat while they click.
Stay on Beat Detective Level 1 for extra practice.
extend: Try Beat Detective Levels 3-5 (Double Trouble to Master Beat Champ).
Switch to 16 steps and find where ti-ti and ti-ka-ti-ka appear in Notate Song.
Add a second measure that is different and read both.
access: Project the grid large and number the beats under it; students with motor needs can tell a partner where to click.
For ELL students, label the board with pictures: heart = beat, mouth = words/rhythm.
Headphones keep the room calm; volume low for students with sound sensitivity.

formative: Warm-up: can each student show pat (beat) vs. clap (rhythm) when asked?
Beat Detective: note who echoes Level 1-2 correctly.
Notate Song: listen as students read their line with ta / ti-ti.
assessment.summative: Each student shows you (or saves to the class account) an 8-step beat with the kick on every beat and reads one line of its Notate Song notation aloud with ta, ti-ti and shh.

levels: Keeps a steady pat while clapping a different rhythm at the same time.
Pats a steady beat and claps the word rhythm, and names which is which.
Pats or claps but mixes up which one is the beat.
Cannot yet keep a steady pat with the class.
Kick on all beats, clap on 2 and 4, plus an added rhythm that still feels steady.
Kick on steps 1, 3, 5, 7 and clap or snare on beats 2 and 4.
Kick on some beats, or clap pattern not on 2 and 4.
Sounds placed randomly with no steady kick.
Reads all lines with ta, ti-ti and shh and points to each note correctly.
Reads one line correctly with ta, ti-ti and shh.
Reads ta correctly but mixes up ti-ti or shh.
Cannot yet match syllables to notes.

lessons.exitTicket: Point to the board: show me the beat (pat) and then the rhythm (clap) of “Bate, bate, chocolate.” Then read this card aloud: ta, ti-ti, ta, shh.
tips: Beat Detective works best as a whole-class game: everyone stomps and claps in the air, one helper taps the pads.
With 8 steps, every two steps are one beat. Drawing the four hearts above the grid makes this visible.
Notate Song is the bridge from “making a beat” to “reading rhythm”: never skip it.

lessons.title: Groove Builder: A 4-Measure Song in Beat Machine
lessons.summary: Students build a 16-step groove in layers (backbeat, hi-hat subdivision, bass ostinato, pentatonic melody), arrange it into four measures as Intro, A, A and B, then use Notate Song to count it with 1 e & a and share the link.
objectives: build a backbeat groove with the kick on beats 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4
add a hi-hat subdivision and a repeating bass ostinato that fit the groove
compose a short pentatonic melody on the Rainbow Melody grid
arrange four measures into Intro, A, A, B and explain the choices
