read and count their drum notation with 1 e & a
iCan: I can build a groove in layers: drums, bass and melody.
I can organize my music into an intro, a repeated A section and a contrasting B.
I can count my rhythm with 1 e & a and explain my choices.

vocabulary.def: The repeating pattern that makes music feel good to move to.
Accents on beats 2 and 4, usually the snare.
Splitting the beat into smaller equal parts (eighths, sixteenths).
A short pattern repeated over and over, like a bass line.
A five-note scale (do re mi sol la) where every note sounds good together.
The order of the sections in a piece, like Intro-A-A-B.
A section that changes something but still sounds related.

materials: Projector and speakers
One device per student, headphones
[Beat Machine](/?app=beat-machine)
Planning sheet: 4 boxes labeled Intro / A / A / B with a line for “what changes”
Google Classroom (or similar) assignment for share links
prep: Open [Beat Machine](/?app=beat-machine) on the projector; set **16 steps** per measure and choose the Acoustic or TR-808 sound pack.
Prepare a demo groove (backbeat + hi-hats) to reveal layer by layer.
Write the count row on the board: 1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a, with step numbers 1-16 underneath.
Post a Google Classroom assignment “Groove Builder share link.”

steps.do: Body-percussion backbeat: stomp on 1 and 3, clap on 2 and 4 while counting aloud. Then half the class whispers “1 e & a” sixteenths while the other half keeps the backbeat. Switch.
steps.say: Every beat has four little parts: 1 e & a. That is what a 16-step grid shows.
steps.check: Stomps and claps stay together; sixteenths are even.

steps.do: On the projector (16 steps): Layer 1, kick on steps 1 and 9 (beats 1 and 3), snare on 5 and 13 (beats 2 and 4). Layer 2, hi-hat on every odd step (eighths), then every step (sixteenths): ask which feels busier. Layer 3, on the Bass grid make a 4-note ostinato that repeats. Layer 4, on the Rainbow Melody grid add a short melody; point out it is pentatonic so wrong notes are hard to find. Solo each track to hear it alone.
steps.check: Students can name the step numbers for beats 1-4 (1, 5, 9, 13).

steps.do: Students build their own 1-measure groove with all four layers. Success criteria on the board: backbeat (snare on 2 and 4); hi-hat subdivision (eighths or sixteenths); bass ostinato that repeats; melody of at least 4 notes that ends on a long or resting note. Partners listen and give one “keep” and one “try.” Save to the class account or copy the share link before leaving.
steps.check: Circulate with the success criteria; ask “Which step is beat 3?”

steps.do: Students write on a sticky note which step numbers their snare uses and what those are in counting (e.g. step 5 = beat 2).

Clap a 4-phrase pattern: intro (just pats), A, A, B (something changes), and let students label it. Show the planning sheet. Model pressing **+ Measure** to make four measures: Measure 1 Intro (drums only, or drums + bass), Measures 2 and 3 the full groove (A), Measure 4 B (new melody, or a drum fill with toms and crash, or drop the kick).
steps.say: Repeat makes it catchy. Contrast keeps it interesting. Your B should change something on purpose.

steps.do: Students add measures to reach 4 and rebuild their groove in measures 2 and 3, then design the intro and the B variation. They fill the planning sheet with what changes in each box.
steps.check: Measures 2 and 3 match; measure 4 has a clear, intentional change.

steps.do: Students press **Notate Song**, find one measure of the drum part and count it aloud with 1 e & a while pointing (partner checks). Then they copy the share link into the Google Classroom assignment with one sentence: what changes in my B section and why.
steps.check: Counts land on the right notes; sixteenth beams are read as 1 e & a.

steps.do: Play 3-4 grooves. The class identifies the Intro, the A sections and the B by raising one finger (A) or two (B) when each section starts.

support: Start from a Ready Groove and change only the melody and bass.
Use 2 measures (Intro + A) instead of 4.
Give a step chart: kick 1, 9; snare 5, 13; hi-hat odd steps.
extend: Write a different bass ostinato for the B section.
Add a syncopated kick (on an “a” or “&”) and explain why it feels off the beat.
Print the Notate Song page and write the counts under every note.
access: Students who cannot use a mouse precisely can direct a partner step by step.
ELL students may use the step numbers and counting chart instead of written reflection.
Low-vision students can zoom the browser; the grid colors match each sound.

formative: Session 1 sticky note: snare step numbers and their beats.
Partner keep/try feedback is heard and used.
Counting check during Notate Song.
assessment.summative: Share link to a 4-measure Beat Machine song (Intro, A, A, B) posted to Google Classroom with one sentence explaining what changes in B and why.

levels: All four layers fit together and one layer shows a creative choice (syncopation, fill, call and response).
Backbeat, hi-hat subdivision, repeating bass ostinato and a 4+ note melody.
Groove is missing one layer or the backbeat is not on 2 and 4.
Two or fewer layers; no steady backbeat.
Clear Intro, matching A sections and a B that contrasts while still sounding related; explained in writing.
Four measures in Intro-A-A-B order with a clear change in B.
Four measures but sections are not clearly different or A sections do not match.
Fewer than four measures or no recognizable plan.
Counts every drum line in Notate Song with 1 e & a, including rests.
Counts one measure of the drum part accurately with 1 e & a.
Counts the beats (1 2 3 4) but not the subdivisions.
Cannot yet connect the notation to counts.

lessons.exitTicket: On a sticky note: “Step 13 is beat ___. My B section changes ___ because ___.”
tips: Teach the step-to-count map early: steps 1, 5, 9, 13 are beats 1, 2, 3, 4.
There is no copy button for measures: building measure 3 again is good practice in reading their own pattern.
Solo track is the fastest way to find which layer is clashing.
Use 16 steps for grades 4-6 so Notate Song shows sixteenths.

lessons.title: Word Rhythms: Type Your Name as a Beat
lessons.summary: Names and words become drum rhythms. Students clap and say a word first, then type it into Type Beat, learn that spaces are rests and CAPITALS are loud, use a “syllable code” to line words up with ta and ti-ti, and echo a partner’s beat.
objectives: say and clap the rhythm of names and words
type a word rhythm in Type Beat and use spaces as rests
use capital letters to make an accent (a loud sound)
turn a word’s syllables into ta / ti-ti using the 4-characters-per-beat code
echo a partner’s pattern by clapping
iCan: I can clap the rhythm of my name.
I can type a beat with rests and loud sounds.
I can echo my partner’s beat.

vocabulary.def: The pattern of long and short sounds.
One part of a word you say with one push of breath: Ma-ri-a has three.
A silence in music. In Type Beat, a space or a dot.
A note played louder than the others. In Type Beat, a CAPITAL letter.
Copying what you heard right after you hear it.

materials: Projector and speakers
Devices with keyboards (Chromebooks are ideal), headphones
[Type Beat](/typebeat/)
Word cards: names, foods, animals (pizza, apple, watermelon, tamale, dumpling, elephant)
prep: Open [Type Beat](/typebeat/) on the projector; set tempo near 100 and the Acoustic kit.
Write the syllable code on the board: **ta = k...**  **ti-ti = k.k.**  **shh = ....** (4 characters = 1 beat).
Prepare word cards with 1, 2 and 3 syllable words.

steps.do: Keep a steady pat. Each student says their name in rhythm on the beat; the class echoes and claps the syllables. Contrast one-sound names (“Juan”, clap once = ta) and two-sound names (“Ai-sha”, clap twice = ti-ti).
steps.say: Say it, then clap it. Every syllable gets a clap.
steps.check: Claps match syllables; pat stays steady.

steps.do: On the projector type “mr arthur” (one of the starters) and press Play. Then type a student’s name. Point out the colored blocks lighting up: every letter is a drum, the space is silence.
steps.say: Every letter is a drum sound. The space is a rest: the drums take a breath.
steps.check: Students notice the gap where the space is.

steps.do: Type “maria maria” then add more spaces: “maria   maria”. Ask what changed (a longer rest). Change to “Maria Maria” and then “MARIA”: capitals are louder (accents). Then show the syllable code: type k.k.k... (ti-ti ta) and clap it with the class. Type “pizza” as k.k. (piz-za = ti-ti) and “cake” as s... (ta).
steps.check: Students predict which version is louder or has the longer silence before you press Play.

steps.do: Task card: 1) Pick a word card, say it and clap it. 2) Type the word itself and listen. 3) Write it in syllable code (4 characters per beat), for example “wa-ter-mel-on” = k.k.k.k. and add a rest beat (....). 4) Make the first sound a CAPITAL accent. 5) Try two different letters (k = kick, s = snare, h = hi-hat). Students build a 4-beat pattern (16 characters).
steps.check: Patterns are 16 characters; the clapped rhythm matches what plays.

steps.do: Partner A plays their beat; partner B echoes it by clapping (loud claps for capitals). Then switch. Volunteers perform an echo for the class.
steps.check: Echoes keep rests silent and accents loud.

steps.do: Exit ticket on the board, answered by clapping or a thumbs signal.

support: Only use the word itself (no code); focus on spaces and capitals.
Give pre-written codes to copy: k.k.s... = ti-ti ta.
Pair with a strong typist.
extend: Make a 2-word pattern that is 8 beats (32 characters) and has a rest beat in each half.
Write the matching ta / ti-ti / shh under the code on paper.
Try the Latin kit and a different tempo and explain what changed.
access: Large-key or on-screen keyboard for students with motor needs; an adult may type what the student dictates.
Picture word cards for ELL and pre-readers.
Lower volume and headphones for sound-sensitive students.

formative: Name game: who claps the right number of syllables?
Predict-before-play questions on spaces and capitals.
Partner echo accuracy.
assessment.summative: Each student plays their 4-beat word beat for you and claps it back; it must include at least one rest and one CAPITAL accent. Students may paste the share link into the class assignment.

levels: Turns two words into code correctly and explains ta vs. ti-ti.
Says, claps and codes one word so the syllables match the beat.
Claps the syllables but the typed code does not match.
Cannot yet clap the syllables of a word.
Uses rests and accents on purpose to make the pattern interesting and can explain why.
Pattern includes at least one rest and one CAPITAL accent that can be heard.
Includes a rest or an accent, not both.
No rests or accents.
Echoes a partner’s pattern exactly, including accents and rests, first try.
Echoes the pattern with correct rests.
Echoes part of the pattern.
Cannot yet echo the pattern.

lessons.exitTicket: I play k.k.S... twice. Clap it back. Where was the loud sound?
tips: A Chromebook keyboard works best; tablets work but on-screen typing is slower.
4 characters = 1 beat, so the syllable code always lines up with 4/4.
If a beat sounds “too fast,” students usually typed letters with no dots; add dots to spread the sounds out.

lessons.title: Type Beat: Accents, Syncopation and Triplets
lessons.summary: In Type Beat one letter is a sixteenth note, so 16 characters make one 4/4 measure. Students build one-measure grooves, move accents from the beats to the off-beats to create syncopation, add ( ) triplets, set the tempo, and write the rhythm out in standard notation.
objectives: explain that one character is a sixteenth note and 16 characters fill a 4/4 measure
build a one-measure groove with kick, snare and hi-hat letters
compare accents on the beat with accents off the beat (syncopation)
use parentheses to create triplets and describe how they feel
write their groove in standard notation and count it
iCan: I can build a one-measure groove where every character is a sixteenth note.
I can create syncopation by accenting off-beats.
I can write my rhythm in standard notation and count it with 1 e & a.

vocabulary.def: One quarter of a beat; four fit in one beat (1 e & a).
A group of beats; in 4/4 there are four beats (16 sixteenths).
A note played louder; in Type Beat a CAPITAL letter.
Accenting a sound between the beats so the rhythm feels off-balance and exciting.
Three equal notes in the space usually taken by two.
How fast the beat is, in beats per minute (BPM).

materials: Projector and speakers
Devices with keyboards, headphones
[Type Beat](/typebeat/)
Grid worksheet: 16 boxes labeled 1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a, with a blank staff line underneath
Google Classroom assignment for share links
prep: Open [Type Beat](/typebeat/) on the projector; load the **Rock** starter (k.h.s.h.k.h.s.h.).
Draw the 16-box grid on the board with the counts on top.
Print one grid worksheet per student.

steps.do: Class counts sixteenths “1 e & a 2 e & a …” while patting. Then clap only on the numbers (accents on the beat). Then clap only on the “&”s (off-beats). Ask which felt more surprising.
steps.say: Accents on the numbers feel steady. Accents between the numbers feel syncopated.
steps.check: Off-beat claps stay between the pats.

steps.do: Play the Rock starter. Write its 16 characters into the board grid: k on 1 and 3, s on 2 and 4, h on the “&”s. Show k = kick, s = snare, h = hi-hat, dots = rests. Change one dot to h and hear the difference. Then load **Loud and quiet** (Kh.hSh.hKh.hSh.h) and point to the capitals on the beats.
steps.check: Students can say which count any character lands on.

steps.do: Move the accents: change capitals so they fall on the “&” or “a” (e.g. k.hHs.hHk.hHs.hH). Ask how it feels. Then load the **Triplets** starter ((k.h)(s.h)(k.h)(s.h)): three characters inside ( ) take the time of two. Show that (k.k.k.) fills one beat with three even hits: a beat-long triplet, “tri-po-let.” Change the tempo slider from 90 to 140 and back.
steps.say: Inside parentheses, three sounds squeeze into the space of two. That rolling feel is a triplet.
steps.check: Students can clap the triplet beat vs. two even eighths.

steps.do: Task card: 1) Groove A: exactly 16 characters, kick and snare on beats, accents ON the beat. 2) Groove B: copy A, then move at least two accents OFF the beat (syncopation). 3) Add one triplet group somewhere in B. 4) Pick a tempo and kit that fit. 5) Paste both share links into the assignment.
steps.check: Groove A is exactly 16 characters; Groove B has at least two off-beat capitals and one ( ) group.

steps.do: On the worksheet students write Groove A’s characters into the 16 boxes, then write the snare-and-kick rhythm on the staff line with quarter, eighth and sixteenth notes and rests, accent marks (>) where the capitals are, and the counts underneath.
steps.check: Note values add up to four beats; accent marks match capitals.

steps.do: Play 2-3 Groove A/B pairs. Class signals “on” (pat) or “off” (clap) for where they hear the accents. Exit ticket.

support: Start from the Rock starter and only change accents.
Skip triplets; focus on syncopation.
Provide a filled-in count grid to type from.
extend: Write a two-measure groove (32 characters) where measure 2 answers measure 1.
Notate the triplet group with a 3 bracket.
Use the Latin kit and research the clave pattern; type a 3-2 son clave.
access: Students may dictate letters to a partner who types.
Color-code the worksheet boxes by beat for visual processing.
ELL students can show understanding with the grid and claps instead of a written reflection.

formative: Warm-up: on-beat vs. off-beat clapping.
Quick questions: “Which count is character 7?” (the & of 2).
Check Groove A length (16) during work time.
assessment.summative: Two share links (Groove A on-beat, Groove B syncopated with a triplet) in Google Classroom plus the worksheet with Groove A written in standard notation and counted.

levels: Explains and shows how any character maps to 1 e & a, including inside triplets.
Groove A is exactly 16 characters and the student names the count for any character.
Groove is close to 16 characters or counts are partly correct.
Cannot yet connect characters to counts.
Groove B uses syncopation and a triplet musically, and the student explains the effect.
Groove B has at least two off-beat accents and one triplet group.
Has off-beat accents or a triplet, not both.
No difference between Groove A and B.
Notation is accurate including rests, accents and a triplet bracket.
Kick-and-snare rhythm is written accurately with accents and counts, adding up to four beats.
Notation has 1-2 errors in note values or counts.
Notation does not match the groove.

lessons.exitTicket: Write the count for character 7 and character 12 in a 16-character groove, and explain in one sentence what makes a rhythm syncopated.
tips: Have students type dots instead of spaces while learning: dots are easier to count.
Triplets confuse at first: clap “1-trip-let 2-trip-let” over a steady pat before typing.
The share link holds the beat, tempo and kit, so it is a complete record of the work.

lessons.title: Pattern Songs: Same, Different, AB and ABA
lessons.summary: Students hear and show same and different sections, then build AB and ABA songs in Sound Blocks by repeating a column of blocks (A) and changing it for B. They share their song with a link or QR code.
objectives: tell if two sections of music are the same or different
build an A section with a column of blocks and repeat it
build a contrasting B section
arrange sections into AB and ABA form and label them
iCan: I can hear when music is the same or different.
I can build an A section and a B section.
I can make an ABA song and show where the A comes back.

vocabulary.def: Sounds exactly like before.
Something changed.
A part of a song.
The order of the sections, like AB or ABA.
A part, a different part, then the first part comes back, like a sandwich.

materials: Projector and speakers
One device per student or pair, headphones
[Sound Blocks](/soundblocks/)
Letter cards A and B (two A cards)
Optional: teacher iPad to scan QR codes
prep: Open [Sound Blocks](/soundblocks/) on the projector and choose the **Playground** or **Sunny Day** world.
Pre-build a demo: measures 1-2 use one set of blocks (A), measures 3-4 a different set (B), measures 5-6 the same as 1-2 (A).
Put A, B, A cards on the board.

steps.do: Body-percussion patterns: pat-pat-clap-clap (A) then snap-snap-stomp-stomp (B). Perform A A, then A B. Students show thumbs together for same and thumbs apart for different. Then sing a short phrase twice the same, then change it.
steps.check: Thumbs match on every example.

steps.do: Play your pre-built ABA demo. Students pat during A and sway during B. Ask: did the first part come back? Hold up A B A cards as it plays.
steps.say: When the first part comes back, we call it A again. Bread, filling, bread: an ABA sandwich.
steps.check: Movement changes at measure 3 and changes back at measure 5.

steps.do: Clear a new song. Drag 2-3 blocks into the tracks of measures 1-2 (that column is A). Then put the very same blocks into measures 3-4 and play: AA, same. Change measures 3-4 to different blocks: now it is AB. Point to the columns so students *see* the same and different.
steps.check: Students call out “same” or “different” before you play.

steps.do: Task card with pictures: 1) Build A in measures 1-2. 2) Build B in measures 3-4 with different blocks. Play it: AB! 3) Copy A again into measures 5-6. Play it: ABA! 4) Bonus: add one fun sound at the end. Students click a measure’s top bar to start playback there and check each part.
steps.check: Measures 5-6 have the same blocks as 1-2; measures 3-4 look and sound different.

steps.do: Pairs trade devices: the listener holds up A or B cards as each section plays. Two or three songs on the projector (scan the QR code or open the share link). The class labels the form.
steps.check: Listeners label correctly.

steps.do: Exit ticket with body percussion. Students make a share link so you can collect it (or you scan the QR code).

support: Make only AB first; add the return of A with help.
Limit to two tracks.
Give a picture card showing which blocks go in A.
extend: Make ABAB or a rondo (ABACA) with the + button for more measures.
Make B contrast in a specific way (louder, fewer instruments).
Draw the form with shapes (circle-square-circle).
access: Tap-to-place works if dragging is hard.
Almost no words on screen: good for ELL and pre-readers.
Movement responses can be replaced with holding up A/B cards.

formative: Thumbs same/different in the warm-up.
Movement change during the ABA demo.
Quick look at each screen for the A columns.
assessment.summative: Each student’s ABA Sound Blocks song, shared by link or QR code, with the student pointing to the A, B and A sections while it plays.

levels: Labels every section correctly in a classmate’s song and explains what changed.
Shows same/different correctly in the warm-up and the demo.
Correct some of the time.
Not yet able to tell same from different.
ABA is clear and B contrasts in a planned way; may extend the form.
A in measures 1-2, different B in 3-4, the same A in 5-6.
Has AB but A does not come back, or A is not the same.
Blocks placed with no sections.
Points to each section as it plays and names the form without help.
Points to A, B and A as the song plays.
Points with help.
Does not yet identify sections.

lessons.exitTicket: Teacher performs pat-pat / snap-snap / pat-pat. Students hold up fingers: one for AB, two for ABA. Then they whisper “A-B-A.”
tips: Every block in a world shares the same key and tempo, so any choice sounds fine and students can focus on form.
Clicking a measure’s top bar starts playback there, which is perfect for checking a single section.
Songs autosave on the device; collect share links before devices change hands.

lessons.title: Mood Worlds: How Music Paints a Feeling
lessons.summary: Students listen to the Spooky, Sunny Day and Dreamy Sky worlds in Sound Blocks, describe each mood with music words (fast/slow, high/low, which instruments), then compose a short song for a scene from a picture book.
objectives: describe the mood of music with words like fast, slow, high, low, loud and soft
name an instrument or sound that helps make a mood
choose a world and blocks that fit a picture-book scene
explain why their music fits the scene
iCan: I can tell how music makes me feel and why.
I can use music words like fast, slow, high and low.
I can make music that fits a story picture.

vocabulary.def: The feeling music gives you.
How fast or slow the music is.
High sounds are like a bird; low sounds are like a bear.
Anything that makes the music sound: a piano, a drum, a bell.
Music and sounds that paint a picture of a place or a story.

materials: Projector and speakers
One device per student or pair, headphones
[Sound Blocks](/soundblocks/)
A picture book with clear scenes (a calm night, a storm, a party)
Mood word wall: fast / slow, high / low, loud / soft, happy / scary / calm
prep: Open [Sound Blocks](/soundblocks/) on the projector. Pre-build three short songs (2-3 blocks each): one in **Spooky** (slow, minor), one in **Sunny Day**, one in **Dreamy Sky** (slow and floaty).
Choose 3-4 picture-book pages and post them or have them ready to show.
Post the mood word wall.

steps.do: Play a steady drum or clap fast, then slow; high voice then low voice. Students move like a rabbit (fast), a turtle (slow), a bird (high), a bear (low).
steps.check: Movements change with the sound.

steps.do: Play the Spooky song, then Sunny Day, then Dreamy Sky, with eyes closed. After each, students show a face and then answer: fast or slow? high or low? what instrument did you hear? Record answers on a 3-column chart.
steps.say: Don’t just tell me it is scary. Tell me what the music did to make it scary.
steps.check: Answers use at least one music word (Spooky and Dreamy Sky are slower than Sunny Day).

steps.do: Show a picture-book page (for example a quiet night). Think aloud: slow or fast? Which world? Choose Dreamy Sky, drag in two blocks, play it, and change one block if it does not fit.
steps.say: Composers choose sounds on purpose. I picked slow and floaty because the picture is sleepy.

steps.do: Students pick one of the posted scenes, choose a world that fits, and fill at least 2 tracks across 4 measures. Optional: add an echo or reverb effect if it helps the mood. Partners guess which scene the song is for.
steps.check: World choice matches the scene; students can name one reason.

steps.do: Play 3-4 songs. The class guesses the scene. The composer finishes the sentence: “My music fits because it is ___ and ___.”
steps.check: Explanations use music words from the wall.

steps.do: Exit ticket.

support: Offer only two choices (Spooky or Sunny Day) and two scenes.
Use sentence frames with picture icons.
Kindergarten: build one song together on the projector instead of individually.
extend: Make the music change halfway, matching two pages of the book.
Write two sentences comparing two worlds with tempo and instrument words.
Try a world that was not modeled (Hero, Jungle) and describe it.
access: Picture cards for fast/slow/high/low support ELL and nonverbal students.
Students can point to the word wall instead of speaking.
Preview Spooky with anxious students and keep the volume low.

formative: Listening chart answers for each world.
Partner scene guesses.
assessment.summative: A short Sound Blocks scene song (share link or teacher QR scan) plus the student’s spoken or written explanation using at least two music words.

levels: Describes mood using three or more music words (tempo, pitch, instrument, dynamics).
Names the mood and gives one music reason (fast/slow, high/low or instrument).
Names the mood without a music reason.
Does not yet describe the mood.
World, blocks and an effect all match the scene, with a planned change.
World and blocks fit the scene across at least 4 measures.
Song does not clearly fit the scene.
Song not completed.
Explains choices clearly and compares with another world.
Completes “My music fits because…” with a music word.
Explains with help.
Does not yet explain.

lessons.exitTicket: Play 8 seconds of one world. Students hold up a card or say: happy, spooky or dreamy, plus one word (fast, slow, high or low).
tips: Dreamy Sky and Spooky are both slow (70 BPM); Sunny Day is faster (110 BPM). That makes a clear tempo comparison.
Eyes closed listening makes students focus on sound, not the colorful screen.
Kindergarten can do the listening and whole-class composing; grades 2-3 work independently.

lessons.title: Thin and Thick: Building Texture in Layers
lessons.summary: Students learn thin and thick texture by building a Sound Blocks song one layer at a time: start with one track, add a layer every measure or two, then take layers away for the ending. They balance tracks with the volume sliders and may add an effect or a voice block.
objectives: describe texture as thin (few sounds) or thick (many sounds)
build an intro that starts thin and grows by adding layers
create an ending by removing layers
balance tracks with the per-track volume slider
revise their song using partner feedback
iCan: I can hear if music is thin or thick.
I can build my song one layer at a time and take layers away for the ending.
I can make one part softer so another part can be heard.

vocabulary.def: How many sounds are playing at the same time.
Only one or two sounds playing.
Many sounds playing together.
One sound or part stacked on top of others.
The beginning of a song that gets us ready.
How the song finishes (sometimes called the coda).

materials: Projector and speakers
One device per student, headphones
[Sound Blocks](/soundblocks/)
Layer chart: 6 columns (measures) with stick figures added one at a time, then removed
prep: Open [Sound Blocks](/soundblocks/) on the projector in a world your class likes (Hip-Hop, Jungle or Hero).
Pre-build a demo: measure 1 = drums, 2 = + bass, 3 = + melody, 4 = + fun sound, 5 = drop melody, 6 = drums only.
If you plan to allow the voice block, check microphones on a few devices.

steps.do: Make a layered body-percussion piece. Group 1 pats a steady beat. Add group 2 clapping on 2 and 4, then group 3 saying “boom-chicka,” then group 4 snapping. Then remove groups one at a time until only the pat is left.
steps.say: One group is thin. All groups together is thick. Taking groups away makes an ending.
steps.check: Each group stays steady as others join.

steps.do: Play your demo. Students raise one more finger every time a layer is added and lower one when a layer leaves. Show the layer chart.
steps.check: Fingers go up 1-2-3-4 and back down.

steps.do: New song. Measure 1: one drum block. Measure 2: same drum + a bass block. Measure 3: add a melody. Play from the start. Show a volume slider: turn the drums down so the melody can be heard. Show one effect (echo or reverb).
steps.say: Each new layer should be easy to hear. If one is too loud, slide its volume down.

steps.do: Task card: 1) Start thin: 1 track in measure 1. 2) Add a layer in measures 2, 3 and 4 (thickest). 3) Take layers away in measures 5 and 6 for the ending. 4) Balance with the volume sliders. 5) Optional: one effect, or a voice block (record one measure of your voice after the 3-2-1 countdown; it stays on this device and is not in the share link).
steps.check: Measure 4 has the most tracks; measure 6 has the fewest.

steps.do: Partners listen and fill a 2-question card: Can I hear every layer arrive? Does the ending sound finished? Then each student makes one change.
steps.check: Every student changes at least one thing based on the feedback.

steps.do: Play 3 songs. Class counts layers with fingers. Collect share links or scan QR codes. Exit ticket.

support: Use 4 measures: 1, 2, 3 layers, then back to 1.
Give a picture plan to copy.
Skip effects and voice.
extend: Use the + button for 8-12 measures and add a thin B section in the middle.
Use volume slides to make a “fade out” ending.
Write two sentences describing the texture in each section.
access: Headphones with the volume set low; microphone use is optional.
Students who should not be recorded skip the voice block (it never leaves the device anyway).
Finger counting can be replaced with layer cards for students with motor needs.

formative: Finger counting during the demo.
Screen check: layers grow then shrink.
Partner feedback card.
assessment.summative: A 6-measure Sound Blocks song (share link or QR scan) that starts thin, builds to thick and thins out for an ending, plus the student’s one revision noted on the feedback card.

levels: Counts every layer in a classmate’s song and names each section thin or thick.
Shows layers arriving and leaving with fingers during the demo.
Notices some layer changes.
Does not yet hear layer changes.
Clear growth to a thick middle and a planned ending (e.g. fade or single-track finish), balanced volumes.
Starts with 1 track, adds layers to a thick middle, removes layers for the ending.
Layers added but no thinning ending, or order unclear.
All tracks start at once with no plan.
Makes a revision and explains how it improved the texture.
Makes one change based on partner feedback.
Listens to feedback but makes no change.
Does not take part in feedback.

lessons.exitTicket: Draw 6 boxes. Fill them with stick figures to show your song’s texture (thin, thicker, thickest, thinner, thin).
tips: Voice recordings stay on the device and are left out of share links: tell families this if they ask.
Click a measure’s top bar to start from the thickest part when checking balance.
The finger-counting game works with any music; reuse it in listening lessons.

lessons.title: Draw a Soundscape: Kandinsky and Sketch Studio
lessons.summary: Students draw a soundscape for a story, the weather or a place. In Kandinsky, lines become melodies, circles become singing voices and triangles become percussion; in Sketch Studio, the drawing tool and line thickness change the sound. Students perform their soundscape for the class.
objectives: explain that a soundscape uses sounds to paint a place, weather or story
show that higher lines make higher sounds and lower lines make lower sounds
choose lines, circles and triangles on purpose to show parts of a scene
perform their soundscape and tell what it shows
iCan: I can draw music that sounds like a place or the weather.
I can make high and low sounds by drawing high and low.
I can play my soundscape and tell what it shows.

vocabulary.def: Sounds that paint a picture of a place, the weather or a story.
A line of notes that goes up and down.
Sounds can be high like a bird or low like a bear.
Sounds you tap, shake or hit, like drums.

materials: Projector or interactive board, speakers
Devices for pairs (touch screens are great), headphones
[Chrome Music Lab EXTRA](/chromeextra/)
Scene cards: rainstorm, sunny park, ocean, a forest at night, a story the class just read
prep: Open [Chrome Music Lab EXTRA](/chromeextra/) and click **Kandinsky** in the top bar; try a line, a circle and a triangle so you know the sounds.
Optionally open **Sketch Studio** in a second tab and press Test Sound.
Choose a short story or weather scene to model with.

steps.do: Make a rainstorm with the class: rub hands (wind), snap (drops), pat legs (heavy rain), stomp (thunder), then back down to silence. Then use your voice: slide up high like a bird, down low like a bear.
steps.say: We just made a soundscape: sounds that paint the weather.
steps.check: Students follow your conducting from quiet to loud and back.

steps.do: On the projector, in Kandinsky, draw a line going up, then down, and press Play. Draw a circle: it becomes a singing face. Draw a triangle: it becomes a drum. Ask: where should I draw to make a high sound?
steps.check: Students predict that higher on the screen = higher sound.

steps.do: Show the rainstorm card. Think aloud: little triangles for raindrops, a long low line for the wind, a circle for a frog singing. Play it. Ask the class what they hear. Use Undo to fix a shape.
steps.say: I chose triangles for the rain because rain taps. What would you choose for thunder?

steps.do: Pairs pick a scene card. Task: use at least one line (melody), one circle (voice) and one triangle (percussion), and be ready to say what each one shows. Grades 1-2 may try Sketch Studio instead: choose a medium (crayon, chalk, watercolor) and draw thick lines for loud and thin lines for soft. Press Clear only if both partners agree.
steps.check: Drawings include all three shapes; students can name what each shape stands for.

steps.do: Pairs play their soundscape on the projector (or bring the device up). The class guesses the scene, then the pair tells what each shape shows.
steps.check: Classmates can guess the scene from the sound.

steps.do: Exit ticket with hands.

support: Use one scene for the whole class (rainstorm).
Limit to lines only, focusing on high and low.
Adult or buddy helps hold the device steady for drawing.
extend: Make the soundscape tell a 3-part story (calm, storm, calm).
In Sketch Studio, compare Step and Glide and choose the one that fits.
Download a PNG of the drawing in Sketch Studio and write one sentence on it.
access: Touch screens and interactive boards help students with fine-motor needs; finger drawing is fine.
Picture scene cards for ELL and pre-readers.
Kandinsky has very few words, so it works well for newcomers.

formative: High/low predictions during the hook.
Shape-meaning check while circulating.
assessment.summative: Each pair performs its soundscape for the class and tells what each shape shows; the teacher notes it on a checklist (or saves a Sketch Studio PNG).

levels: Draws on purpose to show rising and falling sounds and explains why.
Draws higher for high sounds and lower for low sounds.
Sometimes matches high and low.
Does not yet connect drawing height and pitch.
Every shape is chosen to show a part of the scene, and the scene changes over time.
Uses a line, a circle and a triangle that each fit the scene.
Uses shapes, but they do not clearly fit the scene.
Random drawing with no connection to the scene.
Performs and explains each shape clearly; classmates guess the scene.
Performs and names what at least two shapes show.
Performs with help.
Does not yet perform.

lessons.exitTicket: Show me with your hand: where do you draw a high sound? A low sound? What shape makes a drum sound?
tips: Press any button first if there is no sound: browsers wake up audio only after a click.
Load the “Composition VIII Symphony” sample artwork as an inspiring hook if time allows.
Nothing saves in Kandinsky; take a photo of student work for your records.

lessons.title: Strong and Weak Beats: Meter with the Rhythm Experiment
lessons.summary: Students feel strong and weak beats, compare 3/4 (pat-clap-clap) with 4/4 (pat-clap-clap-clap), and build their own patterns in the Rhythm experiment of Chrome Music Lab EXTRA, with 5/4 as a bonus challenge.
objectives: feel and show the strong first beat of a measure
tell the difference between music in 3 and music in 4 by moving
read the meters 3/4 and 4/4 as “3 beats in a group” and “4 beats in a group”
build a rhythm pattern that shows the strong beat in a chosen meter
iCan: I can find the strong beat.
I can move in 3 and in 4.
I can build a rhythm pattern in 3/4 or 4/4.

vocabulary.def: The first beat of a group; it feels heavier.
The lighter beats after the strong one.
How beats are grouped: in 2s, 3s or 4s.
One group of beats.
The top number tells how many beats are in each measure.

materials: Projector and speakers
Devices for pairs, headphones
[Chrome Music Lab EXTRA](/chromeextra/), Rhythm tab
Large cards: 3/4 and 4/4 (and 5/4 for the bonus)
prep: Open [Chrome Music Lab EXTRA](/chromeextra/), click **Rhythm**. Learn the scenes: Monkeys = 3/4, Monsters = 4/4, Robots = 5/4, Birds = 6/4 (use the arrows or the meter dots).
Notice each beat is shown as two steps, so 3/4 has 6 steps and 4/4 has 8.
Pick a known song in 3 (“Oh, My Darling Clementine” or “Down in the Valley”) and one in 4 (“This Old Man” or “Yankee Doodle”).

steps.do: Sing a song in 4 and pat the steady beat. Then make beat 1 a big pat on the legs and the others light claps: pat-clap-clap-clap. Then sing a song in 3: pat-clap-clap.
steps.say: The pat is the strong beat. It starts every group.
steps.check: Pats land together on beat 1.

steps.do: On the projector play the Monkeys scene (3/4), then the Monsters scene (4/4). Students do pat-clap-clap or pat-clap-clap-clap along. Ask which one is in 3. Hold up the 3/4 and 4/4 cards.
steps.check: Students switch their pattern to match the scene.

steps.do: In the Monkeys scene press Clear. Count the steps: each beat has two. Put the low timpani on the very first step only (strong beat). Add the triangle on beats 2 and 3 (steps 3 and 5). Play it and pat-clap-clap. Then try moving the low sound to beat 2 and ask why it feels strange.
steps.say: The low, heavy sound on beat 1 tells our bodies where the group starts.
steps.check: Class hears and moves to the strong beat.

steps.do: Task card: 1) Monkeys (3/4): heavy sound on beat 1, light sounds on beats 2 and 3. 2) Monsters (4/4): bass tom on beat 1 (and 3 if you like), snare on 2 and 4, hi-hat on every beat. 3) Partner test: play one without telling which; partner moves pat-clap-clap or pat-clap-clap-clap and names the meter. Bonus: Robots (5/4), count 1-2-3-4-5 and try pat-clap-clap-pat-clap.
steps.check: Partners name the meter correctly by moving.

steps.do: Pairs play a pattern on the projector while the class moves and holds up the 3/4 or 4/4 card. Change the tempo slider to show that meter stays the same at any speed.
steps.check: Cards match the scene.

steps.do: Exit ticket.

support: Use only Monkeys vs. Monsters with the default patterns; focus on moving.
Color the strong-beat step on a printed grid.
Say “BIG small small” instead of counting.
extend: Explore 5/4 and 6/4 and explain how they group.
Write the 3/4 pattern on paper with ta and shh, barlines and the time signature.
Listen to a waltz and a march and name the meter.
access: Students can show meter by tapping a desk or a partner’s shoulder instead of moving.
Number the steps on the projector for visual learners.
ELL students can respond with the meter cards.

formative: Warm-up pat-clap patterns.
Partner meter test during practice.
assessment.summative: Each pair demonstrates a 3/4 pattern and a 4/4 pattern they built, and each student identifies the meter of an unknown example by moving and holding up the right card.

levels: Shows the strong beat in 3, 4 and 5 without help.
Shows the strong beat in 3 and 4 with pat-clap patterns.
Shows the steady beat but not the strong beat.
Not yet keeping a steady beat.
Names the meter of new music and explains how they knew.
Names 3/4 or 4/4 correctly for the Rhythm scenes.
Correct sometimes.
Cannot yet tell 3 from 4.
Builds 3/4, 4/4 and the 5/4 bonus with clear strong beats.
Builds a 3/4 and a 4/4 pattern with the heavy sound on beat 1.
Builds one pattern, or the strong beat is not on beat 1.
Pattern does not show a meter.

lessons.exitTicket: Play one scene. Students move pat-clap-clap or pat-clap-clap-clap, then hold up the 3/4 or 4/4 card.
tips: Each beat is two steps in the Rhythm grid: beat 1 = step 1, beat 2 = step 3, and so on.
Reset brings back the scene’s original pattern if a pair gets lost.
Moving first, then seeing, then building makes meter stick.

lessons.title: Scale Mood Lab: One Melody, Four Scales
lessons.summary: Students compose a 4-bar melody in Song Maker, then hear the same melody shape in Major, Natural Minor, Pentatonic and Blues scales and describe how the scale changes the mood. They use Invert and Reverse as composer tools, choose a final version and share the link.
objectives: compose a 4-bar melody with a clear ending in Song Maker
compare how Major, Natural Minor, Pentatonic and Blues scales change the mood of the same melody
use Invert and Reverse to develop a melodic idea
choose a final scale and explain the expressive reason
iCan: I can compose a 4-bar melody that ends in a finished way.
I can explain how changing the scale changes the mood.
I can use invert and reverse like a composer to develop my idea.

vocabulary.def: The set of notes a melody uses, in order from low to high.
A scale that often sounds bright or happy.
A scale that often sounds darker, sad or serious.
A five-note scale used in folk music around the world.
A scale with “blue notes” from African American blues traditions.
Flip a melody upside down: up becomes down.
Play a melody backwards.

materials: Projector and speakers
One device per student, headphones
[Chrome Music Lab EXTRA](/chromeextra/), Song Maker tab
Listening chart: 4 rows (Major, Minor, Pentatonic, Blues) × columns for mood words and why
Google Classroom assignment for share links
prep: Open [Chrome Music Lab EXTRA](/chromeextra/) and click **Song Maker**. In settings (Grid & Scale Settings) set Length 4 bars, 4 beats, Scale Major, Start Note C; press Apply Settings.
Compose a short demo melody that starts and ends on the lowest C.
Practice: changing the Scale in settings keeps your notes in the same rows, so the melody shape stays and the notes change.
Find **Invert Melody** and **Reverse Song** in the Magic tools.

steps.do: Sing “Frère Jacques” in major, then in minor (lower mi, la and ti). Students show thumbs up/down for the mood and describe the difference.
steps.say: Same tune, same rhythm, different scale. Listen to what changes.
steps.check: Students notice the minor version sounds darker.

steps.do: Play your demo in Major. Open settings, change Scale to Natural Minor, Apply, and play again. Repeat with Pentatonic and Blues. Students fill the listening chart with a mood word and a reason (darker, jazzy, folk-like, bright).
steps.check: Charts include a mood and a music reason for each scale.

steps.do: Clear and compose 2 bars live: start on C, mostly steps with one leap, a rhythm with long and short notes. Show Invert Melody (upside down) and Reverse Song (backwards) and talk about when composers use them (Bach, Schoenberg, film composers). Use Undo to go back. Build bars 3-4 from the inverted or reversed idea and end on C.
steps.say: A composer does not throw an idea away. They flip it, reverse it and see what is useful.

steps.do: Task card: 1) Compose bars 1-2 in Major. 2) Make bars 3-4 by developing bars 1-2 (try Invert or Reverse, then edit). 3) End on the home note (lowest C). 4) Play it in all four scales and choose the one that best fits a mood you pick (a mystery, a celebration, a lonely walk, a jazz club). 5) Add drums if you like. 6) Make Share Link and post it with one sentence: “I chose ___ scale because ___.”
steps.check: Melody is 4 bars, ends on C, shows a developed idea; the reflection names a scale and a musical reason.

steps.do: Play 3-4 melodies. Before the composer reveals the mood, the class guesses the scale and the mood. Discuss: did the scale alone create the mood, or also tempo and rhythm?
steps.check: Guesses use scale and mood vocabulary.

steps.do: Exit ticket.

support: Start from the Ode to Joy preset and only change the scale.
Use 2 bars instead of 4.
Provide a word bank for moods.
extend: Try Dorian and describe how it differs from Minor.
Change the Start Note and explain why the mood stays the same.
Export MIDI and open it in Staff Composer to see it in notation.
access: Turn on note names on the grid (the labels button) for students who need them.
Students may record the reflection orally.
Use headphones and limit to two scale comparisons for students who tire with listening.

formative: Listening chart entries for all four scales.
Circulate: is the melody 4 bars and does it end on C?
Class scale-and-mood guesses.
assessment.summative: Song Maker share link to a 4-bar melody in the chosen scale, posted to Google Classroom with a sentence explaining the scale choice and how Invert or Reverse was used.

levels: 4 bars with a clear shape, varied rhythm and a strong ending; development is clearly heard.
4 bars that end on the home note and use Invert or Reverse to build bars 3-4.
Melody is incomplete or does not end on the home note.
Notes placed without a phrase or ending.
Compares all four scales with precise vocabulary and connects to musical traditions.
Describes how each scale changes the mood with a music reason.
Names moods but gives no reasons.
Cannot yet describe a difference.
Chosen scale, tempo and drums all support the mood, explained clearly.
States a scale choice and a clear expressive reason.
States a choice with a vague reason (“it sounds good”).
No reflection.

lessons.exitTicket: Write: “If I wanted a melody to sound mysterious, I would choose the ___ scale because ___.”
tips: Changing the scale keeps notes in the same rows, so the melody shape stays the same: perfect for fair comparisons.
Have students compose in Major first; minor and blues can feel strange when composing from scratch.
A share link only matches the song at the moment it was made: remind students to make it after their final change.

lessons.title: Keyboard Map: Find C, D and E
lessons.summary: Students discover the pattern of black keys (groups of 2 and 3), use it to find C, D and E, play Hot Cross Buns with the song guide, and echo short 3-note patterns by ear. Works with USB MIDI keyboards, computer keys or the on-screen keys.
objectives: identify groups of 2 and 3 black keys on a piano keyboard
find and name C, D and E using the group of 2 black keys
perform Hot Cross Buns (E D C) with a steady beat
echo 2-4 note patterns using C, D and E by ear
iCan: I can find the groups of 2 and 3 black keys.
I can find C, D and E by looking for the 2 black keys.
I can play Hot Cross Buns on the keyboard.
I can listen to 3 notes and play them back.

vocabulary.def: An instrument with white and black keys in a pattern that repeats.
The black keys come in groups of 2 and groups of 3. They are our map.
The white key just to the left of the 2 black keys.
Moving to the very next white key, up or down.
Playing back exactly what you just heard.

materials: Projector with [MIDI MUSIC](/midimusic/) open
One device per student or pair (Chromebook, laptop or iPad)
USB MIDI keyboards if you have them (optional: computer keys and on-screen keys work too)
Headphones (one per student, or a splitter for pairs)
A paper keyboard strip or drawing of a keyboard on the board
prep: Plug MIDI keyboards in **before** opening the page; on iPads, plan on the on-screen keys (iPads have no Web MIDI).
Open [Find C, D and E](/midimusic/?challenge=find-cde) on the projector and test sound.
Have [Hot Cross Buns](/midimusic/?song=buns) and [Echo Me: 3 Notes](/midimusic/?challenge=echo-3) ready in tabs.
Draw a big keyboard on the board with the black keys only (no letters yet).

steps.do: Sing Hot Cross Buns as an echo song: teacher sings each phrase, class echoes. Show high-middle-low with hands (shoulders, belly, knees) for E-D-C (mi-re-do).
steps.say: Our song walks down the stairs: high, middle, low. Show me with your hands.
steps.check: Hands move down on each “hot-cross-buns.”

steps.do: Point to the board keyboard. Students count the black keys in each group aloud: 2, 3, 2, 3. Circle the 2-groups in one color and the 3-groups in another. Have students “play” the groups on their desks: two fingers, then three fingers.
steps.say: The black keys are a map. Two, three, two, three. Find the twins and the triplets!

steps.do: On the projector, press keys under the 2 black keys and name them: C is just left of the 2 black keys, D is in the middle, E is on the right. Start [Find C, D and E](/midimusic/?challenge=find-cde) and solve the first rounds together, students calling out where to press.
steps.check: Students point to the key left of the 2 black keys before you press it.

steps.do: Students open [Find C, D and E](/midimusic/?challenge=find-cde) and earn stars (8 rounds). Early finishers try it on a different C (higher or lower on the keyboard). Then everyone opens [Hot Cross Buns](/midimusic/?song=buns): the song guide lights up the next key. Play it with the guide, then try singing while playing.
steps.check: Fingers find E-D-C without searching; the student can show you their stars.

steps.do: Open [Echo Me: 3 Notes](/midimusic/?challenge=echo-3). Model one round on the projector: listen with hands in lap, then play it back. Students then play on their own with headphones. Task card: 1) Listen first. 2) Sing it back on loo. 3) Play it.
steps.say: Ears first, hands second. Sing it in your head, then play.

steps.do: Two or three volunteers play Hot Cross Buns for the class (projected keyboard or their own device turned up). The class keeps a quiet steady beat on their laps. Ask the audience: Did it go high-middle-low? Was the beat steady?
steps.check: Audience uses the criteria: right keys, steady beat.

steps.do: Exit ticket on the paper keyboard: students write C, D and E on the right keys and circle one group of 3 black keys.

support: Put small stickers on C, D and E of physical keyboards, or turn on note names on screen.
Partner a student who finds C quickly with one who needs more time; they take turns.
Stay with Hot Cross Buns and Find C, D and E only; skip Echo Me.
extend: Try [All the White Keys](/midimusic/?challenge=find-white) or [Echo Me: 5 Notes](/midimusic/?challenge=echo-5).
Play Hot Cross Buns starting on a different C, or try [Mary Had a Little Lamb](/midimusic/?song=mary) (also E D C).
access: On-screen keys work with touch or a mouse; computer keys work for students who prefer typing.
Use visual cues (colored hands, a picture keyboard) for ELLs; the challenge text is short and pictured.
Students who cannot use headphones can play with the volume low or sit next to the teacher.

formative: Can the student point to C, D and E on a fresh part of the keyboard with no labels?
Stars on Find C, D and E (students show their star screen).
Listen to Echo Me: does the student match 2-3 note patterns?
assessment.summative: Each student plays Hot Cross Buns for the teacher (or a partner with a checklist) with correct keys and a steady beat; record the result on a class checklist.

levels: Finds C, D and E instantly on any part of the keyboard and explains the 2-black-key rule.
Finds C, D and E correctly using the group of 2 black keys.
Finds C but mixes up D and E, or needs labels.
Cannot yet find C without help.
Plays all of it with correct keys and a steady beat, and sings along.
Plays all of it with correct keys and a mostly steady beat.
Plays most notes correctly but stops or loses the beat.
Plays only parts of the song with the guide’s help.
Echoes 4-note patterns correctly on the first try.
Echoes 3-note patterns correctly most of the time.
Echoes 2-note patterns; longer ones are mixed up.
Plays notes but does not match the pattern yet.

lessons.exitTicket: On a paper keyboard: write C, D and E on the right white keys and circle one group of 3 black keys.
tips: If no sound comes from the MIDI keyboard, plug it in and reload the page. If MIDI is blocked, click the lock next to the web address and allow MIDI devices.
Stars are saved per device: if students share Chromebooks, have them show stars before logging off.
Hot Cross Buns is a traditional English street-cry song: ask students what songs people sing to sell things today (ice cream trucks, markets).

lessons.title: Partners at the Keyboard: Ostinato, Harmony and Answer
lessons.summary: Partners make music together: one keeps a repeating ostinato while the other improvises, they play melody and harmony at the same time, and they trade musical questions and answers. Works in Duet mode with two MIDI keyboards, or with partners sharing one keyboard.
objectives: perform a steady ostinato while a partner improvises
improvise a short solo using C, D, E, G and A over an ostinato
play a harmony part 3 notes above or below a melody, together in time
create a musical answer that ends on C (home)
iCan: I can keep an ostinato steady while my partner solos.
I can make up a solo with the pentatonic notes C D E G A.
I can play a harmony part in time with my partner’s melody.
I can answer a musical question and end on home (C).

vocabulary.def: A short musical pattern that repeats over and over.
Make up music on the spot.
A second part that sounds at the same time as the melody and fits with it.
A 5-note scale (here C, D, E, G, A) where almost any combination sounds good.
Two short phrases: the question sounds unfinished, the answer sounds finished (it ends on home).
The note that feels like the end. In C major it is C.

materials: Projector with [MIDI MUSIC](/midimusic/) open
One device per pair; one or two USB MIDI keyboards per pair (or on-screen/computer keys)
Headphones with a splitter per pair (or speakers at low volume)
Task card on the board: Ostinato → Harmony → Question & Answer
prep: Decide your setup. **Duet and the Partners challenges need 2 MIDI keyboards plugged into one device** (the app says “Duet needs 2 MIDI keyboards”). If you have only one keyboard per pair, use the one-keyboard version in each step.
Plug keyboards in before opening the page. Test [Duet mode](/midimusic/?duet) on one station: each keyboard gets its own sound.

Open [Ostinato + Solo](/midimusic/?challenge=ost-pop), [Harmony: Hot Cross Buns](/midimusic/?challenge=harm-buns), [Harmony: Ode to Joy](/midimusic/?challenge=harm-ode) and [Question & Answer](/midimusic/?challenge=qa) in tabs on the projector.
Write the riff C-G-A-G (low) on the board for one-keyboard pairs.

steps.do: Half the class pats a body-percussion ostinato (pat-pat-clap-rest) while the teacher improvises a vocal or clapped solo on top. Switch: half the class keeps the ostinato, the other half improvises 4 beats each, one at a time.
steps.say: An ostinato is the floor of the house. If the floor moves, the house falls down. Keep it steady!
steps.check: The ostinato group does not speed up when the soloist plays.

steps.do: Project [Ostinato + Solo](/midimusic/?challenge=ost-pop). Model with a student: one learns the riff C3-G3-A3-G3 (it is shown and practiced twice), then keeps it going over the pop groove while the other improvises on the glowing keys (C D E G A). Then switch. **One-keyboard version:** Player 1 plays the riff on the low C-G-A-G keys with the left hand side of the keyboard; Player 2 solos on C D E G A higher up on the same keyboard, standing side by side.
steps.check: Riff player stays with the groove; soloist uses only the glowing keys.

steps.do: Pairs play Ostinato + Solo at least twice, switching roles. Fast pairs try [Minor Groove + Solo](/midimusic/?challenge=ost-minor) and talk about how the mood changes.
steps.say: Soloists: try short ideas with rests. Space makes a solo sound like talking.

steps.do: Project [Harmony: Hot Cross Buns](/midimusic/?challenge=harm-buns). The melody is E-D-C; the harmony is G-F-E, 3 notes higher. Play it with a volunteer, then pairs play it, swapping parts. Next, [Harmony: Ode to Joy](/midimusic/?challenge=harm-ode), where the harmony is 3 notes lower. **One-keyboard version:** open the [Hot Cross Buns song guide](/midimusic/?song=buns); Player 1 follows the lit melody keys while Player 2 plays the same rhythm 2 white keys higher (G-F-E) on the same keyboard; then switch.
steps.check: Both parts start together and stay together; students can say which part is higher.

steps.do: Project [Question & Answer](/midimusic/?challenge=qa) and play it through with a volunteer: Player 1 asks (ends up high, unfinished), Player 2 answers and lands on C. Then pairs make up their **own** 4-beat question and answer: the question may end anywhere but C, the answer must end on C. **One-keyboard version:** take turns on the same keyboard. Task card: 1) Question = 4 beats, does not end on C. 2) Answer = 4 beats, ends on C. 3) Play it twice the same way.
steps.say: A question sounds like it wants more. An answer sounds like you can stop.

steps.do: Three pairs perform their question and answer (or ostinato + solo) for the class. Audience gives one “glow” (what worked) using the words ostinato, harmony, steady or home.
steps.check: Answers end on C; audience feedback uses music vocabulary.

steps.do: Exit ticket (written).

support: Let the stronger partner learn the ostinato first; the other solos on only 3 keys (C D E).
For harmony, play only the first phrase (hot cross buns) twice.
Lower the challenge pressure: practice in free play before starting the scored challenge.
extend: Try [Boogie Bass + Blues Solo](/midimusic/?challenge=ost-boogie) or [Band: Chords + Solo](/midimusic/?challenge=partner-chords).
Write the pair’s question and answer in letter names or on the staff.
Make a longer piece: ostinato intro, question-answer twice, ostinato ending.
access: On-screen keys and computer keys work for one player while the other uses a MIDI keyboard.
Allow a student to be the “conductor” who cues starts and switches if playing is difficult.
Give ELLs the vocabulary with icons: 🔁 ostinato, 🎵 harmony, ❓/❗ question and answer.

formative: Watch the ostinato player during the solo: does the riff stay steady and in time with the groove?
Listen to harmony pairs: do both parts move together?
Check each pair’s answer phrase ends on C.
assessment.summative: Each pair performs one of: Ostinato + Solo, a harmony part, or their own question and answer for the class or the teacher; score with the rubric on a class checklist.

levels: Keeps the riff steady and in time for the whole solo and can switch to soloing smoothly.
Keeps the riff steady with at most one small slip.
Keeps the riff going but speeds up or stops more than once.
Cannot yet keep the riff going while a partner plays.
Plays the harmony or melody part correctly, starts together and listens to stay together.
Plays the part correctly and mostly together with the partner.
Plays the right notes but drifts apart from the partner.
Plays only some of the part with help.
Solo uses the given notes, has repeated ideas and rests; the answer clearly lands on C.
Solo stays on the given notes; the answer ends on C.
Solo wanders off the given notes or the answer does not end on C.
Plays random notes without a clear idea or ending.

lessons.exitTicket: Explain in one sentence the difference between an ostinato and a solo. Then write which note makes an answer sound finished in C major.
tips: Two keyboards on one Chromebook: the app says “Two keyboards! Press Duet” when it sees them. Press 👥 Duet so each player gets their own sound.
Splitters let pairs hear each other with headphones; otherwise keep the volume at about a third.
Teach the switch signal (teacher raises two fingers) before the first pair activity so roles change without stopping the music.

lessons.title: Chords and the 12-Bar Blues
lessons.summary: Students build C, F and G triads, play the 12-bar blues progression with a swing groove, then improvise with the blues scale over it. Along the way they learn where the blues came from and why it matters to American music.
objectives: build C, F and G major triads (root, 3rd, 5th) on the keyboard
perform the 12-bar blues chord progression in time with a groove
improvise a blues solo with C, E♭, F, G and B♭
describe the origins of the blues in African American communities and its influence on later styles
iCan: I can build C, F and G chords by skipping keys: root, 3rd, 5th.
I can play the 12-bar blues chords in time.
I can improvise a blues solo using the blues scale.
I can explain where the blues came from and what it means to the people who made it.

vocabulary.def: Three or more notes played together. A triad is root, 3rd and 5th (play a key, skip a key, play a key, skip, play).
The note a chord is named after and built on.
An order of chords that repeats under a song.
A 12-measure chord pattern using I, IV and V (C, F, G in C).
Notes with a “bluesy” sound; here C, E♭, F, G, B♭.
A long-short, bouncy feel for pairs of 8th notes.
One voice or instrument calls, another answers; a key part of the blues.

materials: Projector with [MIDI MUSIC](/midimusic/) and speakers
One device per student or pair, MIDI keyboards if available (on-screen/computer keys work)
Headphones
Chart of the 12 bars on the board: C C C C | F F C C | G F C G
A recording of a traditional blues (e.g. a field recording or early blues from the Library of Congress) to play for the class
prep: Test [Build C, F and G](/midimusic/?challenge=chord-cfg), [12-Bar Blues](/midimusic/?challenge=blues) and [Blues Solo](/midimusic/?challenge=jam-blues) on the projector.
Draw the 12-bar grid on the board in 3 rows of 4 bars, chords labeled C (I), F (IV), G (V).
Choose a short blues listening example and a 2-3 sentence background (work songs, spirituals, field hollers, Mississippi Delta, the Great Migration to cities like Chicago).

steps.do: Sing a call-and-response: teacher sings a short bluesy line (“I woke up this morning…”), class answers with a set response. Snap on beats 2 and 4 with a swing feel.
steps.say: In the blues, the music talks back. Call, then response.

steps.do: On the projector, show a triad: play a key, skip, play, skip, play. Build C (C-E-G), F (F-A-C) and G (G-B-D). Then open [Build C, F and G](/midimusic/?challenge=chord-cfg) and solve two rounds together.
steps.check: Students can say which keys are in each chord.

steps.do: Students play Build C, F and G (6 rounds) for stars. Early finishers try [Major Chords](/midimusic/?challenge=chord-major) with no glowing keys.
steps.check: All three keys pressed together, held until the next chord.

steps.do: Point to the board grid and count the bars aloud with the class (one-two-three-four for each bar). Open [12-Bar Blues](/midimusic/?challenge=blues): the swing groove plays at 110 BPM and the keys glow. Model one time through, then students practice. Partners can check each other with the board grid: point to each bar as it goes by.
steps.say: Twelve bars, three chords. Four bars of home, two of F, two of home, then G, F, home, and G sends us back to the top.
steps.check: Chord changes happen on the first beat of the bar.

steps.do: Students write the 12-bar pattern from memory in a 3×4 grid (C/F/G or I/IV/V).

Play the blues listening example. Share the background: the blues grew from African American work songs, spirituals and field hollers in the Southern US, especially the Mississippi Delta, and traveled north to cities like Chicago. It shaped jazz, rock, R&B and hip-hop. Ask: What feelings does the blues express? Why might people sing about hard times?
steps.check: Students name at least one role of the blues (telling stories, sharing hard times, community, dancing).

steps.do: Open [Blues Solo](/midimusic/?challenge=jam-blues): the glowing keys are C, E♭, F, G, B♭ over a swing groove for 40 seconds. Model a solo built from one short riff repeated and changed, with rests between ideas (call and response with yourself).
steps.say: Pick one idea, play it, rest, play it again a little different. That is how blues players talk.

steps.do: Students practice Blues Solo several times. Task card: 1) Start with a riff of 3-5 notes. 2) Repeat it, then change one thing. 3) Leave rests. 4) End on C. Pairs then combine: one plays the [12-Bar Blues](/midimusic/?challenge=blues) chords while the other improvises in free play with the same 5 notes (with two keyboards use [Duet mode](/midimusic/?duet); with one keyboard, chords low and solo high on the same keyboard). Switch.
steps.check: Solos use the 5 blues notes, repeat an idea and leave space.

steps.do: Four or five students or pairs perform a 12-bar chorus. The class gives feedback using the task card criteria. Close with a written reflection.
steps.check: Feedback mentions riff, rests, chords or swing.

support: Play only the root (one note) of each chord in the 12-bar pattern, then add the full triad.
Solo with only 3 blues notes (C, E♭, G) at first.
Point along the 12-bar grid for the student while they play.
extend: Try [Boogie Bass + Blues Solo](/midimusic/?challenge=ost-boogie) with a partner.
Add a 7th to each chord (B♭ on C, E♭ on F, F on G) and describe the change in sound.
Write a 3-line blues lyric (AAB form) and sing it over the progression.
access: On-screen keys allow mouse play for students with limited fine motor control; let them play roots only.
Provide a picture grid of the 12 bars with color-coded chords (C blue, F green, G orange).
Give ELLs sentence frames: “The blues began… It was used for…”.

formative: Stars on Build C, F and G and 12-Bar Blues (students show their star screen).
Board-grid check: can the student point to where the music is in the 12 bars?
Listen to Blues Solo attempts for riffs, rests and an ending on C.
assessment.summative: Each student or pair performs one 12-bar chorus (chords, solo, or both) for the class, and writes 3-4 sentences on where the blues came from and what it meant to the people who created it; collect the writing in Google Classroom or on paper.

levels: Plays all 12 bars with full triads, changing on beat 1 every time, without looking at the grid.
Plays all 12 bars with correct triads and changes mostly on time.
Plays the right chords but loses the place in the 12 bars.
Builds chords only with glowing keys and cannot yet follow the progression.
Solo develops a riff (repeat and change), uses rests, swings and ends on C.
Solo stays on the blues notes, repeats an idea and ends on C.
Solo uses the blues notes but has no repeated idea or clear ending.
Plays random notes or stops after a few seconds.
Explains the blues’ roots (work songs, spirituals, African American communities in the South), its role, and names a later style it influenced.
Describes where and by whom the blues began and one role it played.
Names one fact about the blues but not its role or meaning.
Cannot yet describe where the blues came from.

lessons.exitTicket: Session 2: Write one sentence about where the blues came from and one thing you did in your solo that made it sound like the blues.
tips: Blues Solo is scored on time and staying on the allowed notes; praise musical choices too (repeats, rests).
If students rush the chords, have them say the chord names aloud while playing.
Choose listening examples that are school-appropriate; many early field recordings and traditional blues are in the public domain and on the Library of Congress site.

lessons.title: Loop It! Building a Class Body-Percussion Ostinato
lessons.summary: The class builds a layered loop together on the projector: a beat keeper, a rhythm pattern and a word chant, each recorded on top of the last. Then small groups make their own 3-layer loop and perform it by muting and unmuting.
objectives: perform a steady beat and a rhythm ostinato with body percussion and voice
record a loop layer that lines up with the loops already playing
describe how adding and removing layers changes the music (thicker and thinner texture)
follow the teacher’s cues to start, stop, mute and unmute
iCan: I can keep a steady beat with my body.
I can say it, then loop it: practice my pattern, then record it.
I can add a layer that fits with the loops already playing.
I can watch for the cue to start and stop.

vocabulary.def: A short piece of music that repeats over and over.
One part stacked on top of other parts.
A pattern that repeats again and again.
The steady pulse, like a heartbeat.
Turn a layer off without erasing it.
How many layers we hear: thin (few) or thick (many).

materials: Projector, speakers and a microphone (built-in laptop mic is fine) with [Looper](/looper/)
For groups: one device per group of 3-4, headphones (with splitter if possible)
Rhythm cards on the board in ta / ti-ti / shh (e.g. ta ta ti-ti ta)
A short chant, e.g. “Bounce high, bounce low” or a class-made line
prep: Open [Looper](/looper/) on the teacher computer and allow the microphone.

Run **Sound check** once on each device (in Beat & setup): it plays clicks through the **speakers** and listens with the mic, so do it with speakers on (headphones will not work for the check). After that, record with headphones on.
In Beat & setup, set the metronome with a one-bar count-in at a comfortable tempo (about 90-100 BPM).
Write the 3 layer roles on the board: 1) Beat keeper (pat), 2) Rhythm (clap), 3) Word chant (voice).

steps.do: Teacher pats a steady beat; class echoes 4-beat patterns in ta and ti-ti with pats, claps, snaps and stamps. Then build a live “human loop”: group 1 pats the beat, group 2 adds the clapped rhythm, group 3 adds the chant. Point to a group to stop and start (live muting).
steps.say: When I point at you, freeze. When I point again, come back in right on the beat.
steps.check: Groups re-enter on the beat.

steps.do: Ask: What if one person could be all three groups? Show the 24 loop slots on the projector and explain: the first loop sets the length, and every new loop snaps to it.

Layer 1: the class pats the beat for 1-2 bars while you record loop 1 after the count-in, then stop: it repeats. Layer 2: select a new slot, record the clapped rhythm from the board (say it, then loop it). Layer 3: record the word chant. Show **mute** on each layer, **undo** for a mistake, and the volume slider.
steps.say: Say it first, then loop it. Practice once with the loop, then I will record.
steps.check: New layers line up with the beat; students can name each layer’s job.

steps.do: Mute and unmute layers in different orders. Students show thin texture (hands close together) or thick texture (hands far apart).
steps.check: Students’ hands match the number of layers playing.

steps.do: Groups of 3-4 at one device with headphones. Task card: 1) Each person picks a role: beat keeper, rhythm, word chant (and a 4th: a sound effect). 2) Say it, then loop it. 3) Record loop 1 (beat keeper) first, then add one layer at a time. 4) Practice a start-to-finish: add layers one by one, then mute them one by one.
steps.check: Every group member records one layer; loop 1 is a steady beat.

steps.do: Two groups play their loop on speakers, building up layer by layer and muting down to silence. Audience: What layers did you hear? When was it thickest?
Exit ticket: draw the loop as stacked boxes (one box per layer) and label each one.

support: Give groups pre-made rhythm cards to choose from instead of inventing.
Teacher or an aide records loop 1 for a group so they can focus on adding layers.
Use only 2 layers (beat + chant).
extend: Add a 4th layer: a sung sol-mi-la pattern or a sound effect.
Try a drum groove from Beat & setup under the body-percussion loops.
Plan an ending: mute layers in reverse order and stop together.
access: Students who prefer not to use their voice can be beat keepers, play a classroom instrument, or press record and mute.
Use picture role cards (hand = pat, clap icon, mouth = chant) for ELLs and pre-readers.
If a student is sensitive to loud sound, keep volume low and offer the “mute boss” job.

formative: During the warm-up, does each group keep the beat and re-enter on cue?
Do group layers line up with loop 1 when played back?
Can students say which layer is the beat keeper?
assessment.summative: Each group performs its 3-layer loop for the class, building up and muting down on cue; the teacher scores each student on a checklist (steady part, recorded a layer, followed cues).

levels: Performs and records a part that is steady and matches the beat every time it repeats.
Records a part that is mostly steady and lines up with the loop.
Part speeds up or slows down so it does not line up with the loop.
Cannot yet perform a repeating pattern without help.
Explains each layer’s role and suggests the order to add them.
Adds a layer that fits the loop and names its role.
Adds a layer but it clashes or the student cannot say what it does.
Does not add a layer.
Mutes, unmutes and re-enters exactly on the cue and helps the group stay together.
Follows start, stop and mute cues correctly.
Follows cues late or needs reminders.
Does not follow cues yet.

lessons.exitTicket: Draw our loop as a stack of boxes, one box per layer, and label each box (beat, rhythm, chant). Circle the layer that started first.
tips: If a recording sounds early or late, run Sound check again on that device with speakers on.
With the microphone near the speakers, earlier loops leak into new recordings; headphones fix this.
Recordings stay on the device. Use Save to keep a session on that device; nothing is uploaded.

lessons.title: Build Up, Break Down: A Layered Loop Composition
lessons.summary: Groups compose a layered loop piece with a planned form: an intro, a build-up, a peak, a breakdown and an ending. They mix with volume and pan, add one effect, and perform it live by muting and unmuting loops.
objectives: plan a form for a loop piece (intro, build-up, peak, breakdown, ending) on a form map
record 4-6 loops that fit together rhythmically and have clear roles
use volume, pan and one effect to balance and shape the mix
perform the piece live by muting and unmuting loops according to the plan
iCan: I can plan the form of a loop piece and follow it when we perform.
I can record a loop that fits with the others.
I can use volume, pan and an effect to make the mix clear.
I can explain how our form builds and releases energy.

vocabulary.def: The plan or order of sections in a piece of music.
Adding layers one at a time so the music grows.
Removing layers so the music gets thinner, often before the ending.
How many layers are sounding and how they combine.
Where a sound sits between the left and right speakers.
Balancing the volume, pan and effects of all the layers.
A change to the sound, such as Echo, Big Room, Underwater or Crunchy.

materials: Projector with [Looper](/looper/) and speakers
One device per group of 3-4, headphones (splitters help), a quiet corner per group if possible
Form map worksheet: a grid with sections across (Intro, Build, Peak, Breakdown, Ending) and loops down; students shade where each loop plays
Optional: small percussion instruments or found sounds
prep: On each device, run **Sound check** (Beat & setup) once with speakers on (headphones don’t work for the check); then use headphones for recording.
Prepare a 4-loop demo on your computer (beat, bass voice, melody, sound effect) to model muting a form.
Print or project the form map. Decide a theme option list (e.g. a storm, a city morning, a game level, a celebration) for groups who want a story.

steps.do: Conducted body-percussion piece: four groups each have an ostinato. Teacher conducts a build-up (add groups), peak (all), breakdown (drop groups) and ending. Ask: What made the peak exciting? What did the breakdown do?
steps.check: Students name that energy rose with more layers.

steps.do: Play your 4-loop demo, muting and unmuting to show a form: intro (beat only), build (add bass, then melody), peak (all + sound effect), breakdown (melody alone), ending (stop together). Show volume, the left/right pan drag, one effect (try Echo on the melody), and Undo. Fill in the form map for your demo on the board.
steps.say: Your loops are the ingredients. The form is the recipe: when each one comes in and goes out.

steps.do: Groups choose a theme (or pure music), assign roles (beat keeper, bass voice, melody/chant, sound effect, mixer) and sketch their form map. Rules: loop 1 is a steady beat; 4-6 loops total; one effect only; the peak must have the most layers.
steps.check: Each form map has 5 sections and every loop has a role.

steps.do: Groups record their loops: practice each part with the loop playing, then record (say it, then loop it). Use the beat or a drum groove from Beat & setup with count-in. Later loops may be 2× or 4× long for melodies. Use **Save** at the end so the session stays on the device.
steps.check: Loops line up; nobody records over the beat keeper by accident.

steps.do: Each group writes which loops are finished and what is left, on the back of the form map.

Groups open their saved session. Mixer job: set volume so the beat and melody are clear, pan two loops apart (one left, one right), add one effect where it supports the theme. Listen with all loops on, then with one off at a time.
steps.check: No loop covers the others; pan and effect choices can be explained.

steps.do: Groups rehearse the performance following their form map: one student cues sections, others mute/unmute. Rehearse at least twice the same way. Optional: export a WAV of the full mix.
steps.say: A performance is a plan you can repeat. Run it twice the same way.

steps.do: Each group performs on the speakers (about 1 minute) and shows its form map. Audience gives feedback with the criteria: clear build-up and peak, balanced mix, effect that fits, ending planned. Each student writes one glow and one grow for another group.
steps.check: Critique cites a specific section or layer.

steps.do: Individual reflection: How did your group’s form build and release energy? What would you change?

support: Give a ready-made form map (4 loops, fixed order) and let the group fill in the sounds.
Use a drum groove from Beat & setup as the beat layer so nobody has to record loop 1 first.
Limit to 3 loops and a simple build-up/ending.
extend: Add a contrasting B section by switching to a different set of loops, then return (ABA).
Write the rhythm of each loop in standard notation on the form map.
