Try a second effect on a different loop and compare which version expresses the theme better.
access: Roles let every student contribute: mixer, conductor, recorder, or performer on a classroom instrument.
Provide a visual form map with icons (🌱 build, 🔥 peak, 🌙 breakdown, 🛑 end) for ELLs.
Large on-screen buttons and keyboard shortcuts (Space, R, M, U) help students with motor needs.

formative: Check form maps after the planning step (5 sections, roles assigned).
Listen to loops at the end of Session 1: do they line up and fit?
Watch rehearsal: are mute/unmute moves on the beat and in the planned order?
assessment.summative: Group performance of the loop piece following the form map, plus each student’s written reflection; collect form maps and reflections (and the optional WAV) in Google Classroom.

levels: Performance follows a clear, planned form with a strong build-up, an obvious peak, a breakdown and a planned ending; students explain why.
Performance follows the form map with build-up, peak, breakdown and ending.
Some sections are clear but the peak or ending is missing or unplanned.
Loops play without a recognizable plan.
All loops line up, have distinct roles, and volume, pan and effect make every layer clear and support the theme.
Loops line up and the mix is balanced; one effect is used.
Loops mostly line up, but one layer covers others or the effect distracts.
Loops do not line up or are hard to hear.
Mutes and unmutes exactly on the beat, responds to the cue-giver, and recovers smoothly from mistakes.
Follows the plan with most changes on time.
Changes are late or out of order more than once.
Cannot yet perform the piece in order.

lessons.exitTicket: Draw a line graph of your piece’s energy from start to finish and label the build-up, peak, breakdown and ending.
tips: The WAV export includes volume, pan and mute but **not** effects; tell students before they export.
Sessions are saved on the device only: keep groups on the same device between sessions.
Keep the master loop short (one or two bars); it is capped at 12 seconds.

lessons.title: Song Form in the Studio: Intro, Verse, Chorus, Outro
lessons.summary: Students learn the Studio DAW with its built-in 7-step tutorial, then arrange loops into a full song form (Intro–Verse–Chorus–Verse–Chorus–Outro), marking each section on the timeline and sharing a link.
objectives: identify intro, verse, chorus and outro in a familiar song by listening
use the loop library to add, extend and duplicate loops on the timeline
arrange loops into Intro–Verse–Chorus–Verse–Chorus–Outro with contrast between verse and chorus
mark each section on the timeline and document the form on a form map
iCan: I can hear the difference between a verse and a chorus.
I can add, stretch and duplicate loops in the Studio DAW.
I can arrange my song into intro, verse, chorus and outro.
I can explain how my chorus is different from my verse.

vocabulary.def: The order of sections in a song.
The beginning that sets the mood before the main part.
A section that usually changes words each time; often calmer.
The repeated, catchy section with the most energy.
The ending section.
A short recording that repeats; in the DAW it follows the song’s tempo and key.
The area where you place clips in order from left to right.

materials: Projector with [Studio DAW](/?app=daw) and speakers
One Chromebook or laptop per student (plugged in), headphones
A school-appropriate song with a clear verse/chorus (any familiar class song)
Form map: six boxes in a row: Intro | Verse | Chorus | Verse | Chorus | Outro
prep: Open [Studio DAW](/?app=daw) and run through the 7-step tutorial yourself.
Make a short demo song with three sections so you can show the difference between verse and chorus loops.
Check that students are signed in to the class account if you want projects saved there (they also save on the device).
Decide where share links go (e.g. a Google Classroom assignment).

steps.do: Play a familiar song. Students show a flat hand for the verse and hands up for the chorus. Map the form on the board as they hear it.
steps.check: Hands change at the chorus.

steps.do: On the start screen, choose a template (e.g. Pop Song) or Empty Song, then show where the Loop Library is, the timeline, play (Space) and the tutorial.
steps.say: Today you learn the studio. Next time you become the producer.

steps.do: Students do the built-in **7-step tutorial**: find a drum loop, add it to the song, press play, add more layers (bass, keys or guitar), make it longer by dragging the edge or Ctrl+D, add an effect, and save. Circulate; students who finish help a neighbor.
steps.check: Each student has at least 3 tracks and has saved.

steps.do: Students search the library by instrument, genre and mood. They choose two groups of loops: calm ones for a verse and bigger ones for a chorus. Loops follow the song tempo and key, so they fit.
steps.check: Students can name one verse loop and one chorus loop.

steps.do: Students write on the form map which instruments will play in the verse and which in the chorus. Save (Ctrl+S).

On the projector, arrange a short version: Intro (2 layers), Verse (3-4 layers), Chorus (all layers + one new one). Right-click an empty spot of the timeline at the start of each section and choose **Add marker here**; markers are numbered (Section 1, 2, …), so write which number is which on the form map. Duplicate a section with Ctrl+D.
steps.say: Contrast makes a chorus feel like a chorus: add something, take something away, or change the energy.

steps.do: Students arrange Intro–Verse–Chorus–Verse–Chorus–Outro (about 1-2 minutes). Task card: 1) Each section is at least 4 bars. 2) The chorus has more energy than the verse. 3) The intro and outro are thinner. 4) A marker at each section. 5) Save, then use **Share** to copy a link.
steps.check: Sections are visible on the timeline; verse and chorus clearly differ.

steps.do: Three or four students play their song; the class raises hands when they hear the chorus arrive. Students post their share link and write two sentences: How is your chorus different from your verse? Where did you put the most layers?
steps.check: Listeners spot the chorus by ear.

support: Start from a template (Pop Song or Lo-Fi Hip-Hop) so the verse layers already exist.
Shorter form: Intro–Verse–Chorus–Outro.
Give a printed checklist of the 7 tutorial steps.
extend: Add a bridge with completely different loops before the last chorus.
Use automation or an effect to make a build into the chorus.
Record a short spoken or sung hook in the chorus with the microphone.
access: Keyboard shortcuts (Space, Ctrl+D, Ctrl+S) reduce dragging for students with motor needs.
Loop library filters use icons and short words; pair ELLs with a buddy for the search.
Plug Chromebooks in during DAW work; older devices may lag with many tracks, so cap at 6 tracks.

formative: Tutorial completion: each student has 3+ tracks, an effect and a saved project.
Listening warm-up: can students identify verse vs chorus?
Look at the timeline: are sections marked and in the right order?
assessment.summative: A 1-2 minute song in Intro–Verse–Chorus–Verse–Chorus–Outro form, submitted as a share link in Google Classroom with the form map and a two-sentence explanation of the contrast between verse and chorus.

levels: All six sections are present, marked and balanced in length; the form is easy to hear and an extra section (bridge) may be added.
All six sections are present in order and marked on the timeline.
Some sections are missing, out of order or not marked.
Loops are placed without a recognizable form.
Verse and chorus differ in several ways (layers, instruments, energy) and the intro/outro frame the song.
The chorus clearly has more energy or different layers than the verse.
Verse and chorus sound almost the same.
No difference between sections.
Uses library filters, duplicate, markers and an effect efficiently and saves and shares without help.
Adds, extends and duplicates loops, adds markers, saves and shares.
Needs help to extend loops, add markers or share.
Cannot yet place loops on the timeline without help.

lessons.exitTicket: Session 2: Write the form of your song using letters or words (Intro, Verse, Chorus…) and one sentence about how your chorus stands out.
tips: Have every student complete the built-in tutorial in session 1; it saves a lot of help requests later.
Teach form first and let the loops do the harmony; the piano roll comes in the next lesson.
Share links open as a credited remix, so classmates can listen and build on each other’s songs.

lessons.title: Chords, Bass and Groove in the Piano Roll
lessons.summary: Students compose their own harmony: the I–V–vi–IV progression with the piano roll’s Chord tool in the song key, a bass line on the chord roots and a drum-grid groove. They arpeggiate chords and compare swing and humanize by ear.
objectives: build the I–V–vi–IV progression in a song key using the Chord tool
write a bass line that plays the root of each chord
program a drum groove on the drum grid
compare versions with and without arpeggiate, swing and humanize and describe the difference in music words
iCan: I can build a I–V–vi–IV chord progression in my song’s key.
I can write a bass line on the roots of my chords.
I can program a drum beat on the grid.
I can explain how swing and humanize change the feel.

vocabulary.def: The home note and scale a song uses, e.g. C major.
Chord numbers from the scale: I is built on note 1, V on note 5, vi on note 6 (minor), IV on note 4.
The note a chord is named after; the bass usually plays it.
The notes of a chord played one at a time.
Pushing every other note a little late for a bouncy, shuffled feel.
Tiny random changes in timing and loudness so it sounds played by a person.
The repeating rhythm feel that makes you want to move.

materials: Projector with [Studio DAW](/?app=daw) and speakers
One Chromebook or laptop per student (plugged in), headphones
Board chart: In C major, I = C, V = G, vi = Am, IV = F
Optional: [MIDI MUSIC Pop Song Chords](/midimusic/?challenge=pop-axis) to hear and play the same progression
prep: In [Studio DAW](/?app=daw), start an Empty Song and set the song key to C major in the transport bar; make a 4-bar demo with chords, bass and drums.
Find the Chord tool, Arpeggiate, Swing and Humanize controls in the piano roll toolbar so you can point to them.
Write the I–V–vi–IV chart on the board with note names for C major.

steps.do: Sing the roots C–G–A–F on “doo” while the teacher plays the four chords. Students show the chord number with fingers (1, 5, 6, 4).
steps.check: Fingers change with the chords.

steps.do: In an Empty Song, set the key (C major). Add an instrument track (piano or keys), create a MIDI clip and open the piano roll. Choose **Chord (3 notes)** in the Chord tool and click once per bar: C, G, A (minor because of the key), F. Play it back.
steps.say: With a song key set, the Chord tool only uses notes from the key, so A becomes A minor automatically.

steps.do: Students build I–V–vi–IV (4 bars, one chord per bar) in a key they choose (C, G or F major; write the chord names first). Then add a bass instrument track and draw one low note per bar on each chord root. Loop and listen.
steps.check: Chord names match the key chart; bass notes match the chord roots.

steps.do: Pair-share: play your progression for a neighbor. Exit ticket: write your key and four chord names with Roman numerals. Save.

Model the drum grid (step sequencer, 16th-note steps): kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hat on every 8th. Students add a drum machine track and program their own groove, then change at least two steps to make it their own.
steps.check: Groove keeps a steady backbeat.

steps.do: Students duplicate their chord clip and use **Arpeggiate** on the copy. Then a listening test: play the clip with Swing at 0, then turned up; then Humanize at 0 and turned up. Students write which version they prefer for their song and why, using words like bouncy, straight, robotic, relaxed.
steps.say: Producers decide with their ears. Listen to both, then choose.

steps.do: Students build an 8-16 bar piece: chords (block or arpeggiated), bass, drums; optionally a melody. Save and Share the link. Two or three students play theirs; class names the chord numbers they hear.
steps.check: Final piece has chords, bass on roots and drums, and the student can explain one choice.

steps.do: Written reflection: Which setting did you choose (swing, humanize, arpeggio) and how does it change the feel?

support: Stay in C major and use the board chart; bass is just the root, one long note per bar.
Start from the Make a Beat template so drums are ready and focus on chords and bass.
Practice the progression first with [MIDI MUSIC Pop Song Chords](/midimusic/?challenge=pop-axis).
extend: Try the sad-pop order vi–IV–I–V or switch to a minor key.
Use 7th chords from the Chord tool and describe the color.
Write a melody using chord tones on the strong beats.
access: A MIDI keyboard or the on-screen keys can be used to play notes in instead of clicking.
Provide a color-coded chord chart (I, V, vi, IV in different colors) for ELLs and visual learners.
Reduce the number of tracks on older Chromebooks to avoid lag.

formative: Check each student’s written key and chord names against their piano roll.
Are bass notes on the chord roots?
Read the swing/humanize comparison notes for music vocabulary.
assessment.summative: An 8-16 bar piece with I–V–vi–IV chords, a root bass line and a drum groove, submitted as a share link with a short written explanation of the key, chords and one feel choice (swing, humanize or arpeggio).

levels: Correct I–V–vi–IV in the chosen key with a bass that plays roots and adds a passing note or rhythm.
Correct I–V–vi–IV in the chosen key with the bass on each root.
Progression or bass has one or two wrong chords or notes.
Chords and bass do not follow the progression.
Drum groove has a steady backbeat plus original variations that fit the style.
Drum groove has a steady backbeat with at least two personal changes.
Drum groove is uneven or clashes with the chords.
No drum groove.
Compares versions precisely (e.g. “swing makes the hi-hats long-short”) and justifies the choice for the song’s mood.
Describes how swing or humanize changes the feel and states a choice.
States a preference without describing the sound.
Does not compare versions.

lessons.exitTicket: Session 1: Write your song’s key and the four chords of I–V–vi–IV with letter names. Session 2: one sentence on what swing did to your groove.
tips: If chords sound wrong, check the song key in the transport bar; the Chord tool follows it.
Quantize clicked-in notes if students played them in with a keyboard.
This progression is in countless songs; challenge students to notice it on the radio, but keep class listening examples school-appropriate.

lessons.title: Score the Scene: Film Music and Foley
lessons.summary: Students score a short silent video clip or a story scene. They choose music for the mood, add sound effects and microphone Foley or voices (with the voice changer), shape everything with effects and mixing, and critique each other’s scores with class criteria.
objectives: choose tempo, key/mode, instruments and dynamics to match the mood of a scene
create sound effects and Foley with the microphone and loops and place them in sync with events
balance music, effects and voice with the mixer and effects
evaluate peers’ scores with agreed criteria, citing specific musical evidence
iCan: I can choose music that matches the mood of a scene.
I can record and place sound effects so they line up with what happens.
I can mix my score so the important sounds are clear.
I can give feedback using our criteria and music words.

vocabulary.def: Music written to go with a movie or scene.
The feeling the music creates (calm, tense, joyful, spooky).
Everyday sounds recorded to match actions on screen (footsteps, doors, rain).
Lining up a sound exactly with what happens on screen.
A short musical idea that stands for a character or idea.
Setting the volume and effects of each track so everything is clear.
Feedback that names what works and what could improve, with reasons.

materials: Projector with [Studio DAW](/?app=daw) and speakers
One Chromebook or laptop per student or pair (plugged in), **wired** headphones for recording

A short (30-60 second) silent video clip the school is allowed to use (e.g. a public-domain silent film excerpt or a student-made clip), as an MP4 or WebM file on each device or shared drive; OR a written/illustrated story scene
Foley objects: paper, keys, cups, a book, rice in a container
Critique sheet with the class criteria
prep: Pick the clip and check it plays: in the DAW, add a **video track** and load the file (MP4, WebM or MOV). Put the file where students can reach it (shared drive or downloaded to each device).
No video? Use the **Movie Soundtrack** or **Soundscape** start-screen template and a written scene with 3-4 events (e.g. a storm reaches a village; a lost robot finds a friend).
Make a cue sheet template: time | what happens | mood | sound/music idea.
Tell students that microphone recordings stay on their device; they are not uploaded.

steps.do: Play the clip (or read the scene) twice with two very different pieces of music: e.g. a calm Soundscape and a tense Movie Soundtrack loop. Ask: How did the music change what you felt or expected?
steps.check: Students name a musical element (tempo, instruments, major/minor, dynamics).

steps.do: Watch the clip again, pausing at key moments. Students fill a cue sheet: time, event, mood, music or sound idea. Agree the class criteria for a good score: matches mood, sounds in sync, clear mix, changes when the scene changes.

Add the video track (or open the Movie Soundtrack/Soundscape template). Search the Loop Library by **mood** for the opening; drag a loop under the first scene. Show tempo and key, and how loops follow them. Add a marker at each cue time.
steps.say: Score the feeling, not just the action. What should the audience feel right now?

steps.do: Students build the music for each section on their cue sheet, changing loops, instruments or dynamics when the mood changes. Save often (Ctrl+S).
steps.check: Music changes at least once at a cue point.

steps.do: Model recording on an audio track with count-in, wearing wired headphones; make footsteps or rain with objects. Students record 2-4 Foley sounds or a short voice line and drag them to line up with the picture. Try the **voice changer** (e.g. Robot) for a character. Recordings stay on the device.
steps.check: Sounds land on the right moment; recordings are clear.

steps.do: Add effects with presets (reverb for a big space, echo for a dream, filter for underwater). Open the mixer: set the music lower when voices or key sound effects happen. Watch the whole clip with sound and fix sync.
steps.say: The audience should hear the most important sound at every moment.

steps.do: Students write one cue they are proud of and one they still need to fix.

Gallery listen: students rotate to 2-3 other stations with headphones (or play scores on the projector). For each, complete the critique sheet: one strength and one suggestion per criterion, citing a time and a musical element (e.g. “At 0:20 the low strings made it tense”).
steps.check: Feedback names a time and an element.

steps.do: Students revise based on feedback, export the score as WAV/MP3 (share links leave microphone recordings silent, so export is the way to hand in Foley), and write an artist statement (3-4 sentences): what mood each section has and the musical choices that create it. Two or three scores are played for the class.

support: Start from the Movie Soundtrack template with loops already placed; students only change them at cue points.
Limit the clip to 30 seconds and 2-3 cues.
Provide a mood-to-music chart (tense = low, fast, minor; calm = slow, soft, major).
extend: Write a leitmotif for a character in the piano roll and bring it back changed (faster, minor, different instrument).
Use automation to fade music in and out at cues.
Compare their score with a professional film score and describe one technique they borrowed.
access: Students who don’t want to record their voice can use loops or Foley objects only, or a classmate’s voice with permission.
Use a visual storyboard instead of a video for students who need more time to process.
Sentence frames for critique (“At ___, the ___ made me feel ___ because ___.”) help ELLs.

formative: Cue sheet: does each event have a mood and a sound/music idea?
Check sync of 2 Foley sounds per student during Session 2.
Critique sheets cite a time and a musical element.
assessment.summative: The finished score as exported WAV/MP3 audio (share links play recordings silently), with the clip or scene named, plus the artist statement and the completed peer critique sheet, collected in Google Classroom.

levels: Music changes at every cue, and tempo, instruments, mode and dynamics clearly create each mood; the statement explains them with evidence.
Music matches the mood of each main section and changes when the scene changes.
Music fits some parts of the scene but not others.
Music does not relate to the scene.
Foley and voices are clear, land exactly on the action, and the mix always keeps the most important sound on top.
At least 2 sound effects line up with the action and the mix is balanced.
Sound effects are early/late or covered by the music.
No sound effects, or they are unrelated to the scene.
Gives specific, kind, useful feedback citing times and elements for every criterion, and revises own work from feedback.
Gives feedback on each criterion with at least one musical element named.
Feedback is general (“it was good”) with few music words.
Does not complete the critique.

lessons.exitTicket: Name one moment in your score, the mood you wanted, and the musical choice that creates it (tempo, instrument, dynamics, effect or sound).
tips: Use wired headphones for recording so the music does not leak into the microphone.
Microphone recordings stay on the device: keep students on the same device across sessions, and check before exporting whether a voice recording should be shared.
Only use video clips the school has the right to use; public-domain silent films and student-made clips are safe choices.

lessons.title: Sol, Mi and La: Singing with Hand Signs
lessons.summary: Students sing sol-mi, then add la, with Curwen hand signs. The projected Do-Re-Mi bells give the pitch for echo games and playground chants, and the class plays the Ear Training Do-Re-Mi level together.
objectives: sing sol and mi (and then la) in tune with a model
show sol, mi and la with Curwen hand signs while singing
echo short sol-mi-la patterns played on the bells
name the higher and lower sound in a two-note pattern
iCan: I can sing sol and mi like a cuckoo bird.
I can show sol, mi and la with my hand.
I can echo a bell pattern with my voice.

vocabulary.def: A singing name for a higher note. Hand flat, palm facing in.
A singing name for a lower note, under sol. Hand flat, palm down.
The note just above sol. Hand curved, palm down, like it is hanging.
Copy exactly what you hear.
A hand shape that shows which note we sing.

materials: Projector or board with the [Do-Re-Mi Trainer](/?app=solfege-trainer&focus=1) open
Speakers
Optional: a printed [Do-Re-Mi chart](/?app=solfege-trainer&focus=1) (Print button) for the board
Optional: real Boomwhackers or resonator bells in G, E and A
prep: Open the Do-Re-Mi Trainer on the projector and test the sound. Try the Cuckoo (Sol-Mi) button under Play Songs.
Know where the bells are: sol is bell 5, mi is bell 3, la is bell 6 (keys 5, 3, 6 on the keyboard).
Write SOL, MI, LA on the board as a ladder (la on top, sol, then mi with a gap below sol).
Choose two chants: Rain, Rain, Go Away (sol-mi-la) and See Saw (sol-mi).

steps.do: Unplugged: sing hello on sol-mi (Hel-lo, ev-ery-bo-dy). Students echo. Then play "high voice, low voice": slide up like a siren and down like a slide; reach up for high, touch knees for low.
steps.check: Every child moves voice and body up and down together.

steps.do: Press **Cuckoo (Sol-Mi)** on the projected trainer. Ask: Which bird is calling? Is the first sound higher or lower than the second?
steps.say: Listen to the cuckoo bird. Show me with your hand: is the first sound high or low?
steps.check: Hands go up for sol, down for mi.

steps.do: Tap bell 5 (sol) and bell 3 (mi). Teach the hand signs shown on each bell: sol palm facing in, mi flat palm down. Sing them back and forth with signs. Then add bell 6 (la) and its curved-hand sign above sol.
steps.say: Sol is a flat hand, mi lies flat below it. La hangs just above sol.
steps.check: Hand signs move at the right height: la highest, mi lowest.

steps.do: Echo game: tap a 3-4 note pattern (sol-mi, sol-sol-mi, sol-la-sol-mi). The class sings and signs it back. After a few, a student "bell captain" taps a pattern for the class to echo.
steps.check: Class echoes in tune and starts together after the pattern ends.

steps.do: Sing Rain, Rain, Go Away on sol-mi-la with hand signs, then See Saw on sol-mi. Tap the bells to give the starting pitch. Split the room: half sings words, half sings solfège. Mention that these are traditional children's chants sung on playgrounds in many countries, and ask if anyone knows a chant from home.
steps.check: Students switch from words to solfège without losing the pitches.

steps.do: Open the Ear Training Challenge and choose the **Do-Re-Mi** level. The trainer plays a note; students show the hand sign they think it is; a student helper taps the matching bell. Watch the points and streak grow as a class.
steps.say: Listen, sign it, then we check with the bells.
steps.check: Most hands show the correct sign before the helper taps.

steps.do: Sing goodbye on sol-mi-la. Exit ticket: teacher sings one note (sol, mi or la); each child shows its hand sign.

support: Start with sol-mi only for Kindergarten; add la in a later class.
Use body levels (head = la, shoulders = sol, waist = mi) instead of hand signs at first.
Give the starting pitch on the bells before every echo.
extend: Let strong singers lead the echo game as bell captains.
Add do from the Do-Re-Mi level and try Hot Cross Buns (mi-re-do) from Play Songs.
access: Students who cannot sign may point to the board ladder or the colored bell.
Bell colors help pre-readers and English learners; say the syllable and point to the color.
Turn the volume down for students sensitive to sound.

formative: Watch hand signs during the echo game: correct sign at the correct height?
Listen to small groups (one row at a time) sing sol-mi in tune.
Note Ear Training answers shown by hand before the helper taps.
assessment.summative: Each student sings and signs a 3-note sol-mi-la pattern back to the teacher (quiet one-on-one during the chant game); record on a class checklist.

levels: Sings sol, mi and la in tune in new patterns without help
Sings sol-mi-la patterns in tune when echoing
Matches sol and mi but la is out of tune
Speaks or sings on one pitch
Signs all three notes at the right height, even in new patterns
Signs sol, mi and la correctly while singing
Signs sol and mi correctly; la is missing or confused
Does not yet match a sign to a note
Names which note was played on the bells without a model
Tells which of two notes is higher
Tells high and low with a body or hand model
Does not yet tell high from low

lessons.exitTicket: Teacher sings one note on "loo". Students show the hand sign: sol, mi or la?
tips: Sing first, bells second: the trainer is the reference pitch, the children are the instrument.
The bells are in C major (sol = G). If that is too low for little voices, sing the patterns a step higher and use the bells only for the game.
Keep the echo patterns short (3-4 notes) and always start them on sol.

lessons.title: The Major Scale by Ear: Steps, Skips and the Triad
lessons.summary: Students sing the full major scale with hand signs, sort intervals into steps and skips, find the do-mi-sol triad, and use the Ear Training Triad and All 8 levels before taking down 4-note patterns in solfège.
objectives: sing the major scale up and down with Curwen hand signs
tell a step from a skip by ear and on the bell ladder
identify do, mi and sol as the tonic triad
write a 4-note solfège pattern they hear (melodic dictation)
iCan: I can sing the major scale with solfège and hand signs.
I can hear whether a melody moves by step or by skip.
I can write down a 4-note pattern I hear in solfège.

vocabulary.def: Eight notes going up by step: do re mi fa sol la ti do.
Moving to the very next note (do to re).
Jumping over a note (do to mi).
Three notes stacked in skips; do-mi-sol is the home triad.
The home note of the key: do.
Writing down music you hear.

materials: Projector with the [Do-Re-Mi Trainer](/?app=solfege-trainer&focus=1)
Printed Do-Re-Mi chart (Print button in the trainer), one per student or pair
Dictation sheet or whiteboards: 5 rows of 4 boxes
Optional: Chromebooks with headphones for partner ear training
prep: Print the Do-Re-Mi chart (syllables, note names, hand signs).
Write five 4-note dictation patterns for your key, starting on do, mi or sol: e.g. do-re-mi-do, mi-sol-mi-do, sol-fa-mi-re, do-mi-sol-do, sol-la-ti-do.
Draw a vertical scale ladder on the board.

steps.do: Unplugged: review sol-mi-la from earlier grades, then echo-sing short patterns with hand signs. Press **Full Scale** under Play Songs and sing along with signs.
steps.check: Fa and ti signs (thumbs down, index pointing up) are correct.

steps.do: On the projected bells, tap do-re (step) and do-mi (skip). Students show a flat hand sliding for a step and a hop for a skip. Tap ten 2-note pairs; the class shows step or skip.
steps.say: A step goes to the next bell. A skip jumps over one.
steps.check: Most students answer correctly without watching the screen.

steps.do: Tap do-mi-sol, then all three bells together (quickly in a row). Show that the triad is built from two skips. Sing do-mi-sol-mi-do with signs.
steps.say: Do, mi and sol are the home chord. Songs love to land on them.

steps.do: Open the Ear Training Challenge on the **Triad** level (do, mi, sol only). The class sings do first, then listens, signs, and a volunteer taps the answer. Then switch to **All 8** and repeat.
steps.check: Watch which notes cause mistakes (often fa/sol and ti/do).

steps.do: Sing or tap 4-note patterns on the bells (always give do first). Students write the syllables in their boxes (d r m f s l t d). Play each pattern three times. Check together on the projector after each one.
steps.check: Students write step patterns correctly; skips are the main challenge.

steps.do: Partners (on Chromebooks or one at the board) take turns: one taps a 4-note pattern starting on do, the other sings and writes it.
Students write: Which is easier to hear, a step or a skip? Why? Collect the dictation sheets.

support: Limit dictation to do-re-mi, or give the first note of each pattern.
Let students point to the printed chart instead of writing syllables.
Play each pattern a fourth time.
extend: Add letter names under the syllables (C major) using the printed chart.
Dictate 6-note patterns or patterns that start on high do.
Challenge: beat your class streak in All 8.
access: Large-print chart or chart taped to the desk.
Students may sign answers instead of writing.
Headphones for students who need a quieter space during partner work.

formative: Step/skip hand responses during the model.
Error pattern in Triad and All 8 levels (which notes get confused).
Dictation boxes checked after each pattern.
assessment.summative: Five-pattern dictation sheet (collected); score 1 point per correct syllable (20 total).

levels: 18-20 syllables correct, including skips
14-17 correct; steps always right
9-13 correct; mostly first notes and steps
8 or fewer correct
Labels steps and skips and names the skipped note
Identifies step or skip correctly most of the time
Identifies steps but confuses skips
Guesses
Sings scale and triad in tune with correct signs, up and down
Sings the scale up and down with correct signs
Sings the scale with some sign or pitch errors near fa and ti
Needs the bells to sing along

lessons.exitTicket: I play do-mi-sol-do. Write it in solfège and circle every skip.
tips: Always sing do before each dictation pattern so students have a home note.
If the class gets stuck on fa and ti, practise mi-fa and ti-do (the half steps) slowly.
The trainer does not save scores: snap a photo of a good class streak for the board.

lessons.title: Instrument Families: Blow, Buzz, Bow and Hit
lessons.summary: Students learn the four orchestra families by how their sound is made, act out each one, guess instruments from sound alone with the screen hidden, and sort picture cards into families.
objectives: name the four orchestra families: strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion
tell how each family makes sound: bow or pluck, blow, buzz, hit
recognize several instruments by sound alone
sort instrument pictures into the right family
iCan: I can name the four instrument families.
I can show how each family makes its sound.
I can guess an instrument just by listening.

vocabulary.def: Instruments you bow or pluck, like violin and cello.
Instruments you blow into, like flute and clarinet.
Shiny instruments you buzz your lips into, like trumpet and tuba.
Instruments you hit, shake or scrape, like drums and xylophone.
A group of instruments that make sound the same way.

materials: Projector with [Instrument Zoo](/?app=instrument-zoo&focus=1) and speakers
Picture cards of the instruments (one set per table; print or draw them)
Four family signs or hula hoops on the floor
Optional: real classroom instruments (recorder, drum, guitar or ukulele)
prep: Open Instrument Zoo and click through one card in each family to hear the note and the arpeggio.
Make picture cards for violin, cello, harp, flute, recorder, clarinet, trumpet, trombone, tuba, xylophone, timpani, marimba (photos or drawings).
Plan how to hide the screen: turn off the projector image (mute or freeze button) while the sound plays.

steps.do: Unplugged: "Body orchestra". Teach four motions: pretend to bow a violin, blow a flute, buzz lips into a trumpet, tap a drum. Call a family name; students show the motion.
steps.check: Every child shows the right motion for each family.

steps.do: Without showing the screen, play the Andean pan flute card. Ask: What is making this sound? How do you think it is played?
steps.say: Close your eyes. What could make that sound?

steps.do: Show the screen. Use the family filter to show one family at a time. For each family play two cards (note, then arpeggio), read the "Did you know?" fact aloud, and say how the sound is made: strings bow or pluck, woodwinds blow, brass buzz, percussion hit.
steps.say: Brass players buzz their lips like a bee. Woodwind players blow air.
steps.check: Students copy the motion as each family appears.

steps.do: Hide the screen. Play a card; students first show the family motion, then guess the instrument. Show the screen to check. Do 6-8 rounds, mixing families. Teams can keep score on the board.
steps.check: Most students get the family right even when they miss the exact instrument.

steps.do: Tables sort picture cards into four families (or children carry a card to the matching hoop). Ask each table to name one instrument and how it makes sound.
steps.check: Cards are in the right family; listen for "blow, buzz, bow, hit" words.

steps.do: Play a sound from a real classroom instrument (recorder, drum, ukulele). Which family? Point out that the ukulele and pan flute in the Zoo are World & popular instruments; ask where students have heard them.
Exit ticket: teacher plays one card with the screen hidden; students hold up 1-4 fingers for the family (1 strings, 2 woodwinds, 3 brass, 4 percussion).

support: Start with only two families (strings and percussion) for Kindergarten.
Put a picture next to each family motion on the board.
Let students point to a picture card instead of saying the name.
extend: Ask why the tuba sounds lower than the trumpet (bigger instrument, longer tube).
Grade 3: write one sentence per family describing its sound (warm, bright, booming, sparkly).
access: Real instruments to touch help visual and tactile learners.
Family motions let English learners answer without words.
Lower the volume for the brass and timpani cards for students sensitive to sound.

formative: Body orchestra motions match the family called.
Family guesses during the hidden-screen game.
Table sorts checked by the teacher.
assessment.summative: Picture-sort check: each student sorts 8 cards into four families and tells the teacher how one family makes sound (checklist).

levels: Names all four families and an instrument outside the Zoo for each
Names all four families with an example each
Names two or three families
Names one family or none
Explains blow, buzz, bow/pluck and hit and shows each
Shows or tells how each family makes sound
Knows how one or two families make sound
Does not yet connect families to sound making
Identifies the exact instrument by sound most of the time
Identifies the family by sound most of the time
Identifies the family sometimes, often guessing
Does not yet identify by sound

lessons.exitTicket: Listen with eyes closed: show 1, 2, 3 or 4 fingers for the family you hear.
tips: Instrument Zoo has no built-in quiz; hiding the projector image while a card plays turns it into one.
Invite a band student or band teacher to play live: it beats any recording.
Harp and guitar are plucked strings; xylophone and marimba are pitched percussion. Expect good questions.

lessons.title: Timbre Detectives: Range, Clef and the Carnival of the Animals
lessons.summary: Students compare instruments by timbre, range and clef, rank high to low within each family, learn about the ukulele and Andean pan flute in their cultures, and follow a listening map of Saint-Saëns' Carnival of the Animals.
objectives: describe timbre using specific words (bright, mellow, breathy, brassy)
compare range and clef of instruments within one family
explain where the ukulele and pan flute come from and what role they play in their cultures
identify featured instruments in movements of the Carnival of the Animals and explain the composer's choices
iCan: I can describe an instrument's timbre with music words.
I can order instruments in a family from highest to lowest and name their clef.
I can explain why a composer chose an instrument to portray an animal.

vocabulary.def: The tone color of a sound: what makes a flute sound different from a trumpet playing the same note.
The lowest to the highest note an instrument can play.
The sign at the start of the staff that tells which notes the lines and spaces are (treble, bass, alto).
A part of an instrument's range: low, middle or high.
A picture or chart that follows what happens in a piece of music.
A row of tubes of different lengths that you blow across; played in the Andes mountains of South America.

materials: Projector with [Instrument Zoo](/?app=instrument-zoo&focus=1)
A recording of Saint-Saëns, Carnival of the Animals (1886, public domain) that the teacher has access to: The Elephant, The Swan, Aviary, Fossils
Listening map worksheet: four boxes with title, "instrument I hear", "high/low", "why this animal?"
Family comparison chart: instrument, clef, range, timbre words
prep: Cue the four Carnival movements in your recording (each is 1-3 minutes).
Click each card in Instrument Zoo and note the clef and range it lists; fill in a teacher answer key for the comparison chart.
Post a timbre word bank: bright, dark, mellow, breathy, brassy, reedy, sparkly, booming, warm, thin.

steps.do: Unplugged: say the same sentence in a whisper, a robot voice and an opera voice. Same words, different tone color: that is timbre.

Filter Instrument Zoo to **Brass**. Play trumpet, French horn, trombone and tuba. Students order them highest to lowest and note the clef each card lists (treble vs bass). Repeat with **Strings** (violin, cello) and **Woodwinds** (flute, clarinet, oboe).
steps.say: Bigger instrument, longer tube or string, lower sound. Does the clef agree?
steps.check: Students connect bass clef with the low instruments.

steps.do: Hide the screen. Play oboe, then clarinet, then flute (similar range). Students write two timbre words for each from the word bank. Reveal and discuss which words fit best.
steps.check: Students use specific words, not just "nice" or "loud".

steps.do: Show the **World & popular** cards: ukulele and Andean pan flute. Read each "Did you know?" fact. Discuss: the ukulele grew from small Portuguese guitars brought to Hawaiʻi and became a symbol of Hawaiian music; the pan flute (siku/zampoña) is played in Andean communities in Peru and Bolivia, often in pairs that trade notes. If your class plays ukulele or recorder, perform a short folk song and talk about its home culture.
steps.say: Instruments carry stories about the people who play them.

steps.do: Play The Elephant, The Swan, Aviary and Fossils (play the recording you have). Students fill one box per movement: featured instrument, high or low, and why it fits the animal. Answers: double bass (low, heavy elephant), cello (smooth, gliding swan), flute (high, fluttering birds), xylophone (clattering bones).
steps.check: Students explain choices with range or timbre, e.g. "low and slow like a heavy elephant".

steps.do: Written reflection: If you wrote a Carnival movement for your favorite animal, which Instrument Zoo instrument would play it? Give a range reason and a timbre reason. Two volunteers play their chosen card for the class.

support: Give the listening map with instrument choices to circle.
Pair students and limit the comparison chart to one family.
Allow drawing the animal and labeling high/low instead of full sentences.
extend: Compare the Swan in cello with the same melody played on violin (play both Zoo cards): how does the timbre change the mood?
Research another Andean or Pacific instrument and present one fact.
access: Word bank on the desk; sentence frame: "The ___ sounds ___ because ___."
Captions or picture cues for each Carnival movement title.
Lower volume or headphones for students sensitive to sound.

formative: High-to-low order and clef notes during the family comparison.
Quality of timbre words in the hidden-screen round.
Listening map boxes checked during the music.
assessment.summative: Completed listening map plus the "my own Carnival animal" reflection, collected (or posted to Google Classroom as a photo).

levels: Uses precise timbre words and correct range/clef terms throughout
Uses timbre words and range terms correctly most of the time
Uses a few music words, some vague ("good sound")
Does not yet use music words
Identifies all four instruments and explains each with range and timbre
Identifies three or four instruments with a reason
Identifies one or two instruments; reasons are vague
Does not identify the instruments
Explains origin and role of both world instruments and links to another culture they know
Explains where the ukulele and pan flute come from and a role each plays
Names where one instrument comes from
Cannot yet connect the instruments to a culture

lessons.exitTicket: Name one instrument that reads bass clef and one that reads treble clef, and describe the timbre of one of them in two words.
tips: Carnival of the Animals (1886) is in the public domain; any recording you own or stream legally works.
Some recordings put the Swan on solo cello with two pianos: point out the pianos as the "water".
The double bass is not one of the 17 Zoo cards; compare it to the cello card and tuba card for "very low".

lessons.title: Piano and Forte: Loud and Soft with Dynamic Ears
lessons.summary: Students learn piano and forte, then mezzo piano and mezzo forte, test their voices and body percussion on the live mic meter, play the Classroom Quiet Challenge, and move to Haydn's Surprise Symphony.
objectives: tell the difference between loud (forte) and soft (piano) music
use the words piano, forte, mezzo piano and mezzo forte
perform with their voice and body percussion at a chosen dynamic
show dynamic changes with movement while listening
iCan: I can sing and clap piano (soft) and forte (loud).
I can show loud and soft music with my body.
I can make the meter show the dynamic I choose.

vocabulary.def: How loud or soft the music is.
Soft.
Loud and strong.
Medium soft.
Medium loud.

materials: Projector with [Dynamic Ears](/?app=dynamic-ears&focus=1); a computer microphone (built-in is fine)
A recording of Haydn, Symphony No. 94 "Surprise", 2nd movement (public domain) that the teacher has access to
Printed dynamics chart (Print button in Dynamic Ears)
Open floor space for moving
prep: Open Dynamic Ears, press the mic button and allow the microphone. Clap softly and loudly to see where the meter lands in your room.
If the mic is blocked, plan to use the dynamic buttons instead (the tool shows them).
Cue the first 1 minute of the Haydn movement (soft melody, then the sudden loud chord).
Print the dynamics chart and post p, mp, mf, f on the board.

steps.do: Unplugged: "Mouse and Lion". Sing a known song (Twinkle or Bounce High) like a tiny mouse (piano), then like a lion (forte). Then pat-clap the steady beat both ways.
steps.check: Soft is still a real voice, not a whisper; loud is strong, not shouting.

steps.do: Play the start of the Haydn Surprise Symphony 2nd movement. Students listen with hands on knees. When the big chord surprises them, ask: What happened? Why do you think the composer did that?
steps.say: Haydn wanted to wake up anyone who fell asleep at his concert!

steps.do: Show Dynamic Ears. Click the dynamic buttons for p and f, then mp and mf; read each Italian word and its meaning. Then turn on the mic and clap at forte, then at piano, so students see the meter move.
steps.check: Students say the Italian word when the teacher points.

steps.do: Mic game: point to a dynamic on the board (p, mp, mf, f). The class sings "hello" or pats the beat at that level and watches the meter. Then small groups (one table at a time) try to hit a target the teacher names.
steps.check: Groups change dynamic without changing tempo.

steps.do: Start the **Classroom Quiet Challenge**: the room must stay at piano for 60 seconds to keep all 5 stars. Students hum, tap fingertips or sing very softly the whole time.
steps.say: Can we be piano for a whole minute and keep five stars?
steps.check: Stars left at the end; talk about what made the meter jump.

steps.do: Replay the Haydn excerpt. Students tiptoe for piano parts and stomp-in-place or jump for forte. Then lead a second piece or section and let students show changes.
steps.check: Movements change at the right moments.

steps.do: Exit ticket: teacher plays or sings a short phrase; students hold up a p card or an f card (or show small hands / big hands).

support: Use only p and f for Kindergarten; add mp and mf in grades 1-2.
Use pictures (mouse and lion) next to p and f.
Model each dynamic before the class tries it.
extend: Let a student "conductor" show dynamics with hand size and the class follows.
Add pianissimo and fortissimo from the tool.
access: Use the dynamic buttons if a student finds the live mic stressful.
Students with hearing differences can watch the meter as their main cue.
Keep forte at a safe level; remind students that forte is strong, not screaming.

formative: Movement responses to the Haydn piece.
Mic game: groups hit the target dynamic.
Students use p/f vocabulary when answering.
assessment.summative: Small-group performance: each group sings a known song once piano and once forte into the meter; teacher records on a checklist whether the meter shows the change and students name the dynamic.

levels: Identifies p, mp, mf and f in music
Identifies piano and forte in music
Identifies loud and soft only with a model
Does not yet tell loud from soft
Sings and plays at four different dynamics on cue
Sings and plays piano and forte on cue with a good tone
Changes dynamic but shouts or whispers
Does not change dynamic
Uses all four Italian words correctly
Uses piano and forte correctly
Uses loud and soft but not the Italian words
Does not yet use dynamic words

lessons.exitTicket: Listen: hold up p or f for the dynamic you hear.
tips: Run the Quiet Challenge at the start of any noisy class: it doubles as classroom management.
The meter depends on the microphone and the room. Calibrate by clapping before class and talk about the meter as "our room's meter".
Nothing is recorded: the mic is only measured live.

lessons.title: Shaping a Phrase: Crescendo, Decrescendo and the Mountain King
lessons.summary: Students learn the full range pp-ff with crescendo and decrescendo, map the dynamics and accelerando in Grieg's In the Hall of the Mountain King, then plan and perform a dynamic shape for a phrase and check it on the live meter.
objectives: order and define the six dynamics pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff
identify crescendo, decrescendo and accelerando in a recording
plan a dynamic shape for a musical phrase and write it with symbols
perform the planned shape and use the meter and peer feedback to improve it
iCan: I can name and order the dynamics from pianissimo to fortissimo.
I can hear and mark a crescendo in a piece of music.
I can plan a dynamic shape, perform it, and check it on the meter.

vocabulary.def: Very soft.
Very loud.
Gradually getting louder; written as an opening hairpin <.
Gradually getting softer; written as a closing hairpin >.
Gradually getting faster.
A musical sentence.

materials: Projector with [Dynamic Ears](/?app=dynamic-ears&focus=1) and a microphone
A recording of Grieg, In the Hall of the Mountain King from Peer Gynt (1875, public domain) that the teacher has access to
Listening map: a long line divided into 6 boxes for students to mark dynamics and tempo
Printed dynamics chart; a short phrase everyone can perform (recorder piece, a song, or a body-percussion pattern)
prep: Test the mic meter in the room; play pp and ff to see the range.
Cue the Grieg (about 2.5 minutes).
Choose a 4-measure phrase the class knows (e.g. Ode to Joy on recorder, or a folk song like Down by the Riverside sung).
Print the dynamics chart and listening maps.

steps.do: Unplugged: a "volume knob" clap. Students clap steady beats while the teacher turns an imaginary knob from pp to ff and back. Then try it without the teacher: crescendo over 8 beats.
steps.check: Gradual change, no sudden jumps.

steps.do: In Dynamic Ears, click the six dynamic buttons in order and read each Italian word, pronunciation and meaning. Draw < and > on the board and connect them to crescendo and decrescendo.
steps.say: A crescendo is a road that gets wider: more and more sound.

steps.do: Play the Grieg. Students mark on their map where it is pp, where it grows (crescendo), where it gets faster (accelerando), and where it reaches ff. Discuss: how do the dynamics and tempo tell the story of Peer Gynt running from the trolls?
steps.check: Maps start at pp/p, show a long crescendo and accelerando, and end at ff.

steps.do: Groups of 4-5 plan a dynamic shape for the class phrase (e.g. p < f > p or mf then sudden pp). They write the symbols under the words or notes and give a reason (what feeling or story it shows).
steps.check: Each plan uses at least one hairpin and two dynamic levels.

steps.do: Each group performs its shape into the mic while the class watches the meter. The class gives one glow (what matched the plan) and one grow (where the meter did not match). Group performs again to improve.
steps.say: Does the meter show the shape you wrote?
steps.check: Second performance matches the plan more closely.

steps.do: Written reflection: What did you change between your first and second performance? Why did Grieg use crescendo and accelerando together?

support: Give groups a choice of three ready-made dynamic shapes.
Use only p, f and one crescendo.
Provide the listening map with the boxes already labeled pp and ff at the ends.
extend: Add a subito (sudden) dynamic change to the plan.
Compare with another piece: the start of Haydn's Surprise Symphony movement 2. Which composer uses gradual change and which uses sudden change?
access: Students can perform on a classroom percussion instrument instead of singing.
Sentence frame for feedback: "The meter showed ___ when you planned ___."
Visual meter helps students with hearing differences; let students sensitive to sound cover their ears or sit farther from the speakers during the loud Grieg ending.

formative: Volume-knob clapping shows gradual change.
Listening maps checked for crescendo and accelerando.
Glow/grow feedback between performances.
assessment.summative: Group dynamic plan (written symbols + reason) and performance; collect the plan and record a short video or audio clip of the second performance for Google Classroom if your school allows.

levels: Marks dynamics, crescendo and accelerando at the right places and explains their effect
Marks the crescendo and accelerando and the start and end dynamics
Marks one change (loud ending) only
Map is blank or unrelated
Plan uses 3+ levels and hairpins with a clear expressive reason
Plan uses 2+ levels and a hairpin with a reason
Plan has symbols but no reason or uses one level
No plan
Performance matches the plan on the meter and improves after feedback
Performance mostly matches the plan; one improvement made
Some dynamic change but not the planned shape
No dynamic change

lessons.exitTicket: Order these from softest to loudest: mf, pp, f, p, ff, mp. Then draw a crescendo symbol.
tips: Grieg's Peer Gynt music (1875) is in the public domain; use any recording you have legal access to.
The meter jumps on consonants and claps: hum or sing on "loo" for a smoother line.
Remind students that ff should still be a good tone; the meter is not a contest for the loudest.

lessons.title: Steady Beat Heroes: The Tempo Challenge
lessons.summary: Students feel the difference between music with and without a steady beat, explore fast and slow, then play the Tempo Challenge (Starter zone, 80 and 100 BPM) on the projector while the whole class pats the beat and learns what "rushing" and "dragging" mean.
objectives: tell music with a steady beat from sounds without a beat
move and pat a steady beat at a slow and a fast tempo
keep a steady beat alone after the clicks stop
use the words rushing and dragging to describe a beat
iCan: I can pat a steady beat that does not speed up or slow down.
I can keep the beat going after the clicks stop.
I can tell if a beat is rushing or dragging.

vocabulary.def: The heartbeat of music: it stays even, like a clock ticking.
How fast or slow the beat is.
Speeding up when you should stay steady.
Slowing down when you should stay steady.
Beats per minute: a number that tells the tempo.

materials: Projector with [Tap Tempo & Tempo Challenge](/?app=tempo-tapper&focus=1); keyboard (Space bar) or mouse for the tapper
Speakers
Optional: rhythm sticks or a hand drum
prep: Open the Tempo Challenge tab, choose 80 BPM and the 🌱 Starter (±5 BPM) zone. Try one round yourself.
Pick two chants with a strong beat: Bounce High, Bounce Low and Engine, Engine Number Nine.
Prepare a few "no beat" sounds: wind or rain sounds, a sustained hum, a crinkled paper.

steps.do: Unplugged: chant Bounce High, Bounce Low while patting the beat on knees. Then walk the beat around the room; freeze when the chant stops.
steps.check: Feet and pats land together.

steps.do: Alternate examples: a chant with a beat, then wind/rain sounds or a long hum without a beat. Students pat if there is a beat and wave arms like wind if there is not.
steps.say: Is there a heartbeat in this sound?

steps.do: Tap the Tap Tempo button at a slow speed, then a fast speed. Students watch the BPM number and the animal change. Pat along both ways.
steps.check: Students say whether the number went up (faster) or down (slower).

steps.do: Switch to the Tempo Challenge tab (80 BPM, Starter). Explain: 4 clicks, then the clicks stop and the tapper keeps going for 32 taps. Teacher demonstrates once, rushing on purpose, so the class sees "Rushing!".
steps.say: When the clicks stop, the beat lives inside you.

steps.do: One student taps (Space bar or button) while the whole class pats the beat silently on their knees. Switch tappers each round. After two rounds at 80, try 100. Celebrate the best score shown for each tempo.
steps.check: Class pats stay together after the count-in; tapper's feedback shows few rushing/dragging messages.

steps.do: Ask: What helps you keep a steady beat? (Counting 1-2-3-4 in your head, watching a friend, breathing.) Show rushing with tiny fast steps and dragging with a slow heavy walk.
Exit ticket: teacher pats a beat that speeds up. Students show a cheetah (rushing) or turtle (dragging) or thumbs up (steady).

support: Let the class pat along out loud for the first round.
Give K-1 students a partner to tap with.
Start at 100 BPM if 80 feels too slow for little hands.
extend: Try the 🏆 Pro (±2 BPM) zone.
Try 60 or 120 BPM.
Keep the beat while chanting a rhythm over it.
access: A student can tap with a large button switch or the mouse instead of the Space bar.
Students with hearing differences can watch a partner's pats or the count-in numbers.
Students who need movement can walk the beat instead of patting.

formative: Beat/no-beat responses.
Whole-class patting stays together after the clicks stop.
Tapper feedback messages (rushing/dragging) during each round.
assessment.summative: Each student takes one Tempo Challenge turn (over this and later lessons); record the score and whether they kept the beat for most of the 32 taps on a class checklist.

levels: Keeps a steady beat alone at 80 and 100 BPM in the Starter zone with few warnings
Keeps a steady beat alone at one tempo for most of the 32 taps
Keeps the beat with the count-in but drifts after it stops
Does not yet keep a steady beat
Identifies beat/no beat and explains how they know
Identifies beat/no beat correctly
Identifies some examples correctly
Does not yet tell the difference
Uses fast/slow, rushing and dragging correctly and corrects their own tempo
Uses rushing and dragging correctly
Uses fast and slow only
Does not yet describe tempo

lessons.exitTicket: Listen to my beat: is it steady, rushing or dragging? Show thumbs up, cheetah or turtle.
tips: The best scores stay on the classroom computer: post the class record on the board and try to beat it next week.
Quiet patting (not clapping) keeps the room calm and lets the tapper hear the count-in.
Practice games like this a few minutes every class rather than one long session.

lessons.title: Animal Tempos: From Sleepy Turtle to Supersonic Rocket
lessons.summary: Students meet the Metronome's animal presets and the Italian tempo words behind them, move like each animal to the beat, and use silent mode with the screen flash to practise keeping the beat inside.
objectives: move to a steady beat at slow, medium and fast tempos
match animal presets to Italian tempo words (Largo, Andante, Moderato, Allegro, Presto, Prestissimo)
keep a steady beat by watching a visual flash with no sound
choose a tempo that fits an animal or story
iCan: I can move like an animal to the beat.
I can say if the tempo is slow (largo) or fast (presto).
I can keep the beat by watching the flash.

vocabulary.def: How fast or slow the beat is.
Very slow, like a sleepy turtle.
Walking speed, like a penguin.
Fast and happy, like a galloping horse.
Very fast, like a cheetah.
A tool that ticks a steady beat.

materials: Projector with [Metronome](/?app=metronome&focus=1) and speakers
Printed tempo chart (Print button in the Metronome) or animal pictures on the board
Open space for moving
Optional: a recording of Saint-Saëns, The Tortoises from Carnival of the Animals (public domain) for a slow-tempo example
prep: Open the Metronome and click each animal preset: Sleepy Turtle, Walking Penguin, Hopping Kangaroo, Galloping Horse, Sprinting Cheetah, Supersonic Rocket.
Pick a click sound (woodblock is friendly); find the silent sound option and the flash option.
Print the tempo chart and post it.
Clear a movement space; set a "freeze" signal.

steps.do: Review from Steady Beat Heroes: pat a steady beat to a chant, then ask: was that fast or slow? Students show with their hands (slow wave, fast flutter).
Click the Sleepy Turtle preset, then jump to Supersonic Rocket. Students guess which animal fits each speed. Show the animal and Italian word on the screen.
steps.say: Musicians around the world use Italian words for tempo. Largo means very slow.

steps.do: Go through the presets in order. For each, say the Italian word together (LAHR-go, ahn-DAHN-teh...) and pat a few beats. Point to the matching row on the tempo chart.
steps.check: Pats match the click at every tempo.

steps.do: Students move to the beat as the teacher changes presets: crawl-turtle at Largo, waddle-penguin at Andante, hop at Moderato, gallop at Allegro, run in place at Presto, rocket blast-off (jump on beat 1) at Prestissimo. Freeze when the metronome stops.
steps.check: Steps land on the clicks, not just "fast" or "slow" movement.

steps.do: Switch the click sound to silent and turn on the flash. Students pat each time the screen flashes. Then turn the screen off for 4 beats and back on: are we still together?
steps.say: Now the beat is a light. Can your hands find it without the sound?
steps.check: Pats line up with the flash when the screen comes back.

steps.do: Students choose a tempo word for a story: a sleepy bear waking up, a mouse running from a cat. A volunteer picks a preset and the class moves to it. Exit ticket: point to the slowest and the fastest animal on the chart and say their Italian words.

support: Use only three animals (turtle, kangaroo, cheetah) for Kindergarten.
Say the English meaning along with each Italian word.
Let students pat instead of moving around the room.
extend: Grade 2: read the BPM number on the screen and order the animals from smallest to largest number.
Invent a new animal for a tempo in between.
access: Silent + flash mode is ideal for students with hearing differences; use it for them all lesson.
Students who use wheelchairs can move arms and upper body.
Picture cards for the Italian words help English learners.

formative: Movement matches the clicks at each preset.
Choral answers for the Italian words.
Silent-beat check when the screen comes back.
assessment.summative: Tempo match: teacher plays three presets in random order; each student points to the matching animal on the chart and moves 4 beats with it (checklist over two classes).

levels: Moves exactly on the beat at all tempos, including Prestissimo
Moves on the beat at slow, medium and fast tempos
Moves fast or slow but not on the beat
Does not yet change speed with the music
Matches all six Italian words to animals and meanings
Matches largo, andante, allegro and presto
Matches largo and presto
Does not yet use tempo words
Keeps the beat steady through a blank screen
Keeps the beat with the flash and no sound
Follows the flash but is late
Does not yet follow the visual beat

lessons.exitTicket: Point to the slowest animal on the chart and say its Italian word. Then the fastest.
tips: Prestissimo is very fast: keep movements in place to stay safe.
The flash option helps every child, not only students with hearing differences.
Hang the printed tempo chart all year; students will start using the words on their own.

lessons.title: Tempo Detectives: Finding the BPM of Famous Music
lessons.summary: Students tap along to public-domain pieces with Tap Tempo to measure their BPM, match each one to an Italian tempo term on the printable tempo chart, check their answer with the Metronome, then take on the Tempo Challenge in the Pro (±2) zone.
objectives: measure the tempo of a recording in beats per minute by tapping
match BPM values to Italian tempo terms from Largo to Presto
explain why a composer chose a tempo for a piece's purpose or mood
keep a steady internal beat within ±2 BPM
iCan: I can find the BPM of a piece of music by tapping the beat.
I can name the Italian tempo term that fits a BPM.
I can explain how tempo changes the mood of music.

vocabulary.def: Beats per minute: how many beats happen in 60 seconds.
Broad and very slow (under 60 BPM).
Walking pace (about 60-79 BPM).
Medium speed (about 80-107 BPM).
Fast and lively (about 108-139 BPM).
Very fast (about 140-179 BPM).

materials: Projector with [Tap Tempo](/?app=tempo-tapper&focus=1) and the [Metronome](/?app=metronome&focus=1)
Printed tempo chart, one per student or pair (Print button in either tool)

Recordings the teacher has access to of four public-domain pieces, e.g. Brahms, Lullaby (Wiegenlied, 1868); Satie, Gymnopédie No. 1 (1888); Sousa, The Stars and Stripes Forever (1896); Rimsky-Korsakov, Flight of the Bumblebee (1900)
Detective log: piece, my BPM, class BPM, tempo term, mood words
Optional: Chromebooks for partner Tempo Challenge
prep: Tap each recording yourself first and write the BPM you get; recordings differ, so use your own answer key, not a published number.
Cue 30-second excerpts with a clear beat.
Print the tempo chart (BPM ranges per term).
Open both tools in two browser tabs.

steps.do: Unplugged: one student claps a beat; the class guesses "turtle, penguin, kangaroo, horse or cheetah". Review that tempo is the speed of the beat.
Play Sousa. Tap the Space bar on the beat in Tap Tempo for 8-10 taps; read the BPM, animal and Italian term shown. Show that the first few taps jump around and the number settles as you keep going.
steps.say: Detectives gather lots of evidence: keep tapping until the number settles.

steps.do: Play each remaining excerpt. Volunteers tap on the projector while everyone else counts beats for 15 seconds and multiplies by 4 on their log. Compare the two methods, record the class BPM, then match it to a term on the printed tempo chart.
steps.check: Logs show a BPM and a matching term; differences of a few BPM are fine.

steps.do: Set the Metronome to the class BPM and play it with the recording. Does it line up? Adjust by a few BPM if needed. Discuss why the Bumblebee may show half or double the expected number (tapping every other beat).
steps.check: Students notice half-time / double-time tapping.

steps.do: Pairs choose one piece and write: why did the composer pick this tempo? Connect it to purpose: a lullaby to calm a baby, a march for soldiers and parades, a bee flying.
Open the Tempo Challenge tab: 🏆 Pro (±2 BPM) zone at 100 BPM. Volunteers try while the class pats silently; or pairs rotate on Chromebooks. Try 60 or 120 for the next round.
steps.check: Feedback shows few "Rushing" or "Dragging" messages.

steps.do: Exit ticket: A piece measures 126 BPM. Which tempo term fits, and would it fit a lullaby? Why or why not?

support: Let students use only Tap Tempo (no math method).
Give a word bank of mood words.
Use the Starter (±5) zone for the challenge.
extend: Find the BPM of a school-appropriate song they love at home and place it on the chart.
Find a piece with an accelerando (Grieg's Hall of the Mountain King) and measure start and end tempo.
access: Partners can split jobs: one taps, one records.
Large-print tempo chart.
Calculator for the 15-seconds-times-4 method.

formative: Detective logs during the investigation.
Metronome check: does the class BPM line up?
Discussion of half-time/double-time results.
assessment.summative: Completed detective log for four pieces (BPM, term, mood, and one tempo-purpose explanation), collected or posted to Google Classroom.

levels: BPM within 5 of the key for all pieces and explains half/double-time results
BPM within 5 of the key for at least three pieces
BPM found for some pieces but often far off
Cannot yet measure BPM
Matches every BPM to the correct term and gives its meaning
Matches most BPM values to the correct term
Matches only slow vs fast terms correctly
Does not yet use tempo terms
Explains how tempo serves purpose and mood with specific evidence
Gives a reasonable purpose or mood reason
States the tempo without a reason
No explanation

lessons.exitTicket: A piece measures 126 BPM. Which tempo term fits, and would it make a good lullaby? Why?
tips: Always use your own measured BPM as the answer key: tempos vary between recordings.
Students often tap every other beat on fast pieces: that is a great teaching moment about pulse levels.
Best Tempo Challenge scores are saved on the device; keep a class record board.

lessons.title: Practice Like a Pro: Meter, Subdivision and Slow Practice
lessons.summary: Students use the Metronome's accents and subdivisions to feel meter in 2, 3, 4 and 6, then learn a slow-practice routine (start slow, add 4 BPM after each clean repetition) for a recorder, ukulele or band passage and assess their own progress.
objectives: feel and conduct meters in 2, 3 and 4 and count a 6-beat pattern using accented downbeats
count subdivisions: eighths, triplets and sixteenths
follow a slow-practice routine with a metronome, raising the tempo in small steps
evaluate their own practice with clear criteria
iCan: I can hear the strong beat and count the meter.
I can count eighth notes, triplets and sixteenths with a metronome.
I can use slow practice to play a hard passage correctly, then faster.

vocabulary.def: How beats are grouped (in 2, 3, 4 or 6), shown by the time signature.
Beat 1 of each measure; the metronome accents it.
Splitting the beat into smaller equal parts.
Three equal notes in one beat (trip-o-let).
Playing a passage slowly enough to play it right, then speeding up a little at a time.

materials: Projector with [Metronome](/?app=metronome&focus=1)
Instruments the class uses: recorders, ukuleles, or band instruments (or voices and body percussion)
A short, hard passage (2-4 measures) from a piece the class is learning
Practice log: start tempo, tempo after each clean repetition, final tempo, self-check
Optional: Chromebooks with headphones so pairs can run their own metronome
prep: Pick the passage and decide a safe start tempo (often 60-70 BPM).
In the Metronome, try beats per measure 2, 3, 4 and 6 and each subdivision (Quarter, Eighth, Triplet, 16th).
Print practice logs; write the routine on the board: Slow → Clean x2 → +4 BPM → repeat.

steps.do: Set 4 beats per measure, 100 BPM. Students pat on beat 1 and tap lightly on 2-3-4. Switch to 3 (waltz) and 2 (march). Conduct each pattern.
steps.check: Pats land on the accented click.

steps.do: Set 6 beats per measure. Count 1-2-3-4-5-6 with a pat on 1 and a lighter pat on 4. Explain that the tool accents only beat 1, so musicians feel the second group themselves.
steps.say: In 6, the beats come in two groups of three.

steps.do: At 80 BPM, switch Quarter → Eighth (1-&) → Triplet (1-trip-let) → 16th (1-e-&-a). Students say the counts, then clap them. Ask which subdivision a tricky rhythm in the passage needs.
steps.check: Counts stay even with the clicks; no rushing on 16ths.

steps.do: Teacher (or a confident student) plays the passage too fast and makes mistakes. Then demonstrates the routine: start slow, play it clean twice, raise the BPM by 4, repeat. Fill in the log on the board.
steps.say: Slow and right beats fast and wrong. Speed comes from clean repetitions.

steps.do: Pairs or sections practise the passage with the routine and fill in their logs (projector metronome for the class, or Chromebooks with headphones per pair). One partner plays, one watches the music and says "clean" or "again".
steps.check: Logs show several 4-BPM steps; the teacher circulates and listens.

steps.do: Self-assessment on the log: How many BPM did you gain? Which measure still needs work? What will you practise at home tonight, and at what tempo?
Exit ticket: Write the slow-practice routine in your own words in three steps.

support: Use a one-measure passage and a start tempo of 50-60.
Use only quarter and eighth subdivisions.
Partner a newer player with a confident one.
extend: Practise with the eighth or sixteenth subdivision on to tighten the rhythm.
Set a stretch goal tempo and use +2 BPM steps near the goal.
Switch the click to silent + flash for the last repetition.
access: Flash option for students with hearing differences.
Students without an instrument can practise the rhythm on body percussion or voice.
Headphones for students who find many clicking devices overwhelming.

formative: Pats and counts against each meter and subdivision.
Practice logs during the practice phase.
Partner "clean / again" calls.
assessment.summative: Completed practice log plus a short play-through of the passage at the student's final clean tempo (teacher listens or students submit an audio clip if your school allows).

levels: Counts all four meters and all subdivisions accurately, and chooses the right one for the passage
Counts meters in 2, 3, 4 and eighths and triplets accurately
Counts quarters and eighths but loses triplets or 16ths
Does not yet count with the metronome
Follows the routine independently, adjusts step size, and explains why
Follows the routine and logs each clean step
Raises the tempo before playing it clean
Does not use the metronome to practise
Names the exact measure and fix needed and sets a specific home goal
Names what improved and a tempo goal
Gives a general comment ("it got better")
No reflection

lessons.exitTicket: Write the slow-practice routine in three steps, and the tempo you will start with at home.
tips: Ask band teachers which passage their students are stuck on: this lesson pays off in rehearsals.
Many clicking devices at once is noisy; one projector metronome for the whole class works well too.
Students often push the tempo too soon: insist on two clean repetitions before each +4.

lessons.title: Tuning Lab: Pitch, Hertz and Cents
lessons.summary: Students learn that pitch is frequency (Hz) and that A = 440, read sharp, flat and in tune in cents, tune a ukulele, guitar or violin with a preset, hold a steady sung pitch on the history view, and band students try their transposition setting. Voices and recorders work if there are no string instruments.
objectives: explain that pitch depends on frequency, measured in hertz (Hz), with A4 = 440 Hz as the usual reference
read the tuner to say whether a note is sharp, flat or in tune and by how many cents
adjust an instrument or their voice to bring a note in tune
explain why transposing instruments read a different written note
iCan: I can explain what hertz and A = 440 mean.
I can tell if a note is sharp, flat or in tune and fix it.
I can hold a steady pitch and show it on the history view.

vocabulary.def: How many times per second a sound vibrates; more vibrations = higher pitch.
Vibrations per second. A4 is usually 440 Hz.
A little too high.
A little too low.
A tiny step of pitch: 100 cents make one half step.
Close enough to the target pitch that it sounds right.
An instrument (like B♭ clarinet or trumpet) whose written note is different from the note you hear.

materials: Projector with the [Instrument Tuner](/?app=tuner&focus=1) and a microphone
Instruments available: ukuleles, guitars, violins; otherwise voices and recorders; band students may bring clarinet, trumpet or saxophone
Optional: a rubber band or a long ruler on a desk edge to show vibration
Worksheet: note, Hz shown, cents, sharp/flat/in tune, what I changed
prep: Open the Tuner and allow the microphone. Try the Chromatic preset with your voice, then the Ukulele preset.
Set tolerance to **Kids ±8¢** to start; make sure **Pitch history** is on.
Slightly de-tune one ukulele or guitar string so you can demonstrate.
If band students attend, check the transposition menu for B♭, E♭ and F.

steps.do: Unplugged: pluck a rubber band or twang a ruler on the desk edge, short then long. Shorter = faster vibration = higher pitch. Students hum a siren low to high.
steps.check: Students connect "faster vibration" with "higher".

steps.do: Use the Chromatic preset. Press the speaker button to play the reference pitch. Show that A4 = 440 Hz (the A4 reference setting). Sing low and high notes and read the note name and frequency. Explain that some orchestras tune slightly higher or lower, which is why the reference can change (415-466 Hz).
steps.say: 440 vibrations every second: that is the A almost every band and orchestra tunes to.

steps.do: Play the de-tuned string. Read the needle: flat or sharp, how many cents. Turn the peg slowly while the class calls "higher" or "lower" until it shows in tune. Mention 100 cents = one half step.
steps.check: Class calls the right direction before the needle moves.

steps.do: Groups rotate: (1) ukulele/guitar/violin group tunes with the matching preset, string by string; (2) singers sing a long "loo" on a given note with Chromatic and watch the **history view** stay flat and steady; (3) recorder players play A and B and check them; (4) band students choose their transposition so the tuner shows their written note. Fill in the worksheet.
steps.check: Each group records at least three readings and one fix.

steps.do: On the projector, volunteers hold a pitch for 5 seconds. The class reads the history line: steady, wobbly, or drifting flat at the end? Switch tolerance to Standard ±5¢ for a harder try.
steps.say: A straight line means a steady pitch. Breath support keeps it from sagging.

steps.do: Written reflection: Explain to a younger student what "sharp" and "flat" mean and how you fixed one note today. Why do band players tune together before a concert?

support: Use Kids ±8¢ tolerance all lesson.
Pre-tune all but one string so students fix one at a time.
Give a needle diagram labeled flat / in tune / sharp.
extend: Try Pro ±2¢ and the strobe view.
Calculate: if A4 = 440 Hz, what is A5? (880 Hz, double) and A3? (220 Hz).
Try the Drop D guitar preset and explain what changes.
access: Students with hearing differences can tune by watching the needle and history view.
Singers who are uncomfortable singing alone can hum in pairs.
Quiet corners help the microphone hear one instrument at a time.

formative: Direction calls (higher/lower) during the de-tuned string demo.
Station worksheets: readings and fixes.
History-line readings during the challenge.
assessment.summative: Tuning worksheet plus a written explanation of Hz, sharp/flat and cents, collected; for string players, a teacher check that one string was tuned within the Kids tolerance.

levels: Explains Hz, A = 440, cents and octaves (double frequency) correctly
Explains Hz, A = 440 and that more vibrations mean higher pitch
Knows higher pitch means "more" but not Hz
Cannot yet explain pitch
Reads note, cents and direction instantly and predicts the fix
Reads sharp, flat or in tune and the direction to fix
Reads in tune vs not in tune only
Does not yet read the tuner
Tunes an instrument string or holds a sung pitch steady within Standard ±5¢
Tunes a string or holds a pitch within Kids ±8¢
Gets close but overshoots or wobbles
Does not yet adjust pitch

lessons.exitTicket: The tuner shows A, 20 cents sharp. Is the note too high or too low, and which way do you adjust?
tips: Tune one instrument at a time near the computer; other instruments in the room confuse the microphone.
If you have no string instruments, voices and recorders make an excellent tuning lab.
Nothing is recorded: the microphone is only measured live.
