units.title: Steady Beat & Tempo
units.big: Music has a heartbeat. We can feel it, show it, keep it alone, and make it faster or slower.
also: Beat-keeping songs and chants (Bounce High, Engine Engine #9, Bee Bee Bumblebee).
Patsch, march, and pass-the-beat games with a ball.
Unpitched percussion: play the beat on hand drums while the class sings.
units.culminating: Each student keeps a steady beat alone for 16 beats (Tempo Challenge Starter zone, or patting with the metronome muted) and shows fast vs slow with movement.

units.title: Sounds Around Us: Loud, Soft & Instruments
units.big: Every sound has a color (timbre) and a size (dynamics). Composers choose sounds on purpose to paint a picture.
also: Sound walk: list the loud and soft sounds around school.
Live instrument visit (older students, band teacher).
Read-aloud with sound effects on classroom instruments.
units.culminating: Groups perform a soundscape for a short story using at least two dynamic levels and two instrument families, then name them.

units.title: Reading Rhythm: Ta, Ti-Ti & Shh
units.big: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds. We can read, write and play it with symbols.
also: Rhythm flashcards and stick notation on the board.
Say-clap-play: chant words, clap them, play them on instruments.
Holiday/winter concert repertoire: find ta and ti-ti in the songs.
units.culminating: Students read and clap a 4-beat pattern on sight, then write their own 4-beat pattern (paper or Big Staff) and perform it for a partner.

units.title: Pitch: Sol, Mi & La
units.big: Melodies move up, down and stay the same. Solfège and the staff help us sing and read them.
also: Singing games: Doggie Doggie, Lucy Locket, Rain Rain.
Hand-sign echo and “inner hearing” (sign it, don’t sing it).
Barred instruments: play sol-mi patterns.
units.culminating: Students sing a 4-measure sol-mi-la melody with hand signs and play it (bells, keyboard or Staff Composer).

units.title: Meter & Music Symbols
units.big: Beats group into twos, threes and fours. Symbols on the page tell us how to play.
also: Waltz vs march: move to music in 3 and in 4.
Symbol word wall: add each new symbol with a picture and a movement.
Grade 3: recorder or barred instruments reading B-A-G.
units.culminating: Students identify 3/4 vs 4/4 by ear, match 8 symbols to their meanings, and (grade 3) name treble lines and spaces.

units.title: Making Songs: Form & Texture
units.big: Songs have a plan: sections repeat and change, and parts layer up and drop out.
also: Find AB and ABA in class songs (Twinkle Twinkle is ABA).
Body-percussion rondo: class A section, solo B/C sections.
Listen: a march vs a lullaby — what changes?
units.culminating: Students compose a Sound Blocks song in ABA form with an intro and ending, share it by link/QR, and tell the class which world and why.

units.title: Perform & Share
units.big: Musicians rehearse, fix, and perform for an audience — and audiences listen respectfully.
also: Rehearse a favorite song from the year with instruments.
Practice audience etiquette and bowing.
Folk dance from another culture (NY Cn10.1c).
units.culminating: A class “Music Lab Showcase”: live loops, a sung song with hand signs and a playlist of student Sound Blocks songs for families.

units.title: Tempo, Meter & Practicing Like a Musician
units.big: Tempo and meter organize time. Good musicians practice slowly and steadily, then build speed.
also: Recorder, ukulele or keyboard unit starts: daily metronome warm-up.
Conducting patterns in 2, 3 and 4 (NY Pr5.1c cues).
Find the BPM of a school-appropriate song students choose.
units.culminating: Students perform a short instrument passage with a metronome at two tempos and fill in a practice log with BPM goals.

units.title: Rhythm Literacy & Grooves
units.big: Sixteenths, syncopation and triplets make grooves feel alive. If we can count it, we can create it.
also: Bucket-drumming or body-percussion ensemble with written parts.
Rhythmic dictation: 4-beat patterns, 2 a class.
Listen: ragtime (Joplin) and Latin clave patterns.
units.culminating: Students compose a 4-measure groove in Beat Machine, print its notation, count it aloud and perform one part on percussion.

units.title: Reading Pitch: Solfège, Treble & Bass
units.big: Two clefs and solfège unlock any melody. Fluency comes from short, frequent practice.
also: Daily 3-minute Staff Wars round as a bell-ringer.
Sight-sing 4-measure melodies with hand signs.
Read a part from the winter concert music.
units.culminating: Note-name check in treble and bass (target: 20 notes in a minute) and a 4-note melodic dictation in solfège.

units.title: Expression & Timbre
units.big: Performers and composers use dynamics, tempo and timbre to create feeling. Listeners can name and explain those choices.
also: Listening journal: one public-domain orchestral piece a week.
Compare two recordings of the same piece (Re9.1a).
Instruments of the world: link to students’ family heritage (NY Cn11.1a).
units.culminating: Written listening response: name the instrument families, dynamics and tempo changes in an unfamiliar piece and explain the mood with evidence.

units.title: Melody & Harmony at the Keyboard
units.big: Scales make melodies and chords make harmony. Ostinatos and the blues let us improvise right away.
also: Ukulele or barred instruments: C, F, G7 chords.
History of the blues and its influence on rock, jazz and pop (NY Cn11.1a).
Major vs minor listening sort.
units.culminating: Partners perform a 12-bar blues: one plays the chords, one improvises with the blues scale, then they switch.

units.title: Composing & Arranging
units.big: Composers shape ideas into phrases and forms, and arrangers give a melody new colors with new instruments.
also: Peer feedback circles with the lesson rubrics.
Perform student compositions on classroom instruments.
Study one arrangement: the same tune for band vs orchestra.
units.culminating: A printed, titled 8-measure composition with dynamics, plus a short artist statement on what they revised and why (Cr3.1a, Cr3.2a).

units.title: Music Production
units.big: Producers build songs from layers and sections and mix them so every part can be heard. Music can tell a story with picture.
also: Analyze the form of a school-appropriate song students choose.
Careers in music technology: producer, engineer, film composer.
Digital citizenship: CC0 loops, credit and remix etiquette.
units.culminating: A finished DAW song or film score shared by link, presented with a 3-sentence producer’s note, and scored with the class rubric at a listening party.

resources.title: Tech setup checklist
resources.summary: Run this once on a student Chromebook or iPad before the first Music Lab lesson.

ul: Chrome (Chromebooks, Windows, Mac) or Safari (iPad) kept up to date. Every tool runs in the browser; nothing to install.
**Headphones for every student** (wired is most reliable; Bluetooth adds delay that makes rhythm games feel late). Label them by seat number.
Turn the device volume to about 70% and let students adjust inside each tool.
Open [mrarthurmusic.com](/) on one device and press Play in [Beat Machine](/?app=beat-machine). If you hear nothing, unmute the tab and tap the page once (browsers only start sound after a tap).
If your district filter blocks a page, tell IT: every sound file comes from mrarthurmusic.com itself, so allowing that one site is enough.

body.h: Microphone tools (Looper, Sound Blocks voice block, Tuner, Studio DAW recording)

ul: The browser asks “Allow microphone?” the first time. Students choose **Allow**. If they blocked it, click the lock icon in the address bar → Microphone → Allow, then reload.
On managed Chromebooks the mic may be blocked by policy; ask IT to allow microphone for mrarthurmusic.com.
Use headphones while recording so the speakers don’t leak into the take.
Plug the USB keyboard in **before** opening the page (Chrome and Edge support Web MIDI; iPad Safari does not, so iPads use the on-screen keys).
If the keyboard isn’t found, unplug and replug it, then reload the page.
No keyboard? Every keyboard tool also plays from the computer keys and the on-screen piano.
Most tools need no login. Staff Composer, Beat Machine and Studio DAW can also save to a student’s class account (class sign-in on the Music Lab home page).
Share links (Staff Composer, Beat Machine, Sound Blocks, Type Beat, Studio DAW) are the easiest way to collect work: students paste the link into Google Classroom or Seesaw.

head: Problem
Try this
rows: Tap the page, check the tab isn’t muted, check headphones are fully plugged in, reload.
Close other tabs, use wired headphones, plug the Chromebook in to power.
Most tools autosave on that device and that browser. Ask students to share a link at the end of every class.
Reload. Saved work comes back from autosave.

resources.title: Classroom routines for device music
resources.summary: Procedures that keep a room of 25 headphones, keyboards and loops calm and productive.

head: Signal
Meaning
rows: Screens tilted down halfway, headphones around the neck. Eyes on the teacher. Practice it until it takes under 5 seconds.
Teacher claps a 4-beat pattern; students echo it. Doubles as a rhythm warm-up.
A student needs help. Use “ask three, then me.”
Green: working. Red: stuck. The teacher scans the room instead of answering shouts.

body.h: Structure every tech lesson the same way

ol: **Unplugged warm-up** (3-5 min): sing, move, clap. Music first, screens second.
**Model on the board** (5 min): project the tool, show only what today needs.
**Guided try** (5 min): everyone does the same small task together.
**Create / practice** (15-20 min): the main task, with a visible timer.
**Share** (5 min): 2-3 volunteers play their work through the projector; peers give a “glow and grow.”
**Save + close** (2 min): share link submitted, headphones wrapped, devices charged.

body.p: Pairs work well with one device: a **Driver** (mouse/keys) and a **Navigator** (reads the task, keeps time, suggests). Switch roles at the halfway timer.

ul: Listen to the whole piece before commenting.
Start with a glow (“I liked how…”) before a grow (“Next time try…”).
Use music words from the word wall.

resources.title: Family letter (editable text)
resources.summary: A short note home explaining the Music Lab and how families can explore it.

body.p: This year our music class uses **Mr. Arthur’s Music Lab** (mrarthurmusic.com), a free set of music tools made for students. In class we compose with Staff Composer and Sound Blocks, practice note reading with Staff Wars and Rhythm Rock Stars, explore instruments in the Instrument Zoo, and produce songs in the Studio DAW.

You can explore it at home on any computer or tablet with a web browser; no download or account is needed. Ask your child to show you something they made, or to play a round of Staff Wars against you!

Student privacy: most tools save only on your own device. Songs saved to a class account store only a first name and last initial. Voice recordings made in Sound Blocks stay on the device. See the NY Ed Law § 2-d notice at the bottom of the site for details.
Thank you for supporting music at home,

resources.title: Accessibility and differentiation guide
resources.summary: Ways to adapt any Music Lab lesson for IEP/504 plans, English learners and advanced students.

ul: Most tools have a **?** help button with one-sentence instructions you can read aloud.
Tempo controls on Beat Machine, Type Beat, Metronome, MIDI MUSIC and Studio DAW let students slow music down.
Sound Blocks is almost word-free: pictures and colors only. Great for emerging readers and English learners.
Every keyboard tool plays from the computer keys, so students who can’t use a mouse precisely can still play.

head: Need
Adaptation
rows: Partner Driver/Navigator roles; touchscreen or large mouse; fewer measures to fill.
Visual feedback tools (Tuner needle, Tap Tempo BPM number, Rhythm Rock Stars lanes); feel the beat with hand on a speaker or drum.
Browser zoom (Ctrl +), high-contrast mode, describe the screen aloud; ear-based tasks (Dynamic Ears, Do-Re-Mi) work well.
Short timers, one task card at a time, a fidget-friendly body percussion role.
Word wall with pictures, sentence frames (“I hear ___ because ___”), demonstrations before directions.
Low headphone volume, allow over-ear headphones, a quiet corner for recording.
Add a constraint (only 3 pitches, must use a crescendo), notate the work, teach a peer, try the next band’s lesson.

resources.title: Teacher-side Music Lab tools
resources.summary: Parts of the site made for teachers rather than students.

ul: **The Staff Room** ([/Hub/](/Hub/)): Mr. Arthur’s teacher planning area.
**Class accounts**: the class sign-in on the Music Lab home page lets students save Staff Composer, Beat Machine and Studio DAW work to their class; teachers see it in the teacher portal.
**MIDI MUSIC teacher links**: `?challenge=<id>`, `?song=<id>` and `?duet` open MIDI MUSIC straight to a challenge or song (the 🔗 on a challenge card copies its link). The lessons here use them.

**Tool Box printables**: Metronome and Tap Tempo print a tempo chart, the Do-Re-Mi Trainer prints a solfège chart, and Dynamic Ears prints a dynamics chart. Every Tool Box tool also has full-screen, “How to use” and copy-link buttons.
**Projector mode**: every tool works full-screen (F11 on a Chromebook/PC) for whole-class games.
